Flappy Bird  
Be careful what you wish for, especially if you want to invent something new. Recently, Dong Nguyen, the creator of the mobile game Flappy Bird, removed it from app stores. He said its success – it had been downloaded more than 50 million times and was making him about £30,000 a day from ads – had ruined his simple life. He wrote on Twitter: “I cannot take this anymore.”  
Regretting making Flappy Bird is not as serious as regretting making a gun, but Nguyen is just the latest in a long list of inventors who wish they had not created something that became a problem.  

2 The labradoodle  
The labradoodle is not a monster – it is very cute. But the problem is how crossbreed dogs have been bred and sold since the labradoodle’s inventor, Wally Conron, first made the breed in the 1980s. “I’ve done a lot of damage,” he told the Associated Press. “I’ve created a lot of problems. There are many unhealthy and abandoned dogs out there.” Conron created the labradoodle when he worked for the Royal Guide Dog Association of Australia. He wanted to help a blind woman whose husband was allergic to dog hair. He did not expect that the labradoodle – and other poodle mixes, many with health problems – would become so popular.  

3 The AK-47  
Six months before he died in December 2013, Mikhail Kalashnikov, the designer of the AK-47 rifle, wrote to the head of the Russian Orthodox Church: “My spiritual pain is unbearable. I keep asking myself: if my rifle killed people, does that mean that I, Mikhail Kalashnikov, 93 years old, the son of a farmer, Christian and Orthodox, am responsible for people’s deaths, even if they were enemies?”  

4 Electronic tagging  
The electronic tag was first thought of in the 1960s as a way to track former prisoners’ attendance at schools and workplaces, and to reward them for good behavior. Its inventors, Bob Gable and his brother Kirkland, were later shocked that the tag had become a tool for control and punishment. “It’s not pleasant,” Kirkland Gable told the Guardian in 2010, “but I’m not in control of the universe. I have to realize there are some things out of my control.”  

5 Pepper spray  
After police used pepper spray on peaceful protesters at a University of California campus in 2011, one of the scientists who helped develop it in the 1980s spoke against its use. “I have never seen such a wrong and improper use of chemical agents,” Kamran Loghman told The New York Times.  

6 The office cubicle  
In the late 1960s, a new type of office was created to give workers privacy and help them work better by giving them more space. Instead, it became a way for companies to put more employees into smaller spaces, making offices look the same and feel lifeless. Its inventor, Bob Propst, said in 1997, “the cubiclizing of people in modern companies is complete madness.”

Apple’s brand and logo are the most valuable in the world, worth almost $119 billion. This is more than the total value of all goods and services produced in Morocco, Ecuador, or Oman. Apple is already the biggest company in the world, with a stock market value of $591 billion. In the last year, Apple’s brand value grew by 21%, according to the Interbrand Best Global Brands annual report.

Apple is known everywhere for its simple logo: an apple with a bite taken out. In the 2014 report, technology companies like Apple became more valuable, while older brands like Coca-Cola, McDonald’s, and Gillette moved down the list.

Google’s brand value went up by 15% to $107 billion, making it second on the list. Coca-Cola is third, up 3% to $81.5 billion, followed by IBM at $72.2 billion and Microsoft at $45.5 billion.

Facebook had the biggest increase, with its brand value rising 86% to $14.3 billion. It is now in 29th place, ahead of well-known companies like Volkswagen, Kellogg’s, and Ford.

Jez Frampton, the head of Interbrand, said that brands like Apple have become stronger because of digital and mobile technology. New companies like Google, Amazon, and Facebook have changed what customers expect and made brand experiences better.

Apple was started by Steve Jobs in his garage in Los Altos in 1976. It only entered the top ten of the Interbrand study in 2011. The Apple logo was made by Rob Janoff in 1977. He added a bite to the apple so people would not confuse it with a cherry. Janoff said the logo is a symbol of desire, knowledge, hope, and even a little rebellion.

Graham Hayles, Interbrand’s chief marketing officer, said it makes sense that Apple’s brand is worth about one-fifth of the company’s total value. He said Apple earns a lot of money because its brand is very strong, and there is a close link between a strong brand and making profits.

Interbrand has done this study every year since 2000. They calculate brand value by looking at a company’s financial results, how loyal customers are to the brand, and how strong the brand is.

Some technology companies did not do well. Nokia, the Finnish phone company, fell 41 places to 98th, with a brand value of $4.1 billion, just ahead of Nintendo, which is now 100th after dropping 33 places. Hayles said this shows how important it is to keep innovating. If companies do not keep up, they lose value quickly.

For the first time, a Chinese company is in the top 100. Huawei, a mobile phone and broadband company, is 94th with a brand value of $4.3 billion. The US and Australian governments have partly banned Huawei because they worry its equipment could be used for spying.

Most of the top 100 brands are American. The highest non-US brands are Samsung from South Korea (6th), Toyota from Japan (8th), and Mercedes-Benz from Germany (10th). The top British brands are HSBC (33rd), Shell (65th), and Burberry (73rd).

Other fashion brands in the top 100 are Boss, Prada, and Ralph Lauren. Louis Vuitton is the highest fashion brand at 19th, worth $23 billion, just ahead of H&M, which is 21st with a value of $21 billion.

Nike is 22nd with a brand value of almost $20 billion, much higher than Adidas, which is 59th with $7 billion.

They are people who look for darkness, and their numbers are increasing. On Black Fell, above the beautiful Kielder Water reservoir in Northumberland, a group of people wait in a car park next to a strange, modern wooden building. This is Kielder Observatory, the center of Britain’s new astrotourism industry. The people waiting outside are lucky because many more wanted to come for a night of stargazing, but only a few can join each night.

Inside, near a woodburner and under soft lights, Gary Fildes, the founder and main astronomer of the observatory, talks to his team. Fildes used to be a bricklayer and has long hair. He and his team talk about the chance of seeing the northern lights, but Fildes thinks it is unlikely. Instead, they decide to use their strong telescopes to look at Jupiter and Venus, and later at stars like Capella and Betelgeuse. They will also watch for the International Space Station.

Fildes tells his team, “Remember, it’s about talking with people, entertaining them, and inspiring them.” He plays music by Pink Floyd, the Jam, and the Pogues. “By 9:30, the sky will look amazing,” Fildes says. “It’s going to be great.”

Fildes, who is 49, is a leader in the UK’s growing astrotourism industry. A big moment for Northumberland happened in 2013, when the whole national park with Hadrian’s Wall, Kielder Water, and Forest Park—about 1,500 square kilometers—became a Dark Sky Park, the only one in England. Dark Sky Parks are rare. In 2013, a Star Count showed that only 5% of people in the UK can see more than 31 stars on a good night.

The International Dark-Sky Association (IDA), based in Tucson, Arizona, gives this status only to places that work hard to stop light pollution. These places must also prove their night skies are very dark. In Northumberland Dark Sky Park, it is so dark that Venus can make a shadow on the ground.

Duncan Wise, who works for the Northumberland National Park Authority, helped lead the campaign for dark-sky status after a group found that Northumberland was one of the quietest places in Britain. “We usually look at the land up to the horizon,” Wise said. “But what about the sky above it?” Wise and others spent years preparing their application to the IDA. They collected lots of light measurements and worked with local councils, park groups, and community groups to make a lighting plan for new buildings in the area.

Their hard work paid off. Many of the 1.5 million people who visit Northumberland each year now know about its Dark Sky status. “We get a lot of people coming here to see the sky now,” says a man at a car-hire company in Newcastle. “They come in autumn and winter, when it’s darkest. It’s good for the bed and breakfasts because they get business all year now.” Local hotels now give guests night-vision torches and put out deckchairs at night. Hotels that learn about astronomy can get a badge showing they are “Dark Sky Friendly.”

Wise says Northumberland should do more to use its special dark skies and thinks the area needs a few more observatories so visitors can see what they came for. A new £14 million national landscape discovery center, which he calls the north’s answer to the Eden Project, will have an observatory when it opens in a few years.

Fildes has big plans. He wants to build Britain’s first “astrovillage,” which would have the largest public observatory in the world, a 100-seat auditorium, a 100-seat planetarium, a one-meter wide telescope, and special telescopes for radio and solar observation. The project would cost millions of pounds, include a hotel, and attract 100,000 people a year—four times more than the current observatory. Fildes does not say much about who is supporting him, but he believes the astrovillage will be real by 2018.

However, Northumberland has competition. Galloway Forest Park in Scotland also has Dark Sky Park status. Since Exmoor became Europe’s first International Dark Sky Reserve (one level below Dark Sky Park) in 2011, many local businesses there now offer stargazing trips and tours. The UK still has a long way to go to catch up with northern Chile, which has more than a dozen tourist observatories and some of the clearest skies in the world. Teide National Park in Tenerife is also becoming a popular place for astrotourism.

Why do people want to look at the night sky? The media has helped. TV presenters like Brian Cox have made more people interested in stargazing. “Brian Cox has made astronomy easy to understand,” says Wise. “Now, it’s not just for professors with old telescopes.” Technology has also helped. Apps like Stellarium can turn smartphones into small planetariums. In the end, Fildes thinks people are starting to enjoy what is above them. “If you had to build a new tourist attraction, what could be better than the universe?”

Benjamin Carle is 96.9% "made in France," including his underwear and socks. He could not reach 100% because he owned six Ikea forks, a Chinese guitar, and some wall paint with no known origin. 

In 2013, Carle, who was 26 years old, tried to live for ten months using only products made in France. He did this for a TV documentary. The idea came from Arnaud Montebourg, the Minister for Economic Renewal, who asked people to buy French products to help the country’s factories.

Carle’s experiment meant he had to give up his smartphone, TV, and refrigerator (all made in China), his glasses (made in Italy), his underwear (from Morocco), his morning coffee (from Guatemala), and his favorite David Bowie music (from Britain). Luckily, his French girlfriend, Anaïs, and his French cat, Loon, stayed with him.

Carle said, “Politicians say many things and expect us to follow. I wanted to see if it was really possible to do what the minister asked.” He spoke to the Guardian in a Paris café after finishing his documentary, drinking non-French coffee.

He made three rules: eat only food produced in France, avoid all foreign-made goods, and live on €1,800 a month (which is more than the minimum wage of €1,430, because living in Paris is expensive).

At the start, Carle was surprised to find that only 4.5% of the things in his apartment were made in France. He had to get rid of almost everything, including lightbulbs (from China) and green beans (from Kenya). After the movers left, his home was almost empty.

He had no refrigerator (none are made in France) or nail clippers, so he kept food cold on the window ledge and cut his toenails with a penknife. He replaced all his foreign clothes, even his underwear, with French-made ones, which were much more expensive: underpants (€26), socks (€9), polo shirt (€75), espadrille sandals (€26). He could not buy jeans because none are made in France.

During the experiment, Carle searched supermarkets for 100% French products, learned to cook with French fruits and vegetables, and brushed his teeth with the last French-made toothbrush from a small company in Picardie. He washed his underwear by hand until he found the last French-made washing machine, which was top-opening and did not fit under his kitchen counter.

Going out with friends was hard—he could not watch American films, drink Belgian beer, or eat sushi or pizza. At home, he had no sofa for months and no TV, so he listened to French singer Michel Sardou and read French books. He could drink French wine and listen to French-Canadian singer Céline Dion, but not French bands like Daft Punk because they sing in English.

He could not use his British-made bicycle or a French car, because most affordable Peugeot, Renault, and Citroën cars are made outside France. So, he bought an old orange Mobylette moped that gave off smoke.

The last things he replaced were his computer, which he swapped for a Qooq (a French recipe tablet that connects slowly to the internet), and his iPhone, which he changed for an old Sagem mobile phone. In the documentary, Carle, realizing he was addicted to his iPhone, smashed it with a new French Tefal saucepan. His girlfriend shouted, “Are you crazy? Those are new pans!”

Carle told viewers his goal was to “save the French economy. After all, I like Mission Impossible.” He said the experiment was both serious and a joke. He even asked a French language expert if he should use words like “cool” (an English word). The expert told him to use the French word “chouette” instead.

Carle found out that France does not make refrigerators (except wine coolers) or TVs, but does make airplane seats and windmills. He joked, “Great. Nothing that will fit into my apartment.”

At the end, Carle took out a bank loan to buy new furniture and clothes. An auditor said he was 96.9% “made in France,” and Montebourg gave him a medal.

Carle’s conclusion: “It’s not really possible or even a good idea to live 100% made in France, especially with new technology. But that was not the main point. This was not about French nationalism or patriotism. It was to make people think about how we buy things and to make different choices. This is true in every country. If we want to save jobs and industries, we should think about supporting them.

“A T-shirt is more expensive in France, but I know the workers are paid well and have good working conditions. I cannot be sure about a cheaper T-shirt from Asia or Morocco.”

He also said, “It is not fair to blame business people for a country’s economic problems when people could do more as buyers.”

Carle says he wants to keep supporting French industry and producers, but not 100%. “It is a full-time job just to find these things,” he said.

The first thing he did after the experiment was invite his friends over to eat cheese and listen to the David Bowie album “Aladdin Sane.” He said, “It was hard not being able to invite people because there was nowhere to sit ... but I’d choose the Bowie over a sofa any day.”

Virunga National Park in DR Congo is home to rare mountain gorillas. A British company wants to look for oil there, but a WWF report says the park could earn DR Congo $400 million each year from tourism, hydropower, and carbon credits instead. The park is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and is on the equator.

If oil is found and used in the park, as the Congolese government and SOCO International hope, it could cause serious pollution and more conflict in an already unstable area, says WWF. SOCO International is the only company trying to explore for oil inside Virunga. SOCO says their work will only be in a part of the park called Block V and will not harm the gorillas.

SOCO’s chairman, Rui de Sousa, said that SOCO understands how important Virunga is for the environment. He said oil companies are still important for the world’s energy and a successful oil project could help the country’s economy and people. He also said the park has been getting worse for years and that development could help improve it.

However, Raymond Lumbuenamo, the WWF director in DR Congo, said that security in and around the park would get worse if SOCO starts exploring for oil. He said, “The security situation is already bad. The UN is fighting there and the M23 rebel group is inside the park. Oil would make things worse. It always brings more conflict and could lead to sabotage. The park could become like the Niger Delta. Oil will not help.”

He also said the area is already crowded, with over 350 people per square kilometre. If land is used for oil, there will be more pressure on the rest of the land. Oil would not create many jobs, but many people would come looking for work. Another worry is that the area has volcanoes, and an eruption could damage oil equipment and cause oil spills in the lakes. Lumbuenamo said, “Virunga’s natural resources should help the Congolese people, not foreign oil companies. Our country’s future depends on sustainable development. Choosing conservation is the best option. Once you start drilling for oil, you cannot go back.”

Lumbuenamo also said that, even though the gorillas are safe now, it is unlikely the park will make $400 million a year soon. “It would be hard to make that much money. Virunga used to be peaceful and can be again, but right now the security is bad. The UN is fighting there. It is not as quiet as before.”

The WWF report says the park’s ecosystems could support hydropower, fishing, and ecotourism. The park also helps provide clean water, control the climate, and stop soil erosion. Virunga is Africa’s oldest and most diverse park, with over 3,000 kinds of animals. Many poor people now live there, including people who fled after the Rwanda massacre in 1994.

The report says the park could support about 45,000 permanent jobs. People around the world also value knowing the park is safe and well managed for the future. The report says Virunga is a valuable asset for DR Congo and Africa, but oil exploration puts this value at risk.

Lasse Gustavsson, head of WWF International, said, “Oil companies are close to one of the world’s most precious and fragile places, but we will not stop until Virunga is safe from this possible disaster. Virunga has snow and lava fields, but it should not have oil fields.”

The UNESCO World Heritage Committee asked for all oil permits in Virunga to be cancelled and asked companies Total SA and SOCO International not to explore for oil in World Heritage Sites. Total has agreed not to explore inside Virunga, so SOCO is the only company with plans to look for oil in the park.

Two mothers in South Africa found out they are raising each other’s daughters because the babies were accidentally switched at birth in a hospital in 2010. One mother wants to fix the mistake and get her real daughter back, but the other mother does not want to give up the girl she has raised. This has created a big legal problem.

Henk Strydom, a lawyer for one of the mothers, said the swap was a terrible mistake and a sad situation that probably will not end happily. Both mothers gave birth at Tambo Memorial Hospital in Boksburg, near Johannesburg, on the same day in 2010. At first, nobody knew anything was wrong.

In 2013, one mother, who is 33 years old and does not have a job, asked her ex-partner for money to help raise her daughter. The man said he was not the father. A DNA test showed that he was not the father and that the girl was not her biological daughter either. The mother was very upset and did not know what to do.

Later, she met the other mother. Since December 2013, both mothers have been going to counselling sessions together, arranged by the hospital. They have also met their real daughters. Strydom said his client noticed that her real daughter looks like her. He said it has been very hard for her because she is raising a child who is not hers, while someone else is raising her real daughter.

The woman became unhappy with the situation and went to the children’s court to try to get her biological daughter back, but the other mother refused. Strydom agreed to help her for free. He said, “It’s a tragedy. She wants her baby back, but the other mother does not want to give up the child. It has been four years, so you can understand why.”

The High Court in Pretoria has asked the University of Pretoria’s Centre for Child Law to find out what is best for the children, which is the most important rule in South African law. The Centre must report back in 90 days.

Strydom said, “No one knows what the court will decide. It is a terrible situation. How can you fix it after four years? The longer it takes, the harder it will be. No matter what happens, someone will be unhappy.”

He also said that, for now, he and his client do not want to sue the hospital or the government health department, which is helping with the case and giving counselling.

The Centre for Child Law will talk to the mothers, fathers, and anyone else who is important in the girls’ lives. The children and mothers will have full medical and psychological checks and may see a psychologist.

Karabo Ngidi, a lawyer at the Centre, said, “What happens must be best for the children. Biology is important, but it is not the only thing.” The families are Zulu, so Zulu tradition, culture, and law will also be considered. It is also possible that the ex-partner of the mother who went to court could be the real father of the other girl.

This is not the first time a baby swap has happened in South Africa. In 1995, two mothers got money after their sons, born in 1989, were switched at a hospital in Johannesburg. In 2009, in Oregon, USA, Dee Ann Angell and Kay Rene Reed found out they were switched at birth in 1953 when a nurse brought them back from a bath. In 2013, in Japan, a 60-year-old man who was switched at birth and grew up poor got money after learning his real family was rich. He became a truck driver, while his real brothers and the boy raised in his place went to private schools and universities.

Bruce Laing, a psychologist in Johannesburg, said that being switched at birth can have very serious and painful effects for a long time. He told The Times of South Africa that parents might feel angry or sad towards a child who is not really theirs and might always wonder, “What if?”

The final season of Downton Abbey begins with a sad feeling and a sense that times are changing. It is 1925, and early signs of economic problems are starting to appear. The neighbors are selling their large house, and Lord Grantham wants to reduce the number of servants because he says under-butlers are too expensive.

However, at the real Downton Abbey, called Highclere Castle and owned by George “Geordie” Herbert, the 8th Earl of Carnarvon, the financial situation is much better. Lady Fiona Carnarvon says that the worldwide success of Downton Abbey has paid for ongoing repairs to the building, helping to protect Highclere for future generations.

She said, “It’s been an amazing experience for all of us. It has given us a great way to promote the house and made it famous around the world. I am very thankful. My husband and I love the house and the people here. Now, millions of other people love it too.”

Right now, only the ground and first floors of Highclere, which is on the border of Hampshire, are used. But they have started fixing up the old tower rooms. Soon, visitors will be able to climb the tower and see an exhibition about Sir Charles Barry, the architect who rebuilt the house between 1839 and 1842 and also designed the Houses of Parliament.

When the Downton Abbey producers first contacted Highclere in 2009, the family needed almost £12 million for repairs, with £1.8 million needed urgently. But by 2012, the popularity of Downton Abbey was helping with these costs. Lord Carnarvon said, “It was just after the banking crisis and things were difficult. We had been hosting business events, but those became rare. Then Downton Abbey started, and the house became a major tourist attraction.”

The number of visitors doubled to 1,200 a day as Downton Abbey, written by Julian Fellowes, became popular in the UK in 2010 and then in the US. Now, it is shown in 250 countries. The ticketing system, which used to be simple, is now computerized and allows people to book in advance, making it easier for foreign visitors to get tickets. Highclere Enterprises’ accounts for 2014-15 show that their assets have almost tripled to about £1 million since 2012. Gareth Neame, the executive producer, said, “I think Downton Abbey saved Highclere’s future.”

Peter Fincham, ITV’s director of television, remembers when Highclere was chosen for the show. “I thought, ‘So what?’ because I had never heard of Highclere Castle. I thought all big houses looked the same. I was wrong. The castle became a very important character in the show.”

The tourists who come because of Downton Abbey are part of a bigger trend. VisitBritain says that almost 30% of foreign visitors, or about nine million people, visit castles and historic houses. Almost half of people who might visit Britain now say they want to do “set jetting,” which means visiting places seen in movies or on TV. More than a million people tour historic buildings each year, spending over £1 billion. From the biggest new tourist markets, 51% of Brazilians, 42% of Russians and Chinese, and 35% of Indian visitors are likely to visit a famous site during their trip. Patricia Yates, VisitBritain’s director, said, “Tourism, films, and TV are strongly connected.” She also said that period dramas have made areas outside London more popular.

Neame is now an ambassador for the GREAT Britain campaign, which is supported by the government and the British Council to promote the UK worldwide. There are special Downton-themed events at British embassies.

Neame said, “They asked me because of the show’s reach. Many people here think it is just entertainment, but in other countries, people respect our actors, writers, and production teams. I am very passionate about this. I believe in soft power. We should be prouder of our achievements.”

“Downton Abbey is famous for showing British culture. Really, it is a fantasy world set in a certain time in history. It is the first TV period drama that has become a big part of popular culture.”

Lady Carnarvon still wants people to know that Highclere’s future is not completely safe. “The profit is still small,” she said. “The show has let us spend more quickly on repairs and restore the garden buildings.”

They are planning a Tutankhamun centenary event in 2022, 100 years after the 5th Earl of Carnarvon and Howard Carter discovered the tomb that changed our knowledge of ancient Egypt. Another event will celebrate the 300th birthday of Lancelot “Capability” Brown, who designed the gardens.

Lady Carnarvon said, “You should never relax and think everything is fine. Every day, you must not take things for granted. For all these big houses, you have to invest in them. There has been a shortage of money since the 1930s. In the past, the estate and house supported the family, but now it is the other way around: my husband and I have to find ways to support and care for Highclere.”

“From my point of view, I try to show people that visiting is fun and offer special events, not just a walk around an old house. We have to compete with attractions like the London Dungeon.”

Health warnings that cover almost two-thirds of cigarette packs and a ban on menthol cigarettes across the EU are closer to happening after a vote in the European Parliament. Menthol and other flavored cigarettes will be banned from 2022. However, Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) decided that most electronic cigarettes, which are becoming more popular as alternatives to tobacco, do not need to be regulated like medicines. This is a setback for the UK government.

Health officials and the e-cigarette industry in Britain are trying to understand what this means. For example, they want to know if companies in the fast-growing e-cigarette market will face the same bans on sponsorship and advertising at sports events as tobacco companies.

The Department of Health did not comment on the advertising issue until officials have studied the MEPs’ decisions. But in a statement, the Department of Health said: “We are very pleased to see stronger action on tobacco, with Europe-wide rules banning flavored cigarettes and stricter rules on health warnings on the front of packs. However, we are disappointed that the proposal to regulate nicotine-containing products (NCPs), including e-cigarettes, as medicines was rejected. We believe these products should be regulated as medicines and will continue to argue this in future talks.

“Figures show that smoking levels in England are at their lowest since records began – 19.5 percent – but we want to reduce smoking even more and believe this important step will help.”

The UK e-cigarette industry, which mostly welcomed the parliament’s vote, said it is already talking with the Advertising Standards Authority. However, it added that banning all advertising would not be “sensible, fair, reasonable, or useful.”

MEPs decided that e-cigarettes should only be regulated as medical products if manufacturers claim they can help people stop smoking tobacco. The government’s main medicines regulator criticized this decision.

The regulator wants to put e-cigarettes, used by about 1.3 million people in Britain by 2014, under the same rules as gums, patches, and mouth sprays that help smokers quit. But the e-cigarette industry says the expensive process of getting a license would make it hard for tobacco alternatives to stay on the market.

MEPs voted to put health warnings on 65% of each cigarette pack, instead of the proposed 75%. Right now, warnings cover at least 30% on the front and 40% on the back. The UK government has delayed a decision on whether to follow Australia by introducing plain packaging until there is proof that such measures reduce tobacco use.

The MEPs’ votes in the first reading of the draft tobacco law, which could become law in 2014, will be followed by talks with the EU Council of Ministers.

The Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Authority had already asked manufacturers to choose voluntary regulation in June 2013, before what it still hopes will become compulsory across Europe. “The law-making process is not finished and there will be more talks. The UK still believes that regulating NCPs as medicines is the best way to help public health,” said a spokesman.

Linda McAvan, Labour MEP for Yorkshire and the Humber and spokesperson on tobacco issues for the parliament’s Socialists & Democrats group, said: “We know that it is children, not adults, who start smoking. And, even though the number of adult smokers is going down in most member states, World Health Organization figures show worrying increases in young smokers in some countries.

“We need to stop tobacco companies from targeting young people with many new products, and we need to make sure that cigarette packs have strong warnings.”

Martin Callanan, the Conservative MEP for North East England, said: “Forcing e-cigarettes off the shelves would have been completely wrong. These products have helped many people stop smoking more harmful cigarettes, but some MEPs wanted to make them harder to make than ordinary tobacco.”

Katherine Devlin, president of ECITA, the e-cigarette industry association, said the important decision by MEPs not to support medicines regulation means that idea is now finished.

British American Tobacco said the larger health warnings demanded by MEPs go “well beyond” what is needed to inform consumers about health risks from smoking, and that a ban on menthol cigarettes would increase demand for illegal products.

It is difficult to know exactly where the noise is coming from, but you can hear it everywhere in Damascus. All day and night, there are dull thuds and loud booms from artillery, rockets, or planes attacking rebel positions. The sounds of war are getting closer to Syria’s capital. After more than two years of the Syrian crisis—the longest and deadliest of the Arab uprisings—people in Damascus have become used to the sounds of death and destruction nearby.

Over the weekend, men smoked water pipes in a park with palm trees, children played among the flowers, and couples talked on benches. At the same time, the loud explosions of bombs could be heard just a few miles away, with smoke rising near an old Ottoman mosque. No one seemed to pay attention.

“Actually, you do get used to it after a while,” said George, an IT technician from a village on the coast. “But you never know exactly what they are hitting.” Usually, people find out later from video clips posted by opposition media on YouTube.

The constant noise is even more disturbing because the government tries hard to act like everything is normal. “As you can see, everything here is fine but we have to hit the terrorists, these extremists,” an army officer said. An official, whose way home has been attacked by rebels in Daraya, said, “If I was afraid, I would just stay inside. I have to work and I am not afraid. If I don’t defend my country, who will?”

Ordinary people, when speaking privately, are less confident. In the city center, a shopkeeper sadly said that his baby daughter cries when she hears the shelling. Zeina, a student in her twenties, is afraid she is getting used to suffering and maybe to danger as well. “At first, when the explosions started, I used to have nightmares,” she said. “Now I can sleep through anything.”

The risks are getting closer to home. In Sabaa Bahrat Square, which was supposed to be the safest part of Damascus, a car bomb exploded. It left a blackened building, broken windows, twisted metal, and damage to the Syrian Central Bank next door. Notices for two of the 15 victims—Muhammad al-Sufi and Manal al-Tahan—are stuck to the wall opposite. Armed militiamen walk around the square, which is often used for pro-government rallies with civil servants brought in to chant slogans under large banners of President Bashar al-Assad.

That bombing was not the worst Damascus has seen as things have gotten worse. In February, 80 people, including schoolchildren, reportedly died near the Ba’ath Party headquarters in Mazraa. The crater is still there, covered by a large patch of new asphalt on the main road north. “I live nearby but luckily I wasn’t there,” said Munir, a university lecturer.

Mortar bombs, fired from rebel-held areas now close to the city, are a new and frightening danger. On March 28, these bombs killed 15 students in a university cafeteria. The real target was probably a government building.

Security has become much tighter since the big bombing of the national security crisis cell in July 2012, when four of Assad’s top aides were killed. Concrete barriers, often painted with the Syrian flag’s colors, now protect official buildings, not just military sites. The Iranian Embassy in Mezze, with its blue mosaic front, now looks like a fortress. “The regime did manage to set up a ring of steel around Damascus,” a foreign diplomat said. “But now the perimeter is starting to be broken, and that shows the reality of the war.”

Because of all this, moving around the city has become difficult, unpredictable, and slow—another part of the new normal in this nervous city. Checkpoints on main roads stop traffic for ID checks and baggage searches with handheld bomb detectors, which are important to stop future bombings. Only drivers with special security clearance can use fast lanes to avoid waiting.

Still, everyone is thinking about the same question: will there be a battle for Damascus—the world’s oldest continually inhabited city, as the guidebooks say—like the one that has badly damaged Aleppo? Some parts of the city already feel like a war zone. The city’s fanciest hotel is almost empty, though many rooms are used as offices by international agencies because of the crisis. Blue helmets and bulletproof vests are piled up on Persian carpets in the fancy reception room, and white UN vehicles are parked behind blast barriers outside. The streets become empty soon after 9pm.

Some people think the fight for Syria’s capital is coming, but not yet—maybe in the summer, when the rebels are stronger in the south. Others believe that neither side will win completely and hope for a political solution from other countries. But few people here expect things to get better.

Passing clouds  
One enjoyable part of flying is seeing clouds up close. Even though clouds look light, they actually hold a lot of water—about 500 tonnes in a small cumulus cloud. Water is heavier than air. So why don’t clouds fall from the sky like rain? They do, but the water droplets fall very slowly. A normal cloud would take a year to fall just one metre.

On cloud nine  
Most people call clouds “fluffy” or “dark,” but weather experts, called meteorologists, have more than 50 types of clouds based on their shape and height. These types are put into groups numbered one to nine. Cloud nine is the huge, tall cumulonimbus cloud. So, when someone says they are “on cloud nine,” it means they feel very happy, like being on top of the world.

Around the rainbow  
The best place to see a rainbow is from a plane. Rainbows happen when sunlight hits raindrops. On the ground, we see a half-circle because the Earth blocks the rest, but from a plane, you can see a full circle rainbow. When flying over clouds, the plane’s shadow appears right in the middle of the rainbow.

Mr blue sky  
Sunlight is white and has all the colours. When sunlight goes through the air, some of it bounces off gas molecules. Blue light bounces more than other colours, so the sky looks blue to us.

There’s life out there  
Besides clouds and other planes, we don’t expect to see much outside a plane window. But the air is full of bacteria—up to 1,800 different types have been found over cities, and they can go twice as high as a plane usually flies.

Turbulence terror  
Even experienced flyers can feel sick during turbulence. Turbulence can cause shaking or sudden drops. The good news is that no modern passenger plane has ever crashed because of turbulence. People can get hurt or even killed if they are not wearing seatbelts or if loose luggage hits them, but the plane itself is safe.

In-flight radiation  
When airport body scanners were introduced, some people worried about radiation. But the amount of radiation from a scanner is the same as what you get in one minute of flying. The Earth is always hit by cosmic rays, which are natural radiation from space, and these are stronger at higher altitudes.

You can’t cure jet lag  
The world has different time zones. When you travel far, your body’s time is different from the local time, causing jet lag. You can’t stop jet lag, but you can make it less severe by eating plain food for 24 hours before flying, drinking lots of water, and changing to your destination’s time as soon as you get on the plane.

Supersonic 747s  
Many people have flown faster than the speed of sound. There are fast-moving air currents called jet streams high in the sky, especially between the US and Europe, where air can move up to 250 mph. If a plane flying at 550 mph enters a jet stream, it can reach 800 mph, which is faster than sound (740 mph).

Flying through time  
Time zones make it feel like you are traveling through time, but according to special relativity, flying actually makes you move a tiny bit into the future. However, it is so small that flying across the Atlantic every week for 40 years would only move you 1/1,000th of a second ahead.

Terrible tea  
If your tea tastes bad on a plane, it’s not the flight attendant’s fault. Water should be almost 100°C to make good tea, but on a plane, water can only get to 90°C. So, it’s better to choose coffee.

I can’t hear my food  
Airplane food often tastes bland. This may not be because of bad cooking. Planes are noisy, and studies show that loud noise can make food taste less flavorful.

Needle in a haystack  
It may seem strange that a plane like Malaysian flight MH370 could disappear, but finding a missing plane is very hard. The plane knows its location using GPS and other systems, but this information is not sent out in real time. Ships have had tracking since the 1980s, so the problem is not technology, but that there is no law requiring planes to send their location all the time.

Volcanic fallout  
Flights can be stopped by volcanic eruptions. Ash from volcanoes melts in the hot engines and then hardens on the engine parts. It is safer to avoid flying through ash clouds, even if it causes delays, because flying through ash is very dangerous.

The wing myth  
For a long time, people explained wrongly how wings keep planes in the air. Most of a plane’s lift comes from Newton’s Third Law of Motion. The wing is shaped to push air down. As the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up, lifting the plane.

Forget electric planes  
Some small, light electric planes exist, but large electric passenger planes will not happen soon. Airplane fuel has a lot of energy, but batteries are much less powerful. To get the same energy as one tonne of fuel, you would need 100 tonnes of batteries. A 747 uses 150 to 200 tonnes of fuel. Unless batteries become much better, electric airliners will not be possible.

Beware the vortex  
Pilots often wait before taking off. This is because the wingtips of planes create spinning air called vortices, which can last two or three minutes. If another plane takes off too soon, the swirling air can make it hard to control. Waiting gives the air time to settle.

The doors aren’t locked  
Airplane doors do not need to be locked. To open a plane door, you first pull it inwards, then move it out of the way. After take-off, the pressure inside the plane is much higher than outside, which pushes the door tightly shut. It is impossible for a person to open the door during flight because the air pressure is too strong.

In October 2012, the Taliban sent a gunman to shoot Malala Yousafzai while she was riding home on a bus after school. Their goal was to stop her from speaking out and fighting for girls’ education. 

Nine months later, after many surgeries, Malala stood up at the United Nations on her 16th birthday to give a strong answer. She said, “They thought that the bullet would silence us. But they failed.”

Malala’s 16th birthday was very different from most. Instead of having a birthday cake, she sat in a main council room at the United Nations, in a seat usually for world leaders. She listened as Ban Ki-moon, the UN secretary-general, called her “our hero, our champion.” Gordon Brown, the former British prime minister and now a UN education envoy, said, “the words the Taliban never wanted her to hear: happy 16th birthday, Malala.”

The event, called Malala Day, was the result of four amazing years for Malala, a girl from Mingora in the troubled Swat valley of Pakistan. She became known after she wrote a blog for the BBC Urdu service about her struggles to get an education while the Taliban was gaining power.

By age 11, Malala was already very determined. She spoke directly to Richard Holbrooke, the US special representative to Pakistan, asking him to help fight the Taliban’s actions against girls’ education. At 14, Archbishop Desmond Tutu nominated her for the International Children’s Peace Prize. At 15, she became the youngest person ever nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

But this worldwide attention was dangerous. As more people learned about her, she received death threats. On October 9, 2012, after a meeting of Taliban leaders, a gunman was sent to kill her because they called her a “symbol of infidels and obscenity.”

After the attack, Malala had many surgeries in Pakistan and the UK. Doctors put a titanium plate in her forehead and gave her a cochlear implant to help her hear again. Now, she lives with her family in Birmingham, England, and goes to school every day, which is what the Taliban tried to stop.

In the UN chamber, Malala said, “I am not against anyone. I am not here to speak for personal revenge against the Taliban or any other terrorist group.” She answered the Taliban’s violence with words, not hate. “I do not even hate the Talib who shot me. Even if there is a gun in my hand and he stands in front of me, I would not shoot him.”

Malala spoke with confidence, though her face still showed signs of her injuries. She wore a white shawl that belonged to Benazir Bhutto, the former prime minister of Pakistan, who was also attacked by extremists but did not survive.

Malala said, “The extremists are afraid of books and pens. The power of education frightens them. They are afraid of women.

Researchers were very surprised, not by how hard people found the challenge, but by how much they tried to avoid it. The challenge was simple: sit in a chair and do nothing except think. Some people found this so boring that they chose to give themselves small electric shocks just to break the boredom.

During a 15-minute period alone, two-thirds of men pressed a button to give themselves a painful shock. A quarter of women did the same. Scientists think this is because men usually like new and exciting experiences more than women.

Psychologists from Virginia and Harvard Universities wrote a report about this. There are not many studies that ask why most people find it so difficult to do nothing. In more than 11 different studies, the researchers found that people did not like being left alone with their thoughts, no matter their age, education, income, or how much they used smartphones or social media.

Timothy Wilson, the leader of the study, said these results do not just show that modern life is fast or that mobile devices and social media are everywhere. Instead, he thinks these things are popular because people always want to do something, not nothing.

In the first experiments, students were taken alone into a plain room with no phones, books, or anything to write with. They were told to sit and think for six to 15 minutes. They had to stay seated and not fall asleep. After the time was up, the students said they did not enjoy the experience. They found it hard to focus, and their minds wandered even though there was nothing to distract them. Even when they were given time to plan what to think about, it did not help.

To see if the strange room made it harder to think, the researchers tried the experiment again with people at home. The results were similar, but people felt even worse and often cheated by getting up or checking their phones.

To check if this only happened with students, the scientists also tested more than 100 people aged 18 to 77 from a church and a farmers’ market. These people also did not like being left alone with their thoughts.

But the most surprising result came next. The researchers wanted to see if people would choose something bad over nothing at all. The students could choose to give themselves a mild electric shock. Earlier, they had rated how unpleasant the shocks were, compared to things like looking at pictures of cockroaches or hearing a knife scrape a bottle. All the students said they would pay money to avoid the shock after trying it once.

But to the researchers’ surprise, 12 out of 18 men and 6 out of 24 women gave themselves up to four shocks during the experiment.

The scientists wrote in the journal Science that it was amazing how just being alone with their thoughts made many people give themselves a shock they had said they would pay to avoid.

Jessica Andrews-Hanna from the University of Colorado said many students might shock themselves to make a boring lecture more interesting. But she said we need to know more about why people chose to shock themselves in Wilson’s study.

She said, “Imagine the situation – a person is told to sit in a chair with wires on their skin and a button that gives a harmless but uncomfortable shock. They are told to just sit and think. As they sit there, their mind starts to wander and they think about the shock – was it really that bad? What do the experimenters really want to know? Maybe this is a case where curiosity caused people to do something they normally would not do.”

Organic food has more antioxidant compounds, which are linked to better health, than regular food. It also has lower levels of toxic metals and pesticides. This is according to the most complete scientific study so far. The international team of scientists suggests that eating organic fruits and vegetables could give the same health benefits as eating one or two extra portions of the recommended five fruits and vegetables a day.

The team, led by Professor Carlo Leifert from Newcastle University, found “statistically significant, meaningful” differences. Organic food had between 19% and 69% more antioxidants than regular food. This is the first study to show clear and wide differences between organic and regular fruits, vegetables, and cereals.

The researchers say the higher antioxidants in organic food are equal to eating one or two more portions of fruits and vegetables each day. This could be important for human nutrition, if future studies confirm that these compounds really give health benefits.

These findings add to the debate about whether organic food is better for people. Some experts think the results are exaggerated. Tom Sanders, a nutrition professor at King’s College London, said the research did show some differences, but he is not sure if they are important. He also said that Leifert’s work has caused arguments before. Sanders added that organic cereals have less protein than regular cereals.

The results are based on an analysis of 343 peer-reviewed studies from around the world, which is more than ever before. These studies looked at the differences between organic and regular fruits, vegetables, and cereals. Helen Browning, head of the Soil Association, which supports organic farming, said, “This research proves that the way we farm affects the quality of our food.”

Plants make many antioxidant compounds to protect themselves from pests. Organic crops may have more antioxidants because they are not protected by chemical sprays. Other reasons could be that organic plants are bred to be tougher and are not given too much artificial fertilizer.

Leifert and his team say that many antioxidants are linked to a lower risk of long-term diseases, such as heart disease, brain diseases, and some cancers. However, they also say that there are no long-term studies yet that show health benefits from eating a lot of organic food. The researchers found much higher levels of cadmium, a toxic metal, in regular crops. Pesticide residues were found four times more often on regular crops than on organic food. The research was paid for by the European Union and an organic farming charity.

Some people will criticize the research. Including so many studies could mean that poor-quality studies affect the results, but the team checked this and found that removing weaker studies did not change the results much. Also, the higher levels of cadmium and pesticides in regular food were still below legal safety limits. But the researchers say cadmium builds up in the body over time, and some people may want to avoid it. They also say that safety limits are set for each chemical alone, not for the mix of chemicals used on crops.

Another criticism is that the differences found may be due to different climates, soil types, or crop varieties, not just organic farming. The researchers say that using many studies should balance out these differences. The biggest criticism is about the possible health benefits. A major study in 2012, which looked at 223 studies, found little evidence that organic food is more nutritious. Earlier, smaller studies in 2009 and by the UK Food Standards Agency also found little difference, though the 2012 study did say that organic food might help people avoid pesticides. Sanders said he is not convinced by the new research. He said, “You will not be better nourished if you eat organic food. What matters most is eating fruits and vegetables, not whether they are organic or regular. People buy organic food for a lifestyle. They want to know it is not grown with chemicals or by big companies.”

Surveys show that the main reasons people buy organic food are for healthy eating (55%) and to avoid chemicals (53%). Many people also care about the environment (44%), animal welfare (31%), and taste (35%). Browning said, “This research supports what people think about organic food. In other countries, there is more support for organic food and farming. We hope these findings will help the UK catch up with the rest of Europe.”

Emmanuel Limal, a 43-year-old actor from France, was tired of meeting women who did not want to start a family or did not say so. He lived in Copenhagen for 20 years, hoping to find love and have children. Recently, he tried online dating but was disappointed. 

“I got frustrated because everyone talked about being active, traveling, or having many hobbies, but no one mentioned wanting children,” Limal said. “Some dating sites let you click ‘I’d like kids someday,’ but when you read their profiles, you think: ‘You will never have time!’ If someone goes to the gym eight times a week and travels every month, they are not focused on having a family.”

Limal already has a six-year-old daughter from a past relationship. He comes from a big family—his father has 11 siblings—so he always wanted more children. “I couldn’t find anyone who wanted to make starting a family a priority. I also didn’t know when to talk about wanting kids when I met someone new. It’s a difficult topic in dating,” he said. “One day, I read a profile from a 38-year-old woman who said she knew it was ‘really bad to admit’ but she wanted children. I thought: ‘You shouldn’t be ashamed of this.’”

Limal decided to remortgage his apartment to start Babyklar.nu, which means ‘baby-ready now’ in English. It works like a normal dating site, but everyone must be honest about wanting to start a family soon. “We ask people if they are okay with someone who already has children and also wants another baby,” Limal said. “But we don’t ask how many children they want. That would be too much like shopping online.”

The site became very popular. “When we launched in June, we had 50 people sign up every hour. We are already hearing from couples who met on the site and are now together. I think the first Babyklar.nu baby will be born by next summer.” More men than women have joined the site (53% men, 47% women). People have said things like, “It’s so nice to say this out loud,” and “I finally feel brave enough to be honest about what I want.”

The site comes at a good time for Denmark, a country with five million people. Danes are not having enough babies. A report from Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen says the average is 1.7 children per family, which is not enough to keep Denmark’s population stable. People blame women waiting too long to have children and couples living together but not starting families.

“Now, I hope men and women who want a family but haven’t met the right person have another choice,” Limal said. He also said this is not just about having babies: “I want this to be about children and love. My goal is to help people who really want a family and a partner—and who will stay together. I am a romantic.”

There are plans to start the site in France and the UK later in 2013, but for now, only Danes can use it. “In Denmark, people don’t mind having children before marriage, so things can move quickly. Also, Denmark is small, so someone from Jutland can date someone from Copenhagen without traveling too far,” Limal said. Limal has also found love himself. “I’ve met a nice woman and she wants a baby too—so we will see.”

A subway system is like the veins of a city, full of billions of bacteria. These bacteria come from things like Swiss cheese, kimchi, the bubonic plague, drug-resistant germs, and human skin. For the first time, scientists have started to list and map the bacteria found in a city’s subway, and they have discovered many interesting things.

Dr. Christopher Mason, a geneticist at Weill Cornell Medical College, led a team that spent 18 months collecting samples from the New York City subway. They took swabs from turnstiles, seats, ticket booths, and stations to find the tiny life forms living there. Mason called this “the first city-scale genetic profile ever.” His team found bacteria that cause meningitis at Times Square, a small trace of anthrax on a train handhold, and bacteria that cause bubonic plague on a trash bin and ticket machine in uptown Manhattan.

The research was published in the journal Cell Systems. The team said that the findings of plague and anthrax are not a big concern. The amount of anthrax was extremely small, and rats probably carried the plague bacteria. Also, no one has gotten sick with the plague in or near New York for many years.

“The results do not suggest that plague or anthrax is common,” the study says. “Nor do they suggest that New York residents are at risk.”

Most of the bacteria found are either harmless to humans or even helpful. Many of these bacteria help process toxic waste in the city, just like bacteria in the human body help with digestion and other functions.

Some results were expected. Mason said they found some bacteria linked to fecal matter, which should remind people to wash their hands. He also said that many helpful bacteria, like those used to make cheese, were found around New York.

Bacteria in the subway also showed the eating habits of different neighborhoods. Bacteria from cheeses like brie, cheddar, parmesan, and mozzarella (used in New York pizza) were found all over the subway. Swiss cheese bacteria were mostly found in midtown Manhattan and the financial district. Bacteria used to ferment cabbage for kimchi and sauerkraut were found in the financial district and Bay Ridge. The team also found cucumber DNA all over the city.

Bacteria that can cause illness and infections were very common. Species that cause diarrhea and nausea, both harmless and harmful types of E. coli (mostly harmless), and bacteria that can cause skin and urinary-tract infections were found all over the city. The bacteria that cause tetanus were found in Soho, and bacteria that cause dysentery were found at stations in the Bronx and Harlem.

Mason and his team collected more than 1,000 samples from all 466 open subway stations in New York. They used a DNA sequencer and a supercomputer with genetic databases to study the samples. They found 15,152 different species, almost half of which were bacteria.

The good news is that these “potentially infectious agents” are not causing sickness or disease in New York. Instead, they seem to be normal “co-habitants” and “may even be essential.” They “represent a normal, 'healthy' metagenome profile of a city.”

In short, the researchers say the subway and city are as safe as people thought.

Mason said people should not worry about getting urinary-tract infections from subway seats. “You should wash your hands,” he said, “and probably get some sleep, eat salads, and go to the gym. That’s the same advice as before.”

“If anything,” he added, “I feel even more confident riding the subway.”

Many findings made sense. Busy stations like Grand Central and Times Square had more bacteria and more types of bacteria. The subway had the most bacteria linked to human skin. The Bronx, with its many different neighborhoods and stations, had the most types of bacteria. Staten Island, with only three stops, had the least.

The researchers found marine bacteria at South Ferry, a station that flooded during Hurricane Sandy. They were surprised to find some species usually found in Antarctica and in fish.

Next, Mason said, they will study other cities, such as Paris, São Paulo, and Shanghai, and continue to study New York to see how the subway’s bacteria change with the seasons. He hopes this research will give health officials and scientists a starting point for future studies and help them prevent and track diseases.

Nelson Mandela, a key leader in Africa’s fight for freedom and a hero to millions, has died at the age of 95. He was South Africa’s first black president. Mandela died at home in Johannesburg, surrounded by his family, after being sick for many years. Because of his health, he had stopped appearing in public.

The current president, Jacob Zuma, told the country about Mandela’s death in a serious speech on TV. He said Mandela died peacefully around 8:50 pm local time. Zuma called this “the moment of our deepest sorrow” and said, “Our nation has lost its greatest son.” He praised Mandela’s humanity and said that Mandela brought South Africans together. Zuma also said Mandela would have a state funeral and ordered flags to fly at half-mast.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu led a memorial service in Cape Town. He asked South Africans to try to be like Mandela. World leaders also paid tribute. US President Barack Obama called Mandela by his clan name, Madiba, and said Mandela changed South Africa and inspired the world by giving up his own freedom for others. Obama said Mandela’s life showed that people and countries can change for the better, and that his example of forgiveness and sharing power is something everyone should follow.

UK Prime Minister David Cameron said, “A great light has gone out in the world,” and called Mandela “a hero of our time.” FW de Klerk, the former South African president who freed Mandela and shared the Nobel Peace Prize with him in 1993, said the news was very sad for South Africa and the world. De Klerk said Mandela was a great unifier and lived for reconciliation.

People gathered in the streets of South Africa to celebrate Mandela’s life. In Soweto, people sang and danced near his old house. They formed a circle in Vilakazi Street and sang songs from the anti-apartheid struggle. Some wore South African flags and the colors of Mandela’s party, the African National Congress (ANC). Mandela’s death brought deep sadness and reflection to South Africa, almost 20 years after he led the country from racial apartheid to democracy.

Mandela’s death is also felt around the world. Many people saw him as one of the last great leaders and compared him to Gandhi and Martin Luther King. Mandela’s act of forgiveness, after spending 27 years in prison—18 of them on Robben Island—made him famous in history. When South Africa was close to civil war, Mandela chose to forgive the white minority and build a new democracy.

He led the ANC to win the first multiracial election in 1994 and became president. He stepped down after one term.

Mandela was born Rolihlahla Dalibhunga in a small village in the Eastern Cape on July 18, 1918. A teacher gave him the English name Nelson. He joined the ANC in 1943 and helped start its youth league. In 1952, he opened South Africa’s first black law firm with Oliver Tambo.

Mandela was known for his charm and love of boxing. He once joked, “I can’t help it if the ladies take note of me. I am not going to protest.”

When the ANC was banned in 1960, Mandela went into hiding. After the Sharpeville massacre, where police killed 69 black protesters, Mandela decided to start an armed struggle. He was arrested and charged with sabotage and trying to overthrow the government.

At his trial in 1964, Mandela defended himself and said he wanted a free and equal society. He said, “It is an ideal which I hope to live for and to achieve. But, if needs be, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.” He was not given the death penalty but was sentenced to life in prison. This was a big setback for the ANC, but protests grew and international pressure on the apartheid government increased.

In 1990, FW de Klerk ended the ban on the ANC, and Mandela was released from prison. People around the world celebrated.

Mandela’s presidency was welcomed by many, but there were also problems. After leaving politics in 1999, he said he should have acted sooner against HIV and AIDS in South Africa.

Archbishop Desmond Tutu, who led the truth and reconciliation committee after apartheid, said Mandela went beyond race and class, and helped people believe in Africa again.

Mandela sometimes appeared at ANC events and attended Jacob Zuma’s inauguration as president. His 91st birthday was celebrated with the first “Mandela Day” in his honor.

Mandela was married three times and had six children, 17 grandchildren, and 14 great-grandchildren.

Brazil had one of its biggest nights of protest in many years, with more than 100,000 people across the country going into the streets. They were angry about strong police actions, bad public services, and the high costs of the World Cup.

The main protests happened in cities like Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Brasilia, Belem, Belo Horizonte, Salvador, and others. Most protests started peacefully, but some ended with fights between police and protesters, and some cars and buses were set on fire.

The protests grew quickly. Earlier, smaller protests about higher bus prices had already led to complaints about police using too much force, like rubber bullets, tear gas, and beatings.

The protests happened at the same time as the Confederations Cup, a test event for the World Cup. Many different groups joined together because they were unhappy about rising costs, poor public services, lots of money spent on sports events, bad health care, and problems with inequality and corruption.

Most protests in Rio were peaceful, but some police officers were hurt in fights at the city’s legislative assembly. At least one car was turned over and burned, and windows were broken in banks and notary offices.

Later in the night, the situation got worse. A big crowd started fires outside the legislative assembly, broke windows, and wrote graffiti on the walls with messages like “Revolution,” “Down with Paes, down with Cabral” (the mayor and governor), and “Hate police.” Police inside used pepper spray and possibly more. A reporter saw one protester unconscious and bleeding from a wound in his upper arm.

The protesters had many reasons for joining. Oscar José Santos, a 19-year-old from the Rocinha favela, said, “We are here because we hate the government. They do nothing for us.” Nadia al Husin, an unemployed architect, held a sign asking the government to do more for education.

In Brasilia, a smaller protest broke through police lines and entered the high-security area of the national congress. Some protesters climbed onto the roof.

In Belo Horizonte, police fought with protesters who tried to get past a barrier around a football stadium where Nigeria and Tahiti were playing in the Confederations Cup.

In Porto Alegre, protesters set a bus on fire. In Curitiba, they tried to enter the state governor’s office. There were also protests in Belem, Salvador, and other cities.

In São Paulo, where there had been the worst clashes and most reports of police violence the week before, large crowds gathered again. This time, early reports said the marches were peaceful.

Social networks were important for spreading news about the protests. In São Paulo, where between 30,000 and 100,000 people joined, some carried signs saying “We come from Facebook.”

Most protesters were young, and for many, it was their first big protest. Thiago Firbida, a student, said, “My generation has never experienced this. Since the dictatorship, Brazilians never took over the streets. They did not believe they had a reason to. But now Brazil is in crisis, with prices always rising, so people are finally reacting.”

People compared these protests to those in Turkey and other countries. Some protesters wore Guy Fawkes masks, which are linked to the Anonymous group and Occupy Wall Street protests.

The protests in Brazil have been called the “vinegar revolution” (because police arrested people carrying vinegar to protect against tear gas), the “20-cent revolution” (because of the bus fare increase), and Passe Livre (for the demand for free public transport).

Some people said the protests felt unusual for Brazil but also freeing. Deli Borsari, a 53-year-old yoga teacher, said, “Our politicians need to see our strength as one people. Brazilians are usually too nice – they like parties more than protests – but something is changing.”

The high costs of new and improved stadiums for the Confederations Cup football tournament were a main reason for the protests. Before the opening match in Brasilia, riot police broke up crowds of protesters. Video showed scared Japanese fans running away with their children as shots, maybe rubber bullets or tear gas, were heard.

Another protest near Rio’s Maracana Stadium was also met with strong police action.

Most protests started peacefully until they met the police, who are mostly organized by region. President Dilma Rousseff supports peaceful protests, according to her staff. Helena Chagas from the president’s office said, “The president believes peaceful protests are right and normal in a democracy, and that it is natural for young people to protest.”

However, the president was booed at the Confederations Cup opening ceremony. With the economy doing badly and more social unrest, she faces a big political challenge now and in 2014, when Brazil will host the World Cup and have a presidential election.

Amsterdam still seems liberal to tourists. Recently, the Labour Mayor said that the city’s coffee shops, which sell marijuana, would stay open, even though there is a new national law against drug tourism. However, Amsterdam might lose its reputation for tolerance because of a new plan to send troublesome neighbours to “scum villages” made from shipping containers.

The Mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, says his new policy, which costs £810,000, is to protect people who are victims of abuse and homophobia from being harassed. The camps, where antisocial tenants will live for three to six months, are called “scum villages” because the idea is similar to a plan from Geert Wilders, a far-right politician. Last year, Wilders said that repeat offenders should be sent to a “village for scum.”

Bartho Boer, a spokesman for the Mayor, says the plans are not against liberal values. “We want to protect Amsterdam’s liberal values,” he says. “We want everyone to be themselves, whether they are gay, lesbian, or people who stand up to violence and then become victims of harassment. We want to protect them.” Boer explains that the villages are not for small problems, like a neighbour playing loud music on Saturday night, but for people who are very violent and threatening, and where someone is being harassed again and again.

People found guilty of causing “extreme havoc” will be evicted and moved to temporary homes that are very basic, such as converted shipping containers in industrial parts of the city. “We call it a living container,” says Boer. These units have showers and kitchens and have been used before as student housing. This way, antisocial tenants are not “rewarded” by getting better homes.

The Dutch newspaper the Parool said that in the 19th century, troublemakers were sent to villages in Drenthe and Overijssel, which quickly became slums. But Boer says the city has learned from past mistakes and will not put all the antisocial people together.

Boer says it is better to call them “scum houses” instead of “scum villages” because they do not want to put more than one of these families in the same area. After up to six months in these houses, which are spread around the city, the tenants will be given permanent homes. The city expects to move about ten families a year into this programme, which will start in 2013.

The temporary homes will have a lot of police, but the antisocial tenants will also get help from doctors, social workers, and parole officers. “They are taken care of so the same problems do not happen again in their new homes,” says Boer.

Male bosses are getting bonuses that are twice as big as those given to female bosses doing the same jobs. This means that, over a whole career, men can earn £141,500 more in bonuses than women. 

The Chartered Management Institute (CMI) shared these numbers. In 2012, men in management jobs in the UK got an average bonus of £6,442, while women got £3,029. For the highest jobs, female directors got bonuses of £36,270 in the last year, but male directors got £63,700.

These new numbers show that pay in British businesses is still unfair. Because of this, people who want equality at work are asking for changes. Ann Francke, the head of the CMI, said it is time to make this problem important for all managers. She said we need to change how we manage people, make workplaces more flexible, less focused on men, and more open about how people are rewarded. She believes that fixing this problem will help both companies and workers.

Dr. Ruth Sealy from Cranfield School of Management said the results are not surprising. She explained that bonuses can be given in different ways, and she thinks companies should be more open about how they give them.

Some experts said the numbers might be affected because women often work in jobs where bonuses are not common. Still, the big difference in bonus sizes is making the pay gap in Britain worse. The government says the pay gap is getting smaller, but full-time male workers still earn 10% more than women.

Maria Miller, the Minister for Women and Equalities, said the CMI numbers show that women are still not treated equally at work. She said things are getting better, but there is still a lot to do before men and women are truly equal at work.

The government has made it illegal for companies to stop workers from talking about their pay. They have also given courts the power to make companies check their pay if they break equal pay laws. The government started a program called Think, Act, Report to help companies improve how they hire, promote, and pay women. So far, 120 companies, including Tesco, BT, Unilever, and Eversheds, have joined this program. This is up from 54 companies in November 2012, but still not many have joined in almost two years.

The CMI’s data also shows that the pay gap between male and female bosses is getting smaller. The difference in average pay went down from £10,060 in 2012 to £8,502 in the latest numbers. But the CMI warned that the two groups of people they studied in 2012 and 2013 were not exactly the same, so the numbers cannot be directly compared.

A group of 17,000 managers, whose pay has been followed for several years, showed that men’s pay is now rising faster than women’s for the first time in five years. Men’s total pay (salary and bonuses) went up by 3.2%, while women’s went up by 2.8%. 

For the highest jobs, male directors’ pay went up by 5.3% in the last year, but female directors’ pay only went up by 1.1%.

Maria is sitting on a black plastic chair in a community center on a cold Tuesday afternoon, waiting for her number to be called. She is number 34. When it is her turn, Maria goes forward to pick up a brown paper bag filled with basic food like pasta, eggs, and cornflakes. She can also choose between butternut squash or carrots for her vegetables this week.

Maria is the 34th person to come to the East Hampton Food Pantry today. This food pantry is a community project set up near some of the most expensive and exclusive homes in the world. By the end of the day, the organizers expect more than 400 families to come and collect their weekly food package to help them get through the cold, dark winter in Long Island.

In the summer, the Hamptons—a group of old towns and villages by the ocean, 100 miles from Manhattan—are a playground for billionaires. But after Labor Day in early September, when the rich and famous leave their big houses and go back to Manhattan or Beverly Hills, life becomes hard for the mostly immigrant community who live there all year. “The people who come here are rich and famous, but we who live here are not,” says Maria. She works 14-hour days in the summer cleaning mansions, but in the winter, she often has no work at all.

Maria laughs when asked if she has enough money. “There is no work in the winter, only in the summertime,” says Maria, who, like many workers in the Hamptons, is from Latin America. “Here, many people live in one room because they can’t pay the rent.”

She says some families with up to five children live crowded together in basements and still pay more than $1,000 a month in rent. “People come here looking for work, but in the winter, there is nothing.”

Many of her friends cannot pay for heating or medicine, and many would go hungry if it were not for the East Hampton Food Pantry. This is just one of several food pantries in the town.

Vicki Littman, the chairperson of the East Hampton Food Pantry, says the number of people coming for help is always increasing. In 2015, the pantry gave out more than 31,000 food packages. “Once Labor Day comes and the season is over, people’s work hours are cut, and our numbers go up to about 400 families a week,” she says. “When they come to us on Tuesday, they get two to three days’ worth of food. Without us, they would have a much harder time.” Littman says it is hard for outsiders to believe that people are struggling in a place known for its wealth.

“When I talk to the summer visitors about the food pantries, they are always surprised because they only see the glamorous side of the Hamptons—the parties, the beaches, and the mansions. But they don’t see the service workers—the landscapers, nannies, waitresses—who depend on summer jobs to get through the winter. People don’t see that when they come here on holiday.

“There are older people who sometimes have to choose between paying for their medicine, their bills, or buying food, and that should not happen.”

Littman says the town has lost too many important workers—like teachers, police officers, doctors, and dentists—because they cannot afford to live in the community. The food pantry board wants to do more to help people stay. Housing is the biggest cost in the Hamptons. The most expensive property in the country is here: hedge fund manager Barry Rosenstein’s 18-acre beachfront estate at 67 Further Lane, which cost $147 million. It is close to Maidstone Golf Club, the most elite and difficult club to join in the Hamptons.
