Larry Cantwell, East Hampton’s town supervisor and a lifelong resident, says homes often sell for more than $25 million, and the high prices have made even the smallest apartments expensive. “Finding your first home is very hard in a place like this,” Cantwell says. “It’s not just poor people—working and middle-class families also have a hard time. If you can find a home to buy in East Hampton for $500,000, you are very lucky.” Cantwell says more than half the town’s homes are empty most of the year, so the population drops to about 10,000 in the winter, compared to 80,000 in August. “It’s like two different cities. There is a lot of wealth here, but almost all of it is in second homes only used in the summer,” says Cantwell, whose father was a fisherman and mother was a house cleaner. “But the rest of us live here all year.

“There are famous and very rich people, but there are also hard-working and poor people struggling to get by. People should remember that this community started as a farming and fishing town—a real working-class place.”

Cantwell says saving enough money to buy your first house while working as a farmer or fisherman is almost impossible in East Hampton today. “And it’s not just the poor—police officers, teachers, young professionals, and others all struggle to find a place to live here, and many cannot afford to own their own home.”

Being homeless in the Hamptons means spending a lot of time on a bus. Different churches have joined together to make sure there is somewhere for homeless people to sleep during the winter. Churches along the north and south forks of Long Island take turns hosting about 50 homeless people each night, and they are bussed between the churches every day. Eddie Vallone, 22, is one of the people on the bus every night. “People think the Hamptons is a rich town with no problems. But there are a lot of problems here, especially with drugs.

“It’s hard to understand—‘OK, the summer is ending. What am I going to do for the winter?’” Vallone says at Maureen’s Haven, a charity that runs the homeless shelter program. “I want to work, but there is no work to do.”

Vallone, who works cleaning pools and doing small jobs on luxury estates, says that if he saves his money and does not spend too much, his summer earnings can last until November. “But work does not start again until May or the beginning of June.”

Robert Mysłajek suddenly stops. On a muddy mountain path, the scientist finds what he is searching for between two wolf paw prints. “Droppings!” he says excitedly. Seeing a wolf is very rare, so finding their droppings is a good day, even for an experienced tracker.

But it is becoming easier. There are now about 1,500 wolves in Poland, double the number from 15 years ago. Wolves, along with brown bears, lynxes, and wolverines, are Europe’s last big meat-eating animals. Conservationists from Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands come to Poland to learn how the country has protected this animal, which even fairy tales have given a bad name.

Bits of bone and hair stick out from the black droppings. “It ate a red deer,” says the University of Warsaw biologist. “In my lab, I can learn a lot about this wolf—not just what it eats, but also its gender, sexual habits, age, health, and family connections.”

DNA tests show that Polish wolves travel far. “One wolf reached the Netherlands, but sadly, it was hit by a car. Wolves need a lot of space. The average area for a Polish wolf pack is 250 square kilometers,” says Mysłajek.

“Is it possible to bring wolves back to Scotland?” asks Alex Entwisle, a 23-year-old student from the UK, who is visiting southern Poland with his animal science class. The students have spent the day looking for droppings and paw prints in the spruce-covered Beskidy mountains of the Polish Carpathians.

They are discussing if wolves should return to the British Isles for the first time since the 1700s.

Mysłajek visited the Scottish Highlands in 2015 as a guest of the Wolves and Humans Foundation, a British charity. He answered questions from villagers about Poland’s experience. “The big difference between Scotland and Poland is that we eat pork. We do not have many sheep here.

“But we have many wild animals—300,000 red deer and over 800,000 roe deer. We also have too many wild boar—about 200,000—which destroy farmers’ crops. Here, wolves help solve this problem,” he says.

Mysłajek, who often appears on Polish TV, says wolves are amazing animals that can travel up to 30 kilometers in one hunt. “The Beskidy pack is strong, with eight or nine wolves. This year, we have seen five cubs, two yearlings, and two adults.

“We track them with cameras in the forest and by following their tracks in mud and snow. In each family group, only one pair has babies each year. All pack members help care for the young with great teamwork and care.”

Mysłajek, whose father was a shepherd, does not understand why wolves have a bad reputation. “Why do we say ‘lone-wolf gunman’? Why did we need stories like Little Red Riding Hood?”

He is interested in these wild dogs, who stayed in the wild 33,000 years ago, while others became domestic dogs.

Wolves are not pets. Mysłajek says only scientific reasons—like the need to help forests grow and control wild animal numbers—can save Europe’s wild meat-eaters, especially the unpopular wolf. “Natural predators keep the ecosystem balanced. They control plant-eating animals, which lets trees grow tall for birds to nest in.”

Should we just shoot the deer? “That only partly solves the problem,” he says. “In a healthy environment, there is a ‘landscape of fear’, where plant-eating animals do not spend all day eating grass by the river. They move away to avoid predators. This gives plants a chance to grow.”

Wolf hunting was banned in the western Carpathians in 1995 and in all of Poland in 1998. Now, wolf packs live in almost all of Poland’s big forests. Wolves live alongside people, not separated by fences like in African safari parks.

The Polish government pays farmers if wolves kill their animals. Mysłajek advises farmers to use electric fences. He also helped bring back two old ways to scare wolves: red flags hung around sheep pens and the bark of the white Tatra Mountain Sheepdog.

Poland’s wolves have survived and moved around more easily because the country developed its roads and buildings later than others. In 1989, when communism ended, Poland had only one motorway. Big road projects, which had to include studies on wildlife, started after Poland joined the European Union in 2004. Now, Poland has one of the world’s highest numbers of bridges and tunnels for wild animals to cross roads safely.

People’s attitudes have changed too. “For many years, hunting was part of the culture. In 1975, there were fewer than 100 wolves in Poland. From the 1950s, the government encouraged hunting wolves and paid a reward for each one killed—equal to a month’s salary. It was a massacre.”

Mysłajek says the situation for Polish wolves has improved a lot, but it is still not safe. Wolf packs move across borders, and hunting still happens in Russia, Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine, and Slovakia.

He says Poland’s new government, elected in October 2015, does not like wolves. “The Environment Minister, Jan Szyszko, is a hunter. There are 120,000 licensed hunters in Poland, and they have power in parliament.

“The hunters say wolves are a problem and claim there are 4,000 wolves in Poland, but this number is not scientific. This government could undo our progress.”

Being a supporter of wolves is difficult. “You cannot tell politicians that wolves are a big tourist attraction. Most tourists want to see wolves, but wolves avoid people. They have a very good sense of smell.”

The 12 British animal science students leave the Polish Carpathians without seeing a wolf—only photos of paw prints and droppings. Entwisle believes Scotland will never be as successful as Poland.

“It would be great for the environment to have wolves back because there are too many deer. But it would not work because of the roads and sheep.

“There would be problems with farmers. Our industrial revolution happened too long ago. We ruined our chance. In Britain, we like predators to be far away and to watch them on TV,” said Entwisle.

There are worse things to do in life than walk along Rio’s Copacabana beach in the sun on your way to watch a World Cup match. So, it was not surprising that Anthony McDowell, an England fan from Liverpool, was not worried about the negative news before the tournament in Brazil. “This place is beautiful. The people are friendly. There is a party feeling,” said McDowell. “The only thing that could be better is the England team.”

He and about six friends are among many fans from around the world who have turned the beach into a party with national colors and songs. Some people danced, some took photos, some drank, but most just walked and talked about football, waiting for the next game to start on the big FanFest screen nearby. The last time so many people were here during the day was when the pope visited.

The happy and mostly peaceful mood was very different from the protests, transport problems, and stadium issues that happened before the World Cup. Now that the football has started, visiting fans want to enjoy the experience. “If I had known, when I started planning, how difficult and expensive it would be, I wouldn’t have come. But now that we’re here, it’s great,” said Brian Hill, a retired boss from Sunderland.

The trip has not been perfect. Hill traveled for more than 20 hours to get to Rio, then had long delays on the road from the airport at 6:30 in the morning. His son, Andrew, had his sunglasses stolen almost as soon as he sat on the beach. They were also surprised that many bars do not have big screens for the games. But, like many fans, they said they loved the atmosphere, even if the organization was not perfect. The tournament has started very well on the field.

Even the most negative person must have enjoyed Robin van Persie’s amazing diving header for the Netherlands against Spain. There have also been many goals: 28 in the first eight games—almost three times more than at the same point in South Africa in 2010. The party feeling on the streets is helped by many fans from nearby countries, and Latin American teams won every game they played up to this point.

So far, the tournament has avoided the worst problems, but it is not perfect. The stadiums were finished late and some were not completely ready, but there have been no reports of serious problems or trouble getting into the stadiums since the games started.

As in past World Cups, ticketing has been a problem, with many empty seats at some games, including the Netherlands against Spain. FIFA spokesman Saint-Clair Milesi said only 48,000 of the 51,900 seats were filled. FIFA is also looking into security problems after Chilean fans set off fireworks during their win over Australia.

The Globo newspaper listed several problems in the 12 host cities. Almost all had worse traffic than usual. The worst transport problems were in Natal, where bus drivers have been on strike since June 12. In Salvador, some trips took five times longer than normal. “Traffic was already bad, but this week it is chaotic,” said Jecilda Mello, president of a local residents’ group.

But protests have become smaller since the first day, when small demonstrations happened in several cities and police used tear gas and pepper spray. Since then, the only security problems have been small thefts and overly excited fans. Police used pepper spray to break up a street party of Argentinian fans after they blocked roads.

The long distances between cities have led to very different World Cup experiences. The tournament has not had a big effect on São Paulo, South America’s largest city, but far away in Manaus—the remote Amazon city where England played Italy—visitors said World Cup excitement was everywhere, with decorated streets and flags on many cars.

FA chairman Greg Dyke said the change in mood was clear. “We’ve had a really warm welcome in Manaus. It’s a big event for them, even if it is strange to spend so much money on a stadium with no one to use it later. But we were in São Paulo for four or five days before the opening match and you wouldn’t have known there was a World Cup until the last day. It was strange.”

A girl born today in the UK can expect to live almost 82 years, while her brother can expect to live 78 years. In Andorra, they would live even longer (85 years for girls and 79 for boys). In the US, life expectancy is a bit lower (81 for girls and 76 for boys). But in the Central African Republic, life expectancy is much shorter (49 for girls and 44 for boys). Almost everywhere in the world, except in countries like Lesotho that have problems with HIV and violence, people are living longer lives. The best news is that young children are much less likely to die than forty years ago. The number of children under five who die each year has dropped by almost 60%, from 16.4 million in 1970 to 6.8 million in 2010.

This is one reason why the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) in Seattle started a big project over the last five years. Nearly 500 researchers worked together to study health problems around the world. Knowing how many children die and why helps the world focus on saving their lives. The large database they created gives many lessons that can help global organizations and governments take better care of people. This includes focusing on healthy diets, fighting alcohol problems, and continuing the fight against HIV in Africa.

The seven papers published by The Lancet are a big achievement, but not everyone agrees with all the results. IHME used some new and bold methods. When there were no official death records, they sometimes used "verbal autopsies," which means they found out the cause of death by talking to the family. One surprising result was about malaria. In 2012, IHME said that 1.2 million people die from malaria each year, which is twice as many as previously thought. Most of the increase is in adult deaths. Before, people thought malaria mostly killed children under five.

Dr. Christopher Murray, IHME Director, said that doctors used to believe adults in malaria areas became partly immune. At first, IHME agreed with this, but their new data showed more adults dying from malaria, especially in Africa. However, he also said that some of these deaths could be from other diseases with similar symptoms. These findings have led to more studies.

Margaret Chan, Director General of the World Health Organization (WHO), officially welcomed the IHME study, but some WHO staff are careful. Colin Mathers, a senior scientist, said they need to check if the numbers are correct. Dr. Ties Boerma, another WHO director, said people should know that some numbers are very different and WHO cannot accept every new study right away. Still, Mathers said that IHME’s new ideas are interesting and helpful. Murray said one main finding is that the main causes of death are changing very quickly, faster than expected.

Because people are having fewer children and living longer, the average age of the world’s population has gone up in ten years, from 26 to almost 30. In Latin America, for example, countries like Brazil and Paraguay had an average life expectancy below 30 in 1970, but almost 64 in 2010. That is a 35-year increase in average age of death in forty years. Murray said that in places like Brazil, the change is so fast that most organizations are not ready for it.

The second main finding is that, outside Africa, the main health problems are changing from infectious diseases and mother and baby deaths to "lifestyle" diseases like heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and cancer. Some of these diseases are also caused by genes. This change is especially strong in Latin America, the Middle East, and south and southeast Asia.

The third big finding was a surprise. It is about how many people live with disabilities and health problems, even though they live longer. The main causes of disability are not the same as the main causes of death. Disabilities are often caused by mental health problems like anxiety and depression, bone and muscle problems like arthritis and back pain (which people in every country complain about), anaemia, loss of sight and hearing, and skin diseases. Substance abuse is also a problem. Murray said that the rates of these problems are not going down. We are not making progress in reducing these conditions.

In the market square of Rjukan, there is a statue of Sam Eyde, the town’s founder. He was a famous Norwegian engineer and businessman. The statue looks north towards a steep mountain. Behind the statue, to the south, is another steep mountain called Gaustatoppen, which is 1,800 meters high. Between these mountains, in the narrow Vestfjord valley, is the small town of Rjukan. Sam Eyde built this town in the early 1900s for the workers in his factories.

Eyde used the power of the 100-meter-high Rjukanfossen waterfall to make hydroelectricity. At that time, it was the biggest power plant in the world. However, he could not change the position of the sun. Because Rjukan is deep in a valley and surrounded by high mountains, the town and its 3,400 people are in shadow for half the year. From late September to mid-March, during the day, the town is not completely dark, but it is not bright either. Rjukan is about three hours northwest of Oslo.

Recently, something new appeared in the square. High on the mountain opposite the statue, 450 meters above the town, there are three large mirrors. These mirrors are powered by solar energy and controlled by computers. They follow the sun and reflect its light down onto the square, making it bright with sunlight.

Ingrid Sparbo, a retired secretary who has lived in Rjukan all her life, stands in the sunlight and smiles. She says people get used to the shade and stop thinking about it, but the sunlight from the mirrors feels warm, not just on the body but also in the mind.

Two young mothers bring their children to the square to stand in the sun. On a cold day, an old couple sits on a new bench, enjoying the warmth. Children smile, and many people take photos. Silje Johansen, a shop assistant, says it is “awesome.”

Eivind Toreid, an electrical engineer, is more careful. He says it is strange, not real sunlight, but very similar, like a spotlight.

Heidi Fieldheim heard about the mirrors on the radio. She says it is even better than she expected and will bring a lot of happiness.

Across the street, in the Nye Tider café, sits Martin Andersen, the man who made this possible. Andersen is a 40-year-old artist who moved to Rjukan in 2001. He first thought of the Sun Mirror, or Solspeil, in September. He and his family would walk with their child in a buggy, and each day they had to go further down the valley to find the sun. By September 28, the sun disappears from Rjukan’s market square and does not return until March 12.

During these long months, Andersen says they could see the blue sky and the sun on the mountain slopes, but to feel the sun, they had to leave town. He thought it was sad that people had to leave Rjukan to enjoy the sun.

Twelve years after his idea, a German company that specializes in concentrated solar power brought in the three large glass mirrors by helicopter. Andersen says it took longer than they thought.

The mirrors really work. At first, many people in Rjukan did not like the idea. There were petitions, letters, and even a Facebook page against the project. Many people thought it was a waste of money. But now, most people seem to like it.

Nils Eggerud says he was strongly against the mirrors. He thought the money could have been used for better things, like more carers for old people, better schools, bike paths, or fixing roads. He still worries about the cost of keeping the mirrors working and who will pay for it. But he admits it feels nice to stand in the sunlight, and he sees how happy people are.

Rjukan’s young mayor, Steinar Bergsland, is more interested in the benefits than the cost. He says more visitors are coming to Rjukan, and local shops are making more money. A technology company is thinking about moving to Rjukan because of the new technology and the attention it brings.

Bergsland says the mirrors are a strong symbol for Rjukan. With help from government grants and a donation from a local business, the town only had to pay 1 million krone (about £100,000) of the total 5 million krone cost. Compared to the town’s yearly budget of 650 million krone, this was not a lot of money. He believes the mirrors will help the town get more money for better schools and more nursing care. He says, “Just look out of the window. Look at those happy faces. Now it’s actually here, people love it.”

Getting fit in four minutes sounds like something from a magazine or a TV ad that is too good to be true. But when you try Dr. Izumi Tabata’s workout – 20 seconds of very hard exercise, 10 seconds of rest, repeated eight times – you quickly see how tough it really is. You end up out of breath and very tired.

Dr. Tabata first used this method with his university students in the early 1990s. He remembers, “They were exhausted! After four minutes, they were finished. But after six weeks, they saw great results and were surprised. We all were.”

Tabata’s research started when he and coach Irisawa Koichi watched Japan’s speed skating team. They noticed that short, very hard exercises worked as well as hours of easier training. To test this, Tabata did an experiment. One group of students did one hour of steady exercise on a bike, five times a week. The other group warmed up for ten minutes, then did four minutes of Tabata intervals, four times a week, plus one 30-minute steady session with two minutes of intervals.

The results were surprising. After six weeks, the Tabata group, who exercised only 88 minutes a week, increased their anaerobic capacity by 28% and their VO2 max (a measure of heart and lung fitness) by 15%. The other group, who trained for five hours a week, improved their VO2 max by 10%, but their anaerobic capacity did not change. Tabata also found that the heart got bigger after three weeks of this training. New research shows that Tabata training can lower the risk of diabetes in people, something already shown in rats.

But you cannot do this training slowly or easily. You must work very hard, using a bike, rowing machine, sprints, or fast bodyweight exercises. Imagine running eight 100-meter sprints with only ten seconds to rest between each one.

Tabata says, “You must give all your effort, at 170% of your VO2 max. If you feel okay after, you did not do it right. The first three rounds feel easy, but the last two are extremely hard. The goal is eight rounds, but some people can only do six or seven.”

One person on an exercise website said, “If you do it right, you should feel like you met God. Most people cannot do it correctly and should not try.” Tabata does not fully agree. He says, “Everyone can do it, but beginners should start with a trained coach to make sure they work at the right level.” He will soon publish research showing that doing Tabata just twice a week, less than half the original amount, still gives good health benefits.

Another new study shows that the Tabata workout burns an extra 150 calories in the 12 hours after exercise, even when resting, because of the body’s need for more oxygen after hard work. So, while most people use Tabata to get fit, it also helps burn fat.

It is surprising that mostly serious athletes use this plan, but that may change soon. Tabata has made a deal with Universal Studios to create a network of trainers and a DVD series. He says, “I see people doing Tabata on YouTube, but some do it wrong because they do not know how hard they need to work.”

Should everyone add Tabata to their workouts? Richard Scrivener, a former rugby team coach, says Tabata is a good addition, not a replacement, for your favorite sport or training. For example, runners need to practice running to get better, but they can do less long-distance running and add Tabata to help their bodies rest and recover, especially if they often get small injuries. This way, their long runs will be better when they do them.

People who go to the gym can do three strength workouts and three Tabata sessions each week. The rest of us can start slowly, adding more sessions over time. But remember, it never gets easier, because you must always give your maximum effort. That is the tough but effective part of the Tabata method.

In 2005, BlackBerry made it possible to send instant messages on mobile phones. This was the start of a very successful time for the company. Before the iPhone was created, BlackBerry’s new ideas made its smartphone one of Canada’s biggest products sold to other countries.

Six years later, in the summer of 2011, there was violence in London that spread to other cities like Birmingham, Nottingham, Liverpool, and Manchester. BlackBerry Messenger (BBM) was so good at helping people organize that politicians wanted to shut it down for a while. But two years after that, users themselves started to stop using BBM. Fewer people wanted BlackBerry phones, and BBM became quiet. Many new messaging apps appeared, such as Facebook Messenger, Apple’s iMessage, WhatsApp, and Kik (which is also Canadian). These apps are free to download and use. They let people send text messages, pictures, voice messages, stickers, and even videos (in WhatsApp’s case) between most types of phones using the internet.

To try to keep its users, BBM was made available on Android and Apple phones. Even with many competitors, more than 20 million people downloaded BBM. However, many people think this is not enough to save BBM.

James Gooderson, an 18-year-old student who writes about technology, says, “Bringing BlackBerry to the iPhone is four or five years too late. WhatsApp has taken away the reason for young people to use a BlackBerry.” BBM says it has 80 million users each month after its update, but WhatsApp has 300 million. Other apps show what BBM cannot do: BBM does not have video or voice calls like Skype and Viber, does not share locations like Path, does not share videos like iMessage, and does not have stickers, which are very popular with kids. Also, sharing contacts and calendars, which was possible on BlackBerry phones, does not work on the Apple and Android versions.

Messaging is changing from words to pictures. People upload photos to Instagram and get many comments. Snapchat lets people send pictures that delete themselves after ten seconds. Like BBM, all these services are free for any phone with internet. In 2011, BBM was so important that it was said to help start a revolution in Egypt. During the London riots, BBM gave news faster than TV.

Jean-Pierre Moore, 28, manages a youth club in Stockwell, south London, an area with high crime and poverty. He now uses an iPad to communicate. He does not think stopping BBM would have stopped the riots. “Social networking was not the reason,” he says. “Many people were already angry. If you mention ‘stop and search’ here, many young men get angry right away.”

Almost 80% of young people with smartphones use social networking apps, says Enders Analysis, a research company. Two-thirds use more than one app. Among people aged 16 to 24, 60% use Facebook every day, but 46% use other apps too. Benedict Evans, a digital media expert at Enders, says, “It’s much more complicated now. The smartphone is the main platform. All these apps connect to your contacts and photos. Some apps, like Instagram, last a long time; others disappear quickly.”

Thirteen-year-old Bennett has three devices, all given to him by family. He uses his BlackBerry for messaging, an iPhone with wi-fi for games, and an HTC Android phone for calls. His friends still use BBM—at his school, four phones have been stolen this term, all BlackBerrys. With BBM, you can send a message to everyone in your contacts, sometimes hundreds of people. On WhatsApp, you can only send a message to 50 people at once. But for Bennett, Instagram is now very important. “Instagram is Facebook without parents,” he says. “Older people use Facebook now. When I saw my mum on Facebook, I deleted my account.”

For families who have trouble paying for heating, BlackBerry is still attractive because it is cheap. Unlimited BBM messages are available with a used device and a £7-a-month plan from T-Mobile. But people do not trust BBM’s privacy as much as before. Many business people, activists, and rioters liked BBM because they thought messages were safe and could not be traced. After the riots, some people were caught, and this trust was lost.

In South Kensington, a rich area of London, older students all have Apple phones and use WhatsApp. For them, BBM is just a memory. “I still have a BlackBerry, but I’m the only one,” says one teenager. How does he feel about that? “Isolated,” he answers.

A big international argument has started about whether Bolivia’s indigenous Indian tribes have the right to chew coca leaves, which are the main ingredient in cocaine. Bolivia has received a special exception from the 1961 Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs, which is the main international law about drugs. This exception allows Bolivia’s indigenous people to chew coca leaves.

Bolivia said that the convention goes against its new constitution, which was adopted in 2009. The constitution says Bolivia must “protect native and ancestral coca as cultural heritage” and that coca “in its natural state is not a narcotic.”

Indigenous people in South America have chewed coca leaves for hundreds of years. The leaves are believed to give energy and have medicinal benefits. People who support Bolivia praised the country for defending the rights of indigenous people. Danny Kushlick, Head of External Affairs at the Transform Drug Policy Foundation, said, “The Bolivian move is inspirational and groundbreaking. It shows that any country tired of the war on drugs can change how it works with the UN conventions.”

However, the UN’s International Narcotics Control Board (INCB), which checks if countries follow global drug laws, said Bolivia is threatening the international drug control system. Several countries, including the UK, US, Italy, Sweden, the Netherlands, and Russia, opposed Bolivia’s request.

The UK told the UN that it “acknowledges and respects the cultural importance of the coca leaf in Bolivia,” but also said, “The United Kingdom is concerned that the exception could increase coca production and, importantly, the amount of coca used to make cocaine. This would weaken international law and the global fight against the drug trade.”

The right of indigenous people in the Andes to chew coca leaves was removed in 1964 when Bolivia was under a dictatorship and joined the convention. The agreement gave Bolivia 25 years to ban coca chewing. This period ended in 1989, and the issue has been argued about since then.

In 2011, Bolivia’s President Evo Morales, who used to grow coca, officially told the UN that Bolivia was leaving the convention. On Friday, Bolivia rejoined the convention, but with an exception that allows coca leaf chewing.

This is the first time such an exception has happened in the history of UN drug-control treaties. Some people worry that other countries might now ask for changes too. The Russian government said this could lead to “an increase in illegal cocaine” and warned that “it sets a dangerous example that other countries might follow to make drug laws less strict.”

The British parliament’s Home Affairs Select Committee said the UK government should support Bolivia’s request, because it is important for countries to stay in the single convention. Bolivia’s return could only be stopped if one third or more of the 184 countries that signed the convention opposed it. There are reports that the US and UK are trying hard to get enough countries to block Bolivia’s request.

Nancie Prud’homme, Projects Director at the International Centre on Human Rights and Drug Policy, criticized the opposition to Bolivia. She said, “These objections are legally questionable. They support a rule that is too broad and ignore international laws about cultural and indigenous rights, which support Bolivia.”

The decision to ban coca chewing was based on a 1950 report by the UN Commission of Inquiry on the Coca Leaf. People who want drug laws to be less strict say this report was not based on good evidence. In 1949, before the study started, the head of the Commission, Howard B Fonda, said he was against coca chewing. He told an interviewer, “We believe that chewing coca leaves every day is very harmful and causes problems for many Indians. Our studies will confirm this, and we hope to find a way to completely stop this habit.”

Growing coca leaves is legal and controlled in Bolivia. This policy has been linked to a decrease in cocaine production in the country, and some experts think the Bolivian model could be useful for other countries.

A few months before he died, Carl Sagan recorded a hopeful message for future Mars explorers. He said, “Whatever the reason you’re on Mars is, I’m glad you’re there. And I wish I was with you.”

Seventeen years after Sagan shared his dream in 1996, a company from the Netherlands wants to make it real. The company, Mars One, plans to send four astronauts to Mars in 2023 to start a human colony. However, there are some serious problems.

First, the gravity on Mars is only 38% of Earth’s gravity. This would change the astronauts’ bodies so much—their bones, muscles, and blood circulation—that they might not survive if they returned to Earth. Second, because of this, the astronauts will have to say goodbye to their families and friends forever, since there is no return ticket.

The Mars One website says that coming back “cannot be anticipated nor expected.” To return, they would need a fully built and fueled rocket to leave Mars, life support systems for a seven-month trip, and the ability to dock with a space station or land safely on Earth. The website says, “Not one of these is a small endeavour,” and all of them need a lot of technology, weight, and money.

Still, the project already has 10,000 applicants, according to the company’s Medical Director, Norbert Kraft. He told The Guardian that the applicants are between 18 and 62 years old. Most are men, but there are also women.

The reasons people want to go are different. An American woman named Cynthia, age 32, said it was her “childhood imagining” to go to Mars. She remembered a trip with her mother in the early 1990s to a lecture at the University of Wisconsin. The speaker was Sagan, and Cynthia asked him if he thought humans would land on Mars in her lifetime. Sagan asked her if she wanted to be in a “tin can spacecraft” for two years to get there. She said “yes,” and Sagan smiled and told her seriously that he believed humans would reach Mars in her lifetime.

Cynthia said, “When I first heard about the Mars One project I thought, this is my chance—my childhood dream could become real. I could be one of the first people to build a settlement on Mars and show people on Earth that there are still new places for humans to explore.”

Mars One is looking for astronauts who are strong, adaptable, curious, able to trust others, and resourceful, according to Kraft. They must also be over 18 years old.

Mars One was started in 2010 by Bas Lansdorp, an engineer. The company says it has a realistic plan and enough money for the project, using technology that already exists. The website says that the basic things needed for life are already on Mars. For example, water can be taken from ice in the soil, and Mars has nitrogen, which is the main part of the air we breathe. The colony will use special solar panels for power.

Mars One has signed a contract with an American company, Paragon Space Development Corporation, to start working on the life support system and spacesuits for the mission.

The project will cost about $6 billion. Lansdorp hopes to pay for part of this by selling TV rights. He said, “The broadcasting revenue from the London Olympics was almost enough to finance a mission to Mars,” in an interview with ABC News.

Paul Römer, the co-creator of the reality TV show Big Brother, is also working with the project. On the website, Römer said, “This mission to Mars could be the biggest media event in the world. Reality meets talent show with no ending and the whole world watching.”

The goal is to build a permanent human colony. The first team will land on Mars in 2023 to start building, and every two years, four more astronauts will join them.

However, some people doubt the project. They worry about how the astronauts will get to Mars and build a colony with all the things they need to survive.

Professor Gerard ’t Hooft, who won the Nobel Prize for physics in 1999, is an ambassador for the project. He admits there are unknown health risks. The radiation on Mars is “of quite a different nature” from anything tested on Earth, he said.

The mission hopes to inspire people to believe that anything is possible, just like the Apollo Moon landings did.

Mars One says it is not only possible, but necessary to build a permanent settlement on Mars. This will help us learn more about how the solar system was formed, the origins of life, and our place in the universe.

At a special press conference at Leicester University, new details were shared about Richard III. Not only was the identity of the man found in the car park with a curved spine confirmed, but also the terrible way his body was treated after his death was revealed.

There was applause when Richard Buckley, the lead archaeologist, said the university team was sure “beyond reasonable doubt” that they had found the last Plantagenet king. Richard III had scoliosis, which bent his spine, and his body was twisted even more to fit into a small grave at Grey Friars church. The grave was not big enough for him.

By this time, the evidence was very strong. Scientists who did DNA tests, experts who used computer imaging to study the bones, genealogists who found a living relative with matching DNA, and historians who read old texts about the king’s death and burial all shared their findings.

Philippa Langley, from the Richard III Society, said, “What a morning. What a story.” She had worked on the project for years, even when many people did not believe it was possible, and she found money from around the world to keep the project going.

Plans have started for a new tomb for Richard III in Leicester Cathedral, only 100 yards from where he was found. There will be a ceremony to bury him there, probably next year. Leicester’s Museums’ Service is also planning a new visitor centre in an old school building near the site.

Richard III died at the Battle of Bosworth on 22 August 1485. He was the last English king to die in battle. For the first time, researchers showed how he died. People gasped when they saw a picture of the base of his skull, which had been cut off by a single, terrible blow. This was probably done with a halberd, a heavy medieval weapon with a sharp iron axe blade on a wooden pole. The blade likely went several centimetres into his brain. Jo Appleby, an expert on human bones, said Richard would have lost consciousness immediately and died very quickly.

This injury matches old reports that Richard died fighting in the middle of the battle, after being thrown from his horse. This is like the famous line Shakespeare gave him: “A horse! A horse! My kingdom for a horse!” Another sword cut also went through his skull and into his brain, which would have killed him too. Many other injuries happened after he died, suggesting that his body was treated badly on the battlefield and on the way back to Leicester. He was stripped, mocked, and his body was damaged.

One terrible injury was a stab through his right buttock into his pelvis. This happened after death, because his armour would have protected him if he were alive. This supports the story that his naked body was carried back over a horse and abused along the way. Bob Savage, a medieval weapons expert, said this wound was probably made by a sharp knife or dagger, not a war weapon.

Michael Ibsen, a Canadian furniture maker and a descendant of Richard’s sister, heard the news on Sunday and listened quietly to the evidence. He said, “My head is no clearer now than when I first heard the news. Many, many hundreds of people died on that field that day. He was a king, but just one of the dead. He lived in very violent times and these deaths would not have been pretty or quick.”

Mathew Morris was the first to find the body, in the first hour of the first day of digging. He did not believe it was the king at first. The digger was still removing the tarmac from the council car park, which local historians and the Richard III Society thought was the site of the lost Grey Friars church. The priests from this church bravely took the king’s body and buried him quickly, probably still naked, but in a place of honour near the church’s high altar. When Morris first saw the leg bones in the soil, he covered them up again.

Ten days later, on 5 September, more digging showed Morris had found the right place. He returned with Lin Foxhall, head of archaeology, to dig up the body. “We did it the usual way, lifting the arms, legs, and skull first, and then the torso. Only when we saw the twisted spine did I think: ‘My word, I think we’ve got him.’”

Philippa Langley believes Richard was the true king, the last king of the north, a good and brave leader who became a victim of powerful Tudor propaganda, especially from Shakespeare. There is still the mystery of the “princes in the tower.” Richard III declared his nephews, Edward V and his brother Richard, illegitimate, put them in the Tower of London, and they were never seen alive again. It is not certain that the bones found in the tower years later are theirs, so more DNA tests may be needed.

Scientists have put a false memory into the brains of mice in an experiment. They hope this will help explain why people sometimes “remember” things that never happened. False memories are a big problem in court cases. Sometimes, people are found guilty because of eyewitness statements, but later, DNA or other evidence shows they were innocent.

To study how false memories form in the brain, Susumu Tonagawa, a neuroscientist at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT), and his team created memories in mice by changing certain brain cells. Our memories are made from different parts, like records of objects, places, and times. These records are called engrams and are stored as physical and chemical changes in brain cells and their connections.

Tonagawa says that both false and real memories use the same brain systems. His team used a method called optogenetics, which lets them control single brain cells. They changed brain cells in the mouse hippocampus—a part of the brain important for making memories—so the cells would make a protein called channelrhodopsin. When these cells are hit with blue light, they become active. The researchers made sure that only the brain cells used to make memory engrams would produce this protein.

In the experiment, the team put mice in a chamber and let them explore. While the mice explored, the memory-making brain cells made the channelrhodopsin protein. The next day, the mice were put in a different chamber and given a small electric shock to make them afraid. At the same time, the researchers shined blue light into the mice’s brains to activate their memories of the first chamber. This made the mice connect the fear of the shock with the memory of the first chamber.

Later, when the mice were put back in the first chamber, they froze in fear, even though they had never been shocked there. Tonagawa called this “incepting” or putting a false memory into the mouse’s brain.

A similar thing might happen when strong false memories are made in humans. Tonagawa said, “Humans are very imaginative. Even when nothing is happening around us, our brains are always active. So, like the mice, we can connect what we are thinking about with good or bad things that happen. This means we might make a false connection between what is in our mind and what is really happening.”

He also said, “Our study showed that false and real memories are based on almost the same brain systems. It is hard for someone with a false memory to tell the difference. We hope our future work will warn lawmakers and legal experts about how unreliable memory can be.”

Chris French, who leads the Anomalistic Psychology Research Unit at Goldsmiths, University of London, studies false memories in people. He said these results are an important first step in understanding how false memories work in the brain.

He explained that memory does not work like a video camera. It does not record everything exactly as it happened. Instead, memory is a process where we build a memory from pieces of real events and sometimes from other sources. He warned that the false memories made in the mice were much simpler than the complex false memories seen in people, such as false memories of childhood abuse, strange rituals, alien abductions, or “past lives.” These rich false memories use many parts of the brain, and we still do not fully understand how they form.

Mark Stokes, a neuroscientist at Oxford University, said the experiments were very impressive, but we need to keep them in perspective. He said that while the results show that new memories can be made by artificial stimulation, this is still very different from how most people think of memory. It is more like making a person feel uneasy in a place for no clear reason, rather than creating a full, detailed memory. He said it is unlikely that this kind of pairing would create the rich memories we usually have, but over time, it could mix with other memories to make a more detailed false story.

The mouse models made by the MIT team will help scientists ask more complex questions about human memory. Steve Ramirez, a colleague of Tonagawa at MIT, said, “Now that we can turn memories on and off and change them in the brain, we can ask questions that used to be only for philosophers. Are there many ways to make false memories? Can we create false memories on purpose? What about false memories for things like objects, food, or other mice? These are questions that we can now study in the lab.”

French said that as this technology develops, scientists must think carefully about how it is used. “Whatever method is used to put false memories into the brain, we must be very careful about the ethical problems. There is a big risk that these techniques could be misused.”

Music subscription services like Spotify and Deezer have made more than $1 billion in sales worldwide, as more people choose to pay for music online. In 2013, money from streaming and subscriptions went up by over 50% to $1.1 billion. This helped music sales in Europe grow for the first time in 12 years, according to numbers published in March 2014.

There are now about 450 music rental services around the world. Many people still listen for free, but more music fans are paying because they want more choices. In three years, the number of paying subscribers grew from 8 million to 28 million, according to the 2014 digital music report from the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI).

People like subscription services because they are easy to use on smartphones and tablets. These services let people try new music without buying a download or CD. Many users say they like that these services are cheap, easy to use, and legal, unlike pirated downloads. IFPI Chief Executive Frances Moore said, “It is now clear that music streaming and subscription is a mainstream model for our business.” In Britain and America, streaming may soon make more money for the music industry than downloads from online stores like Apple’s iTunes. Subscription services now make up one third of all digital music sales worldwide, while downloads make up the rest. However, the two types are growing at different speeds.

In the US, the number of people using subscription and streaming services went up from 19% in 2012 to 23%, while the number of people downloading music went down from 28% to 27%. In Britain, the number of people downloading stayed the same at one third, but subscribers grew from 19% to 22%. In Sweden, France, and Italy, streaming is already more popular than downloading.

Digital music now makes up 39% of all music sales, or almost £5.9 billion out of £15 billion. Sales of CDs and vinyl dropped a lot in 2013, but they still make up just over half of the music industry’s income. A big drop in music sales in Japan, which makes up one fifth of the world’s music sales and where CDs stayed popular longer, caused total music sales worldwide to fall by 3.9%.

However, vinyl records became popular again in some places. Sales of vinyl went up by 32% in America and by 101% in the UK in 2013.

The IFPI also said that One Direction were the top-selling artists of 2013, with 4 million physical and digital sales for their album Midnight Memories. Katy Perry’s album Prism was the best-selling album by a female artist, coming in sixth place after Eminem, Justin Timberlake, Bruno Mars, and Daft Punk.

Technology companies are also joining the music streaming trend. Apple started iTunes Radio, Google is promoting its Play Store, and smaller companies like Beats Music, made by the team behind Beats headphones, are also joining in.

A thick layer of bird droppings covers the golden railing of one of Britain’s most expensive houses. Pigeon skeletons are found among broken mirrors, and water runs through damaged decorations. This is The Towers, a £30 million palace on “Billionaires’ Row” in north London. Its ruined state has been kept secret until now.

The Towers is one of ten mansions in the middle of The Bishops Avenue, a famous and expensive street in London. These houses have been almost empty for about 25 years. It is believed they were bought for members of the Saudi Arabian royal family. The Greek-style columns are breaking, and the swimming pools, decorated with mosaics, are full of rubble. Nature has taken over so much that owls now live there.

This sad scene is common along the avenue, which Lloyds Bank says is the second most expensive street in Britain. While many people in London struggle to buy a home as prices rise by 11.2% each year, 16 mansions on the most expensive part of The Bishops Avenue are empty. Many are behind locked gates, with steel bars on the windows and overgrown gardens watched by guard dogs.

Across the street, another empty mansion worth £18 million has broken windows and walls covered in anti-climb paint. Another house, sold for £20 million, has metal bars on its windows.

Still, prices keep rising. Dryades, a mansion once owned by a Pakistani politician, sold for £12 million in 2007 and is now worth about £30 million. Heath Lodge, where fashion businessman Aristos Constantinou was murdered in 1984, is now worth £13 million, after being sold for £400,000 in the late 1970s.

Seeing these empty, falling-apart houses is hard for people who struggle to find a place to live in London, one of the world’s most expensive cities. A security guard on the avenue said it was frustrating to see so much empty space—enough for many people—going to waste.

Rich people from Nigeria and Saudi Arabia were some of the first to buy houses on this road near Hampstead Heath. Iranians came after the fall of the shah. Now, Chinese buyers are joining Russians and Kazakhs who have spent millions to get an address that estate agents say is as famous as the Champs Elysées or Rodeo Drive. Recently, two mansions were for sale for £65 million and £38 million, offering Italian marble, leather-covered elevators, and luxury panic rooms.

But in the gardens of the empty mansions, stone fountains are falling apart and lawns have turned into swamps. Inside, water drips through a large crystal chandelier onto a thick carpet that is rotting under a collapsed ceiling. Moss grows through broken bricks, and mirrored tiles are scattered in the bathroom. The swimming pool is filled with dirty water and flowers grow through the tiles. The wooden sauna is coming apart.

The Towers is the most dramatic ruin. It is a large mansion surrounded by many trees. Its big halls are now home to pigeons, and its walls are bright green with algae as water pours through three floors and drips into a huge, empty basement swimming pool. Unopened wooden boxes marked “bullet-proof glass” show that the previous owners were worried about security.

Today, very few people live full-time on The Bishops Avenue. A security guard outside one mansion said the owners were not there. Another, outside Royal Mansion, would not say if anyone was home. A staff member at another mansion only warned about the guard dogs. Magdy Adib Ishak-Hannah, a private healthcare businessman from Egypt worth £45 million, said he is one of the few people who live there all the time.

“It’s not a friendly place where you can talk to your neighbors,” he said. “Honestly, I have never seen my neighbors. Next door, a Saudi princess spent £35 million on a new house and I’ve never seen her. About three houses are lived in all the time, and half the properties are used for three to six months a year. The other half, I don’t know if anyone ever comes.”

These expensive, empty houses show that the world’s richest people see British property as an investment. One Hyde Park, an apartment building in Knightsbridge, is another example, where more than half the flats are registered as empty or second homes.

Still, people are now talking about building £5 million apartments instead of £50 million mansions to bring people back to the area.

Anil Varma, a local property developer, plans to rebuild one of the most valuable sites on the avenue as 20 apartments with a concierge, maid service, a 25-meter pool, spa, and cinema.

“If you build a big house and try to sell it for £30 million or £40 million, it won’t sell,” he said. “Local people won’t buy, so you have to find buyers from other countries.”

But the idea of using these empty houses to help solve the housing crisis is still far away. Andrew Harper, a local Conservative councillor, laughed when asked if some of the empty houses could become affordable homes. He said the land is too expensive.

“Very rich people own property there,” he said. “Sometimes they live in them and sometimes they don’t.”

For Tua Pittman, a master traditional navigator from Rarotonga in the Cook Islands, a canoe is much more than just a way to travel. He says, “The canoe is our island, the crew members are the community, and the navigator is the leader.” He also explains that the opposite is true: “An island is our canoe, the community are the crew members, and the politicians and leaders are the navigators. On a canoe, you are not just traveling from one place to another using the stars, the moon, the sun, and the birds. Navigation also means using leadership skills to guide your crew through life.”

It has been a busy week for the crews of the four sailing canoes since they arrived in Sydney for the start of the World Parks Congress. Tua’s journey started in the Cook Islands on September 25. The first part of the trip took the islanders to Samoa, then Fiji, Vanuatu, and the Gold Coast, before going south to Sydney. About 100 crew members took part in different parts of the journey, and they tried to use only traditional navigation methods. However, Tua said that sometimes they had to use modern navigation equipment to reach Australia in time for the Congress.

The official name of the trip is the Mua Voyage. It is a partnership between the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) Oceania Regional Office and five Pacific Island countries: Samoa, Tonga, New Zealand, the Cook Islands, and Fiji. The main goal of the 6,000-nautical-mile (11,000 km) journey was to bring a special message to the World Parks Congress.

Part of the message said: “We see signs of overuse. We no longer see fish and other sea animals in the same size, variety, or numbers as before. We see foreign fishing boats in our waters, taking our resources quickly. Our coral reefs, which are the best in the world, and our mangrove and wetland breeding areas are disappearing. Our ocean is huge but not endless. Growing world populations and the constant push for unsustainable development are making it harder for our ocean to support life.”

Even though the Pacific Islanders worked hard to bring their urgent message to the Congress, much of the last days of the marine part of the Congress were spent trying to set a new target for how much of the ocean should be protected in marine sanctuaries. According to the IUCN, in 2013, less than three percent of the world’s oceans were in marine protected areas, and less than one percent of that was ‘no take’ (meaning no fishing or taking resources). This was far below the target of 20-30% ‘no take’ areas set by the last World Parks Congress in South Africa in 2003.

Professor Callum Roberts, a leading marine scientist from the University of York, helped set the 20-30% target in 2003. But he said this is not enough. “The IUCN should now raise its target from 30 to 33%. New research shows that the old 30% target should now be higher. If we do less now, it will be very bad for our oceans.”

After difficult discussions, the World Parks Congress delegates agreed on a new plan that will greatly change global marine management. Instead of the old 20-30% goal, the IUCN’s new official position is to “urgently increase the ocean area that is well managed in systems of marine protected areas or other strong conservation measures by 2030. These should include strictly protected areas that make up at least 30% of each marine habitat and protect both biodiversity and ecosystem services.”

Tua Pittman was very happy that a strong decision about the world’s oceans was made at the Congress. “It feels like a big reward for all the effort we made to be here and to be heard. Hearing about this decision is fantastic. It’s a step in the right direction.” He says that while traditional navigation uses things like the sun, moon, and stars that do not change, other effects of environmental damage are becoming clearer when traveling across the Pacific.

He said he was 55 years old and, in his lifetime, it has already become much harder to catch fish in the open ocean. He also said that pollution is getting worse, especially as the canoes get close to big cities like Sydney. The effects of climate change are already starting to seriously affect Pacific Islanders. “The decisions of big countries have two, three, or four times more impact on small countries than on large, developed nations. Many times, people do not even know where our islands are, and from the view of a traditional navigator, our people are very worried because decisions made far away affect our homes.”

The Mua Voyage was a huge task, said Tua. It took years of preparation and planning, and it was very important to the voyagers that the world listened to their message and took action. He said that leaders of rich countries need to think more like traditional navigators, who know their boats are very small in a huge sea. Most importantly, Tua says politicians must find a new way to avoid the coming environmental crises that are starting to affect small island nations. “The world needs to find a different path.”

Dame Sally Davies, the Chief Medical Officer for England, has compared the problem of antibiotic resistance to the dangers of international terrorism. This may sound extreme, but the threat is actually even greater. Every year, many more people die from antibiotic-resistant bacteria than from terrorist attacks.

It is hard to measure the total global effect of antibiotic resistance for all bacteria, but the World Health Organization says that, for tuberculosis alone, more than 150,000 people die each year because the bacteria are resistant to many drugs. Antibiotic resistance is not just a future risk; it is a serious problem right now.

In the last hundred years, our lives have changed a lot. At the start of the 1900s, men in the UK lived about 47 years and women about 50 years, mostly because many children died young from infections. About one third of all deaths were in children under five, mainly because of infectious diseases.

Today, a child born in Britain has a better than one in four chance of living to 100 years old. This is thanks to public health systems, vaccines, and antibiotics. These tools help us prevent and treat diseases caused by germs, and they have helped us win the fight against many illnesses.

We have also improved survival in places like intensive care units, where I chose to work. In these areas, antibiotic-resistant bacteria are most common. Strong antibiotics are used often to treat very sick patients. These drugs kill most bacteria, but the ones that survive are tough and learn how to avoid being killed by antibiotics.

When I became a doctor in the late 1990s, I learned about Methicillin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (MRSA), a type of bacteria that cannot be killed by methicillin or any other penicillin. We had a few special drugs, like vancomycin and teicoplanin, to fight it. These were our last options, but over time, more bacteria became resistant, and new types of resistance appeared. Drugs we rarely used before became common, and new last-resort drugs had to be developed. We got used to this ongoing battle between us and the bacteria.

However, things have been getting worse. In hospitals and doctors’ offices, we have overused antibiotics, often giving them when they were not needed. Even worse, antibiotics have been used in farming, added to animal feed to help livestock grow. We thought antibiotics would always work for us, and we believed drug companies would keep making new ones.

But this is no longer true. New, stronger bacteria have appeared. The vancomycin we used to treat MRSA stopped working. Vancomycin Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus (VRSA) was found in hospitals. Other bacteria, like those in the gut called enterobacteria, also became resistant to vancomycin. Now, infections with very resistant bacteria are common, and drug companies are not making enough new antibiotics. It is getting harder to create new drugs that work against these bacteria. For every new drug, bacteria quickly find a way to survive. All the easy solutions have already been tried.

Antibiotics are now expensive to develop, used only for short times, and quickly become useless because bacteria adapt. Because of this, drug companies do not have much reason to make new antibiotics.

As soon as antibiotics became common in the 1940s, bacteria started to become resistant. At first, these cases were rare and did not seem important. But now, they are a normal part of medicine. Less than 100 years after penicillin was discovered, we are starting to lose the fight.

Since the first deaths from MRSA in healthy children in the US in 1998, the number of deaths from MRSA in the US has grown to tens of thousands each year, more than the number of deaths from AIDS. Bacterial resistance is now everywhere in hospitals. This is a unique and serious war. We need to change how we prescribe antibiotics and use them less in farming. Drug companies also need to be encouraged to develop new antibiotics, even if they are not very profitable.

During my career, antibiotic resistance has changed from being rare to being a huge problem. If we do not act, we could return to the days before antibiotics, when many more people died from infections. We must be brave and protect the progress we have made in fighting diseases caused by bacteria. Losing this advantage would be terrible.

People from all over Rwanda, and even from parts of Burundi, travel to the southern town of Butare to visit a small shop called Inzozi Nziza, which means Sweet Dreams. They come to try something new—ice cream—which most of them have never tasted before.

Inzozi Nziza is the first ice cream shop in Rwanda. Here, customers can buy ice cream in sweet cream, passion fruit, strawberry, and pineapple flavors. They can add toppings like fresh fruit, honey, chocolate chips, and granola. The shop also sells black tea and coffee.

The shop’s sign says “ice cream, coffee, dreams.” The manager, Louise Ingabire, says the shop is making people curious about ice cream and is also “changing lives.” She explains, “Ice cream is important. Some Rwandans like it, but it is still new. We need to tell more people that they will enjoy it.”

The shop’s motto is true—it can help people achieve their dreams. Ingabire, who is 27 years old, says, “Before, I did not have a job. I just stayed at home. Now, I have hope for the future. I am earning money and can help my family.”

Butare has 89,600 people and is 135 kilometers south of Rwanda’s capital, Kigali. The town is home to the National University of Rwanda. Inzozi Nziza has become a popular place for students who want to relax and enjoy something cool and different.

Kalisa Migendo, a 24-year-old agriculture student, says, “It brings people together. If you want to meet a friend, a girl, or a boy, you come to Inzozi Nziza for ice cream.”

Most of the shop’s ingredients come from local sources, and the milk is from a depot in nearby Nyanza. The vanilla beans and cocoa are imported.

The shop was started by Odile Gakire Katese, a theatre director. She met Alexis Miesen and Jennie Dundas, who started Blue Marble Ice Cream in Brooklyn, New York. Together, they opened Inzozi Nziza in 2010.

Miesen says, “Katese thought an ice cream shop could help people feel better and rebuild hope and family traditions.”

At first, Miesen and Dundas owned the shop together with the staff. The shop is a cooperative and non-profit. They did not set financial goals, but after 18 months, they gave their shares to the women working there, who had shown they could run the business well.

Fatuma Ndangiza, deputy chief executive of the Rwanda Governance Board, says the shop’s success is not unusual. “Most small businesses are run by women, but in big business, there are still few women. Women are new to big business. But more women are becoming entrepreneurs, both in Kigali and outside.”

Although ice cream is new in Rwanda, Ndangiza likes the idea of the shop. “I think it’s great. It takes skill and changes how people think, because selling and eating ice cream is not part of our culture. It is interesting to bring something new to the market and learn how to make it.”

The shop in Butare employs nine women. In their free time, they practice with Ingoma Nshya, Rwanda’s first and only all-female drumming group, which Katese started ten years ago.

The drummers are Hutu and Tutsi women, some of whom survived the 1994 genocide, when almost a million Tutsis and moderate Hutus were killed.

Some members of Ingoma Nshya are widows or orphans. Others were affected by the genocide in different ways.

Ingabire says that, in the past, Rwandan women were not allowed to drum, and many people thought the drums were too heavy for women. “But drumming brings people together.”

Ingabire’s father, two siblings, and many cousins were killed in the genocide. She says, “Some of us are survivors; some know someone who was killed. When I drum with the group, it gives me strength because we are still alive and surviving.”

The popular shop is featured in a documentary by Rob and Lisa Fruchtman, who are brother and sister filmmakers. The film, called Sweet Dreams, tells the story of how the women built a better future after the genocide and also shows the female drummers.

The film has been shown in more than twelve countries, including the US, UK, and several African countries. It will be shown in Rwanda in 2014. Lisa Fruchtman, who won an Academy Award for film editing in 1984, says, “We think the film is about strength, hope, courage, creativity, and the ability to change your own life.”

More than one third of all women in the world – 35.6% – will experience physical or sexual violence in their lives, usually from a male partner. This information comes from the first big study on this topic by the World Health Organization (WHO). The report shows that violence against women by their partners is very common, with 30% of women being attacked by their partners. It also says that 38% of murders of women are done by their intimate partners.

Dr. Margaret Chan, the director general of WHO, said, “These findings show that violence against women is a global health problem that is very serious.” She also said that health systems around the world need to do more to help women who experience violence.

The highest rates of violence against women are in Africa, where almost half of all women – 45.6% – will suffer physical or sexual violence. In low- and middle-income countries in Europe, the rate is 27.2%. However, richer countries are not always safer for women. In high-income countries, about one third of women (32.7%) will experience violence at some point in their lives. Of the women who suffer violence, 42% get injuries, which may bring them to hospitals or clinics. The report says that this is often the first time that violence at home is noticed and the woman can get help. Violence has a strong effect on women’s health. Some women come to the hospital with broken bones, while others have problems related to pregnancy or mental health.

The two WHO reports – one about how common violence is, and the other giving advice to healthcare workers on how to help women – were written by Dr. Claudia Garcia-Moreno, a specialist in gender and health at WHO, and Professor Charlotte Watts, an expert in gender, violence, and health from the London School of Hygiene and Tropical Medicine.

Dr. Garcia-Moreno said, “For the first time, we have compared data from all over the world about partner violence, sexual violence by non-partners, and the effects of this violence on health.” These effects include HIV and other sexually transmitted infections, depression, women drinking alcohol, unwanted pregnancies, and babies born with low weight.

There are differences in the rates of violence against women in different parts of the world, but Garcia-Moreno said, “In every region we looked at, the rates are too high.” Even in high-income countries, 23.2% of women will suffer physical or sexual violence from a partner, according to data from 81 countries. The worldwide number for women attacked by partners is 30%.

More sexual assaults and rapes by acquaintances or strangers are reported in high-income countries than in other places. The report says that 12.6% of women in rich countries will be sexually attacked by someone who is not their partner, which is higher than the rate in Africa (11.9%). However, data about these crimes is not collected well in all regions.

The authors say that their earlier research shows that women with better education and those who have jobs are less likely to suffer violence, but this is not true everywhere. Professor Watts said that society’s views need to change. “What does society think about violence against women?” she asked. “In some places, it is not accepted, but not everywhere.”

Dr. Garcia-Moreno said, “I think these numbers are a warning for all of us to pay more attention to this problem.” She said that in the last ten years, people have started to see this as a serious issue, but “it is a complex problem. We don’t have a vaccine or a pill to fix it.”

The new WHO guidelines recommend that healthcare workers should be trained to recognize signs of domestic violence and sexual assault, but they do not suggest asking every woman who comes to a clinic if she has suffered violence.

“But if you see a woman coming back many times with injuries that are not explained, you should ask about domestic violence,” said Garcia-Moreno. “When I was in medical school, we did not learn about this. Later, when I was talking to women, sometimes I could tell something else was wrong, but I did not know it could be domestic violence. Now, I think I would handle these situations very differently.”

The auction of a Banksy mural that disappeared from a shop wall in north London was suddenly stopped just before it was supposed to be sold. The artwork, called Slave Labour, shows a child making Union Flag decorations and is seen as a comment on last year’s diamond jubilee. It was expected to sell for about $700,000 at a street and contemporary art auction in Florida.

Frederic Thut, the owner of Fine Arts Auction Miami, would not say who was selling the artwork or how it came to be for sale in his gallery. He announced that Slave Labour and another Banksy piece were removed from the auction. He did not give a reason, but community leaders in Haringey, who had campaigned to stop the sale after the artwork was taken from a Poundland shop in Wood Green, were very happy.

Alan Strickland, a Haringey councillor, said, “One of our two demands was that it doesn’t sell and the other was that we get it back again, so we’re halfway there.” He said he would write to the auction house quickly to find out what happened and what will happen next. He was pleased that the people of Wood Green had made a difference in the US.

Claire Kober, Leader of Haringey Council, wrote to Arts Council England and the Mayor of Miami to ask them to stop the sale, but it seems the gallery owners decided to remove the artwork after talking to their lawyers. The FBI would not say if they were asked to investigate.

A few hours after the auction ended, the auction house said in a short statement that it had convinced the owners of the two Banksy artworks to remove them from the sale. “Although there are no legal issues with selling the Banksy pieces, FAAM convinced its sellers to withdraw them from the auction.”

About 30 people came to the auction, which had 106 artworks for sale in Miami’s Wynwood area. The auction lasted three hours, and other artworks sold for more than their starting prices.

Some people said the auction house was selling stolen property, but Thut said earlier that the seller, a “well known collector,” was the rightful owner and the sale was legal. He also said his gallery had received many emails and phone calls from the UK, some of which were rude, but he believed selling the pieces would help protect them.

The second Banksy artwork, called Wet Dog, was made in 2007 and taken from a wall in Bethlehem. It was thought to be worth up to $800,000. It disappeared from the auction house’s online catalogue on Saturday afternoon, but Slave Labour was still listed until the auction started at 3pm.

Thut said the two artworks, given to him by different owners who were not British, were important for street art and should go to buyers who care about art and its protection. He said he would keep the seller’s identity private. “We respect our clients and their confidentiality. It’s not our decision to have the Banksy returned. We only sell it. We do not control it.”

A spokesperson for Poundland said they did not know who removed the large artwork from the side of their shop in Turnpike Lane. Lawyers for the building’s owner, Wood Green Investments Ltd, would not say if they were involved.

Banksy has not commented on the Slave Labour situation, but in the past he has spoken against people selling his art, like before a 2011 auction in New York where five of his pieces did not sell.

Stephan Keszler, the dealer behind that auction, thinks selling Banksy’s works without his permission is allowed. “He does something on other people’s property without asking. The owner of the property can do whatever they want with it,” Keszler said.

On an important day at Liverpool’s Anglican Cathedral, the families of the 96 people who died at Hillsborough football stadium focused on one main idea: the truth. This word was used badly by The Sun newspaper, which published stories given to them by the South Yorkshire Police. These stories wrongly blamed the innocent victims for the disaster, instead of the police.

Margaret Aspinall, whose 18-year-old son James died at the FA Cup semi-final between Liverpool and Nottingham Forest, said the families had to fight for 23 years to find out the truth. Aspinall, who leads the Hillsborough Family Support Group, said that even though their loss would never go away, she was happy with the clear and strong apology from David Cameron for the serious mistakes made at Hillsborough.

The Hillsborough Independent Panel looked at 450,000 documents from the police, Sheffield Wednesday football club, and other groups involved. The panel wrote a 395-page report that showed the official failures and proved the victims and football fans were not to blame.

Some facts about the disaster and the police’s attempts to blame others were already known. But the report showed even more clearly how the police tried to avoid responsibility and wrongly blamed the fans. The panel found that the Chief Constable, Peter Wright, led a campaign to say that drunk or ticketless fans caused the disaster. The police even tested the victims’ blood for alcohol, which the panel said was a very unusual decision with no good reason. If alcohol was found, the police checked if the victims had criminal records.

The report, mainly written by Professor Phil Scraton from Queen’s University, Belfast, and agreed by all eight experts, found there was no proof of high levels of drunkenness, people without tickets, or violence among Liverpool fans.

The report also found that while the families were suffering, Wright was meeting with his police federation in a restaurant to plan a “defence” and a “strong story.” Constable Paul Middup, the Secretary of the South Yorkshire Police Federation, said at the meeting that the Chief Constable could not tell the truth himself but allowed the secretary to do what he wanted, with support from many senior officers.

This meeting happened just four days after the disaster. On that day, The Sun published its headline “The Truth” using lies from four senior South Yorkshire police officers. Middup was encouraged to continue blaming Liverpool fans for supposed drunkenness and bad behaviour and to spread this message to the police force.

The panel’s report supported the claim made in parliament that senior South Yorkshire police officers changed junior officers’ statements to create a “black propaganda unit.” These statements, which were supposed to be official police accounts, were changed to remove criticism of the police and to focus on supposed bad behaviour by fans. The panel found that 116 out of 164 statements were changed to remove or change comments that made the South Yorkshire police look bad.

The police said they only removed “opinions” from the statements, but the panel was sure that the real reason was to remove criticism of the police. Professor Scraton said, “It was done to remove criticism of the police.”

This false information did not convince the original inquiry, which decided in August 1989 that the police stories about fan drunkenness and bad behaviour were not true, and criticized the police for making these claims.
