Many people told me they used to secretly colour when their children were in bed. Now, it’s normal for adults to colour. These are books for adults. The art in my books is very detailed.”

Basford, who lives in Aberdeenshire, was surprised by the reaction since she released Secret Garden in 2013. “I had a children’s book planned, but I told the publisher I wanted to make one for adults. It wasn’t a trend then. I made the first book, and they said, ‘Let’s do it.’ I just wanted to make a book I would like. So it’s a big surprise to see how popular it has become.”

She is now working on a third book. Michael O’Mara, which already has 17 adult colouring books, will have 22 by May. New books will include The Classic Comic Colouring Book and The Typography Colouring Book. “It’s a huge trend and it’s not slowing down,” said McLaughlin. She added that people who buy these books like to show their coloured pictures to others.

“The pictures are everywhere on Twitter and Instagram. People are very proud of them because they are so detailed,” she said. “You don’t need to be an artist, but what you make is special. People send us pictures of their coloured pages, framed and laminated. The demand is huge. I think people are taking their children’s pictures off the fridge and putting up their own.”

Not many exercise classes have a tea break in the middle, but Margaret Allen’s class does. After a gentle warm-up and some lively exercises, the 93-year-old great-grandmother lets her group have a cup of tea and a short rest.

Some of the eight people in the class look like they need the break more than others. Allen herself, wearing a thick turquoise shirt, navy blue waistcoat, black trousers, and comfortable shoes, does not look tired at all. Even though she has a very painful trapped nerve in one leg and a knee that needs replacing, she seems like she could keep going for hours.

Usually, people say you should not eat just before or during exercise. But when I visit Allen’s class at a church hall in Saltburn-by-the-Sea near Middlesbrough, slices of fruitcake are handed out during the break. The cake was made for Allen’s recent birthday by her 89-year-old sister, Joan, who is known in the area as the “scone queen of Saltburn.”

The women have just finished their cake when Allen stands up again and leads the group in a lively Scottish dance with lots of toe pointing and leg kicking. After forty-five minutes, the class ends.

Allen, who used to volunteer with the Red Cross, has been leading classes in this seaside town for 45 years. She was not very sporty at school, but during the Second World War, she started playing the piano for a fitness class—just to have something to do during the blackouts. She took over the class in her 40s when the old teacher retired. At its busiest, Allen’s class had more than 18 regular members, each paying £1 per class. Now, there are fewer people. During the tea break, the women talk about a funeral they went to that week for one of the younger members, who died at 68 from motor neurone disease.

Allen is the oldest in the group, followed by her sister. The youngest is 60-year-old Jean Cunion, who says the group helped her when her mother died. She is a bit embarrassed to say she is probably the least fit in the group. “I remember, the first time I came, Margaret said: ‘Who’s that huffing and puffing?’ and I had to say it was me.” Ruth Steere, 76, is amazed that Allen always knows what the group is doing, even with her back turned: “She always tells us if we make a mistake. She’s very good at noticing everything.”

Allen loves dancing but has never had formal training as a fitness teacher. She makes up her own routines using five tapes from the BBC’s first fitness expert, Eileen Fowler, who died in 2000 at age 93—the same age Allen is now. Allen believes her good health comes from staying busy, especially after her husband Joe died in 1997. She started writing poetry when she was 80.

“I write poems about everything. I write a lot. I just can’t stop,” she says. A few days after the interview, she calls me to read a short poem she wrote about the joys of exercise. One of the class members, 84-year-old former teacher Winnie Robertson, thinks the secret to staying fit is to keep active: “Use it or lose it, that’s what I say.”

Allen still plays the piano and gives speeches. She is president of the Women’s Fellowship at the local Methodist church and is one of three people over 90 at the Scrabble club of the University of the Third Age. She took a computer course at 88 and tried to use the internet, but it did not work out.

Allen admits that getting older is not easy. She reads me a few lines from a poem she wrote called “That Beast Called Age.” She happily remembers a doctor who saw her for the first time a few years ago and said she could not possibly be older than 78. “I said, ‘Thank you, doctor. You can go now.’”

She also has a simple view about weight gain: “I just think people shouldn’t eat too much. When someone says, ‘Oh, I can’t lose weight,’ I say: ‘Sellotape.’” She pretends to tape her mouth shut. “I said this just the other day to a big man. My motto is: everything in moderation.”

Earlier in 2013, Allen was watching the news and saw a woman getting the British Empire Medal. I think she means Margaret Chartwood from Horley, who got the award in January at age 77. “She was saying: ‘I’m 80 and I’m the oldest fitness instructor in the country!’ I was thinking: ‘No, you’re not.’ But I won’t be writing to Buckingham Palace.”

It started with a fake scallop, but now a menu scandal is affecting some of Japan’s most famous hotels and department stores. This scandal could damage the international reputation of Japan’s famous food.

The problem began when a luxury hotel chain admitted it lied about where its menu ingredients came from. Since then, Japanese news has reported almost every day about similar problems at restaurants in well-known hotels and department stores.

The scandal started when the Hankyu-Hanshin hotel chain in Osaka said it had given false descriptions for many menu items at some of its restaurants from 2006 to October 2013. About 78,000 customers were affected. One of the main problems was a red salmon “caviar” dish that was actually made with cheaper flying fish eggs.

The hotel group’s president, Hiroshi Desaki, tried to calm people by saying he would take a 20% pay cut and other executives would take a 10% cut. However, this did not make customers feel better. A few days later, Desaki resigned and admitted the hotel group had “betrayed our customers,” but said they did not mean to trick anyone. One of the hotel’s top chefs also refused to accept a government medal of honour.

So far, the company has given refunds to more than 10,000 customers, paying back 20 million yen. The total amount is expected to reach 110 million yen.

This scandal is similar to the horsemeat scandal in the UK and has now spread to other well-known food companies in Japan. Like in the UK, no one has become sick from eating the wrongly labelled food, but people are still very angry. For example, customers who thought they ate expensive kuruma shrimp found out they actually ate the much cheaper black tiger shrimp.

The first case was almost missed. The Prince Hotel in Tokyo admitted the problem after a customer wrote online that a “scallop” dish was actually made with a cheaper type of shellfish. The hotel checked and corrected more than 50 menu items at many of its restaurants. This report made Hankyu-Hanshin and other hotels admit they also tricked customers who thought they were paying for high-quality ingredients.

The Hotel Okura chain, which has had guests like Barack Obama, admitted to many problems, such as injecting beef with fat to make it juicier and calling tomatoes “organic” when they were not.

“We deeply apologize for betraying the expectations and trust of our clients,” the hotel said in a statement.

The list of fake ingredients keeps growing: orange juice from cartons sold as freshly squeezed, Mont Blanc desserts with Korean chestnuts instead of French ones, store-bought chocolate cream called homemade, and imported beef sold as expensive wagyu.

Even the government’s top spokesman, Yoshihide Suga, spoke about the scandal. He said, “These incidents have happened one after another, and this wrong labelling has made consumers lose trust. These are clearly cover-ups.”

The scandal has come at a bad time. Japan is trying to convince South Korea and other countries to lift bans on Japanese food imports after the Fukushima nuclear accident. At the same time, UNESCO is thinking about adding Japanese cuisine to its cultural heritage list.

One local newspaper wrote, “Japan’s proud food culture in tears,” and the popular Yomiuri Shimbun said it was “shocked by the industry’s lack of morals.” The newspaper also worried that the scandal could “harm the credibility of brand Japan, products and services, which are praised by foreign countries and tourists for their safety and security.”

Experts say the global financial crisis in 2008 forced luxury hotels to cut costs, but they still wanted to attract customers with detailed menu descriptions. Hiroshi Tomozawa, a hotel and restaurant consultant, told Kyodo News, “Menu descriptions were made to match what customers wanted. When hotels couldn’t get the ingredients listed on the menu, they just used food from other places.”

Even though their reputations are damaged, the hotels and restaurants involved probably will not face legal action. Menus are not covered by the agricultural standards law or by a new food labelling law that will start in 2015. The only law that can be used is one that bans misleading descriptions of goods and services.

The biggest problem for the industry will be Japan’s careful and demanding customers. In a 2009 survey by an online restaurant guide, 72% of people said the origin of ingredients was the most important thing when choosing dishes from a menu, followed by calorie and nutrition information.

Author Philip Pullman says that illegal downloading is just like stealing someone’s wallet. In an article for Index on Censorship, Pullman, who is the president of the Society of Authors, strongly supports copyright laws. He criticizes people who download music or books without paying. 

Pullman writes that technology is so impressive that people forget how wrong it is to steal an artist’s work. He says it is shocking that people can steal from artists and not be punished. He believes stealing music or books online is the same as stealing a wallet from someone’s pocket.

Pullman’s article was published after music industry leaders met with British Prime Minister David Cameron at Downing Street to talk about web piracy. Pullman, who wrote the His Dark Materials trilogy, says that authors and musicians often work for years in poverty and are not well known. When they finally succeed, people take away their chance to earn money by downloading their work for free. He says, “The rule is simple and does not change with technology: if we want to enjoy someone’s work, we should pay for it.”

Pullman’s article is part of a discussion with Cathy Casserly, the head of Creative Commons. Creative Commons gives creators more control over how their work is shared. Casserly says there are problems with copyright laws, which were made before the digital age. She writes that copyright laws stop people from sharing, improving, and mixing each other’s work in ways that were not possible when the laws were made.

Casserly says artists should find new ways to share and make money from their work. She quotes science fiction writer Cory Doctorow, who said, “My problem is not piracy, it’s obscurity,” meaning it is worse to be unknown than to have your work copied.

Index on Censorship agrees with Casserly. The magazine’s editor, Rachael Jolley, says that current copyright laws do not work well in the digital age and may make ordinary people into criminals. She says we need new ways for artists, writers, and musicians to earn money from their work.

The debate about illegal downloading is very active, and the problem is very big. According to Ofcom, the UK’s communications regulator, between November 2012 and January 2013, people in the UK illegally downloaded 280 million music tracks, 52 million TV shows, 29 million films, 18 million ebooks, and 7 million software or game files.

Ofcom says that 18% of internet users over age 12 admit they have recently downloaded content illegally, and 9% say they are afraid of being caught. Pullman writes that it is still amazing how easy and fast it is to get music as MP3 downloads.

After the Downing Street meeting, Prime Minister Cameron chose Conservative MP Mike Weatherley to advise him on this issue. A spokesman for the BPI, the music industry group, said that Weatherley strongly supports copyright and the artists it protects. They hope that Weatherley and the Prime Minister will help the UK’s intellectual property office support copyright laws.

When Larry Pizzi, a long-time bicycle industry leader, first heard about electric bikes almost 20 years ago, he asked, “Why would anyone want to ruin a bike by putting a motor and batteries on it?” Many traditional bike fans still wonder the same thing. Bike shops have been slow to sell e-bikes, even though they have existed since the late 1990s. E-bike sales in the US have been low.

Pizzi, who is now the CEO of Currie Technologies, the top e-bike seller in the US, thinks this will soon change. Other people in the industry agree. Well-known brands like Trek, Raleigh, and Specialized now sell electric bikes, and they believe the market will grow quickly.

“We’re about to see e-bikes become popular with everyone,” Pizzi said. “More companies are joining the e-bike market every month.”

The US is different from other countries when it comes to e-bikes. In 2014, almost 32 million e-bikes were sold, mostly in China, where people use them mainly for transportation. E-bikes are also popular in many parts of Europe. They are common in the Netherlands and Switzerland. German postal workers use them, and BMW sells an e-bike for about $3,000.

Electric bikes are not the same as motorcycles or mopeds, which use only motor power. E-bikes are bicycles that you can pedal with or without help from an electric motor. Riding an e-bike feels like riding a normal bike with a strong wind behind you; the motor helps you go faster or climb hills, but you still pedal. Unlike mopeds, e-bikes are usually allowed on bike paths and cannot go faster than 20 mph.

There is no official number for how many e-bikes are sold in the US. Estimates say between 50,000 and 175,000 are sold each year. This is similar to the number of electric cars sold in the US—118,000 in 2014. However, while many people know about electric cars like the Nissan Leaf, Chevy Volt, and Tesla, few people have heard of e-bike companies like Currie, Pedego, or ElectroBike.

To succeed in the US, the e-bike business must overcome legal, cultural, and financial problems. E-bikes are banned in some states, like New York, but the law is not always enforced. Traditional bike shop owners and workers do not like putting motors on bikes, partly because it makes the bikes heavier. Some e-bikes weigh almost 30 kg.

E-bikes are also expensive. Some cheap models cost as little as $700, but Court Rye, who runs ElectricBikeReview.com, says you should expect to pay at least $1,500 for a good e-bike with a good battery. The best models cost more than twice that.

E-bike companies say they can solve these problems. E-bike technology, especially batteries, is getting better. “Batteries are getting smaller, lighter, more reliable, and last longer,” says Don DiCostanza, founder and CEO of Pedego, an e-bike company and store.

Big companies like Bosch, a German electronics company, and Shimano, a top bicycle gear maker, are joining the e-bike business. This should help bike shops accept e-bikes. “This has really caught the attention of bike dealers,” says Currie’s Larry Pizzi. Pedego and ElectroBike are not waiting for bike shops to change; they are opening their own stores. At the same time, people are working to change laws so e-bikes can be used everywhere.

Most importantly, as more cities build bike lanes and other cycling infrastructure, more people are riding bikes to work. The US Census Bureau reported in 2014 that the number of people biking to work grew from about 488,000 in 2000 to 786,000 in 2012. This was the biggest percentage increase of any way of commuting. E-bikes make commuting easier and more enjoyable by helping with hills, wind, tiredness, and sweat.

Most customers are “older baby boomers who want to feel like they did when they were kids,” says Pedego’s Don DiCostanza. “The main reason they stopped riding bikes was because of hills.” Pedego has opened almost 60 stores in the US and has sold bikes to tour companies in San Francisco and Washington, DC.

ElectroBike, which has 30 stores in Mexico, opened its first US store in Venice Beach, California, in autumn 2014 and hopes to have 25 US stores in a year. CEO Craig Anderson says, “We want to help reduce traffic, lower our carbon footprint, and promote a healthy lifestyle.” He tells customers, “Ride this once and try not to smile.”

New companies like Pedego and ElectroBike will have to compete with big companies like Trek and Currie. In 2012, Currie was bought by the Accell Group, a public company from the Netherlands that leads the e-bike market in Europe. Accell owns the Raleigh brand and Haibike, a well-known German e-bike.

“Accell has high hopes for e-bikes in North America,” says Currie’s Larry Pizzi. “While baby boomers are still very important, we see that many younger people are using e-bikes for transportation instead of cars.”

Accell’s Yuba brand even sells a cargo bike with a stronger motor and a rear rack. “You can carry two children,” says Pizzi. “You can carry 45 kg of shopping. It’s like a minivan alternative.”

Is this the time when streaming becomes truly popular?
According to the International Federation of the Phonographic Industry (IFPI), only 41 million people around the world used music streaming services in 2014. Streaming is the fastest-growing way for the music business to make money, but it is still not very common. Also, many of these users get streaming as part of deals with their mobile phone companies, so it is not clear how many people really use the service. Apple is very good at taking things that already exist—like downloads (iTunes), digital music players (the iPod), and smartphones (the iPhone)—and making them popular with everyone. Recently, leaked information showed that Apple wants to reach 100 million subscribers. If each subscriber pays $120 a year, Apple would make $12 billion every year. For comparison, all recorded music in the world was worth just under $15 billion in 2014. Apple is good at making products popular, but even for Apple, this is a big challenge.

Is this the end of downloading?
The iTunes Store started in 2003 (2004 in Europe) when many people were illegally downloading MP3s. Apple convinced people to pay for downloads and became the biggest company in this area, with about 70% of the market. Downloads still make up the largest part of digital music income, with 52% of all digital music money in 2014, according to IFPI. Apple is the biggest music seller in the world. However, download sales in the UK reached their highest point in 2013 at £283 million and dropped to £249 million in 2014. Download sales also started to fall in the US in 2013. Because of this, Apple bought Beats in 2014 for $3 billion, not just to sell expensive headphones, but also to move from selling music (downloads) to letting people listen to music without owning it (streaming). Apple and the music industry cannot stop selling downloads yet, so streaming and downloading will both continue under the Apple brand. Streaming is the future, while downloads are slowly becoming less popular. Most people like music but do not want to pay $120 a year to listen to it. They prefer to buy a song or album from time to time. In the UK in 2014, the average music buyer spent only £39.52 a year. It is very hard, even for Apple, to make people spend three times more on music each year.

Has Apple Connect made Apple the most artist-friendly service?
Apple tried before to make a platform for artists on iTunes called Ping, but it failed. Apple Connect is different. It is a mix of YouTube, Facebook, and SoundCloud, where artists can post music, videos, photos, and more on their profile pages. This is very modern. Apple is a big company and treats music as “art,” not just “content.” Because of this, Apple has good relationships with the music industry and with artists. Most artists like Apple. In comparison, Spotify has been criticized by artists like Thom Yorke from Radiohead and Taylor Swift. Apple seems kinder and more supportive. There is a feeling that big changes are coming, and Apple wants to be on the right side when it happens.

Where are the artist exclusives?
This will be interesting when the service starts. Getting exclusive rights to big albums will be very important for streaming services. Spotify paid a lot of money to have Led Zeppelin and Metallica only on their service. Apple has watched this and learned. Apple already has AC/DC and the Beatles’ music only for download on iTunes, but it is not clear if these artists will agree to streaming. Apple also got the surprise Beyoncé album in 2013 before anyone else, so it will want more deals like that. There are rumors that Apple wants exclusive rights to the new Adele album.

Giving iTunes the only right to sell an album as a download was not a big risk for artists because iTunes controls most of the download market. But doing this for streaming is different. Also, streaming now counts for the album charts in places like the UK and US. Artists still care about the charts and do not want to limit their fans by being on only one service.

Is this going to kill Spotify?
Some people say Apple Music will destroy other services like Spotify. But it is not that simple. Apple is joining a market where other companies have been working for many years and have more experience. Apple has a lot to learn. The winner will not be the company with the best service, but the one with the most money. Apple’s competitors started earlier, but they are losing a lot of money. For example, Spotify lost €93.1 million in 2013. Apple, on the other hand, became the most profitable company in history in 2015, with $178 billion in the bank. If Apple Music loses money, Apple will not keep it for long, but the company will try hard to beat the competition before stopping.

When we talk about climate change, we often focus only on the problem and forget about the many solutions that exist. These solutions include recycling more, reducing emissions, and finding better options instead of using plastic, air conditioning, smartphones, and fast fashion.

The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change recently met in Copenhagen to share its latest report about how climate change is affecting the world and how fast it is happening. Climate change is now seen on every continent, and we need to work harder to reduce emissions so that the problem does not get worse. In Copenhagen, they talked not only about the risks and problems but also about the solutions.

To highlight what can be done, the Sustainia Award, led by Arnold Schwarzenegger, celebrated ten top sustainability solutions used in 84 countries. These solutions covered areas like food, fashion, energy, transport, education, and health. The awards showed that there are real alternatives to the negative future we often hear about, and they made sustainability real for inventors, investors, consumers, and leaders in different fields and regions.

For example, in California, people are now making plastics from greenhouse gases, and these plastics are as good and as cheap as normal plastics made from oil. In Switzerland, there is a better system for recycling and reusing old clothes and shoes, now used in over 60 countries. In Canada, smartphones are making bike-sharing easier.

Each of the ten projects offered a special solution to sustainability problems, but the Nigerian project called Wecyclers won the Sustainia Award in 2014, chosen by Arnold Schwarzenegger and the other judges.

Wecyclers helps poor communities earn money from the waste in their streets. They use cargo bicycles to collect and recycle waste in Lagos. Families can trade their garbage for goods using a point system through SMS messages. Recycling companies buy the sorted waste from Wecyclers and turn it into products like mattresses, pillows, and trash bags. Wecyclers helps solve local waste problems, as only about 40% of Lagos’s rubbish is collected. Across Africa, only 46% of city waste is collected, according to the World Bank. More than 5,000 households have joined Wecyclers, and there are plans to expand to other cities in Nigeria.

People often think that solutions to climate change are only high-tech ideas that cut emissions or build new systems. But to solve all the different problems, we need many different solutions. Sustainability is not just about lowering emissions; it is also about using our natural resources wisely and living healthier lives. Some solutions may be simple but can still make a big difference for whole communities.

With many solutions for many challenges, we should focus more on the positive part of the story that inspires people and encourages action for the important changes we need.

Most of BB King’s music was blues, and his best work was in this style. However, he was always open to playing other kinds of music and was friendly and skilled when working with different musicians and cultures. Some people say it is too early to call him “the last of the bluesmen,” but it is hard to think of any future blues artist who will have as much influence as King. He inspired thousands of musicians and millions of fans during his 65-year career.

Riley B King (the “B” did not stand for anything) was born near Itta Bena, Mississippi. He grew up as an African-American farm worker, which gave him few opportunities. He slowly overcame these difficulties by learning guitar from a family friend and singing with a gospel group. In his early twenties, he moved to Memphis.

After a few years, he played regularly at a bar in West Memphis, Arkansas. He also worked as a radio DJ in Memphis. He was called “The Beale Street Blues Boy,” which was later shortened to “Blues Boy King” and then to “BB.” After recording once in 1949 for a Nashville label, King started recording for Modern Records in 1950.

His first big hit was in 1952 with a new version of “Three O’Clock Blues,” which was number one on the R&B chart for 15 weeks. This was the first of many hits, including “Please Love Me,” “You Upset Me Baby,” and “Sweet Sixteen.” On these and many other songs, most of which he wrote himself, King created a style that was new but also respected blues traditions. He often talked about the musicians who influenced him, especially T-Bone Walker.

“I’ve tried my best to get that sound,” he told Guitar Player magazine. “I came pretty close but never quite got it.” In 2001, he said, “If T-Bone Walker had been a woman I would have asked him to marry me.” He also mentioned blues guitarists Blind Lemon Jefferson and Lonnie Johnson, and jazz players Charlie Christian and Django Reinhardt.

King once said his guitar style came from his own limits: “I started to bend notes because I could never play in the bottleneck style, like Elmore James and Booker White. I loved that sound but just couldn’t do it.” He was also modest about his singing, which was a mix of smooth singers like Nat King Cole and strong blues singers like Joe Turner and Dr Clayton. His favorite composer and singer was probably Louis Jordan, whose music he celebrated in his 1999 album “Let the Good Times Roll.”

During the 1950s, King was the top blues artist in clubs and theaters for black audiences, playing many one-night shows. In 1956, he is said to have played 342 shows. In 1962, he tried to change his busy schedule by signing with a big record label, ABC. But his first records with ABC, which tried to make him a pop singer, did not please his fans or the company.

However, his 1965 album “Live at the Regal” showed how strong his blues music was and became very famous, inspiring many young musicians. He had more R&B hits with songs like “How Blue Can You Get” and “Paying the Cost to Be the Boss.” In 1969, he reached the top of the pop charts with “The Thrill Is Gone,” something no blues artist had done for many years.

It took time for King to become popular with rock fans, who mostly liked the Chicago blues of Muddy Waters and Howlin’ Wolf. But musicians who admired King helped introduce him to new listeners. In 1969, he said, “About a year and a half ago, all of a sudden, kids started coming up to me saying, ‘You’re the greatest blues guitarist in the world.’ And I’d say, ‘Who told you that?’ And they’d say, ‘Mike Bloomfield’ or ‘Eric Clapton.’ It’s to these youngsters that I owe my new popularity.” He became even more respected in rock music with his 1970 album “Indianola Mississippi Seeds,” where he worked with Carole King and Joe Walsh.

After that, King was known as “the chairman of the board of blues singers.” With his manager, Sidney Seidenberg, he went on concert tours around the world, visiting Japan, Australia, China, and Russia. He also played concerts for prisoners at Cook County jail in Chicago and at San Quentin, which led him to support rehabilitation programs.

In 1990, King learned he had diabetes and reduced his touring, but he still performed often enough for his fans around the world to see him every year or two. He usually performed sitting down, but his singing and guitar playing stayed strong for a long time. For his 80th birthday in 2005, there was a special album with Eric Clapton, Mark Knopfler, Roger Daltrey, Gloria Estefan, and others, as well as tributes from musicians like Bono, Amadou Bagayoko, and Elton John, and a “farewell tour” that was not really his last.

In 2009, King won a Grammy for best traditional blues album for “One Kind Favor.” In 2012, he played at a White House concert, where President Barack Obama joined him to sing “Sweet Home Chicago.” King was married twice and divorced twice. He had 11 children with different partners; four other children died before him.

Kenton Cool, who usually likes to talk, can hardly speak now. Climbing at high altitude has made his voice rough. He is in Kathmandu, Nepal’s capital, after flying from Everest base camp that morning. Cool is thinking about a series of difficult climbs he finished last weekend. Early Saturday morning, he reached the top of Nuptse, the first and lowest of the three main peaks in the Everest “horseshoe” around the Western Cwm valley. 

On the same day, he climbed to the top of Everest, reaching the summit in complete darkness early Sunday. Then, with his climbing partner, he continued to the top of Lhotse, the third peak, on Monday morning.

“It was a rare chance,” he says. “For the first time since the late 1990s, there were fixed ropes on all three mountains. That doesn’t change the physical challenge of what I did. I’ve set a new standard. But the next person might do it without ropes or bottled oxygen.”

Sixty years after the first climb of Everest, many people are remembering Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay and their time, which was different from today’s commercial and environmental problems. I asked Cool to think about what top climbers might do 60 years from now.

“I don’t like to imagine,” he says, but he talks about Swiss climber Ueli Steck, who left the mountain in April after what Cool calls “an argument” with a group of Sherpas at Camp 2. Steck had planned to climb Everest’s west ridge, which was first done in 1963, go down to the South Col, and then climb Lhotse by a new route, all without fixed ropes. “Ueli trained very hard,” Cool says. “He is a unique climber. He is very skilled and also in amazing physical shape. It would have been incredible to see what he could do.”

Tourism is another issue. One example is the impressive helicopter rescue by Simone Moro, Steck’s climbing partner, whose angry words started the argument at Camp 2. Moro flew back to Everest on Tuesday in a powerful helicopter to rescue a sick climber at 7,800 meters. 

This was the highest rescue ever done on Everest and shows the big increase in helicopter flights in recent years. By 2073, there might be a helipad on the South Col, bringing tourists who use bottled oxygen. For now, helicopters are making it much easier to rescue both climbers and the many trekkers who go to base camp.

It is not clear if the Everest region can handle so many tourists, says mountain geographer and environmentalist Alton Byers. He says that climate change and tourism together are putting new pressure on the Sherpa homeland. Glaciers in the Everest area are shrinking or disappearing, which is already causing big problems. “Everywhere, people say there is less water. There is less water for farming and for all the new hotels being built.”

In the Sherpa town of Namche Bazaar, a new five-mile pipeline is being built to bring water for the growing number of tourists who want showers and flush toilets. The local stream is now polluted with human waste and does not have enough water for the town, which is very crowded in the busy season. “Every village is digging a pit outside the houses for garbage. Khumbu has the highest landfill sites in the world,” he says. Human waste at base camp is now managed well and taken away in plastic barrels. But Byers says these barrels are emptied into a big pit a few hours down the valley, which could leak into the water supply.

“These problems can be solved, but we need to take them seriously,” he says. “One climber can spend $85,000 to climb Everest. That’s fine. But soon we will have to focus on these other important issues. For half a million dollars a year, we could solve most of them.”

Climate change is another big problem. Byers works with local groups to find and plan for the effects of climate change, often by finding new water sources or collecting rainwater. The fast growth of glacial lakes, which could burst and flood the Sherpa homeland, is a constant danger. “One day, people will have to move out of the way.”

Changing weather is also affecting tourism. More clouds during normally clear weather are closing Lukla Airport, the main way into the Everest region, more often. A new road for four-wheel-drive vehicles is being built to Lukla to keep tourists and their money coming, but Byers worries that building roads quickly and cheaply in Nepal is causing soil erosion and landslides.

“Everest is the mountain everyone knows,” he says. “It’s like a warning sign that everyone understands. It’s the perfect place to learn how to deal with problems like climate change and tourism.”

A new international survey in 33 countries shows that people are often very wrong about important facts in their own countries.

For example, British people think the richest 1% of households own 59% of the country’s wealth, but they actually own only 23%. Americans believe that 33% of people in the US are immigrants, but the real number is just 14%. Brazilians think the average age in their country is 56, but it is really 31. Russians think 31% of their politicians are women, but the real number is only 14%.

In Britain, people think 43% of young adults aged 25-34 still live with their parents, but the real number is 14%. In India, people who use the internet think 60% of the country has internet access, but only 19% really do.

Why do people around the world get these facts so wrong? One reason is that many people have trouble with basic math or misunderstand the questions. For example, people in many countries think that 37% of people do not belong to any religion, but the real number is only 18%. This may be because people think about how many people practice religion, not what they write on official forms.

People also use mental shortcuts. They use information that is easy to remember, even if it is not correct. For example, people often overestimate how many people live in rural areas because rural land covers a lot of space, even if not many people live there. Psychologist Daniel Kahneman calls this “fast” thinking, which is quick but not always correct, instead of “slow” thinking, which is more careful.

People also think about their own lives and forget that their experience is not the same as everyone else’s. For example, in India, people who answered the survey online are richer and more connected than most people in the country, so they think more people have internet access than really do. People with more education usually answer these questions more accurately, but even they often think their own situation is normal for everyone.

Social psychologists call this “emotional innumeracy.” This means that when people guess numbers about society, their answers show what they worry about, not just the facts. Sometimes, people’s worries make them guess higher numbers, and sometimes their wrong guesses make them worry more.

In Britain, this helps explain why people think the richest own more than they do, why they think more young people live with their parents, and why they think there are more immigrants than there really are (they guess 25%, but the real number is 13%). People are worried about wealth, housing, and immigration, so they think these problems are bigger than they are.

But sometimes people are not worried enough. For example, in most countries, people guess that fewer people are overweight or obese than really are. In Saudi Arabia, people think only 28% are overweight or obese, but the real number is 71%. In Britain, people think it is 44%, but the real number is 62%.

The real facts from the survey are also very interesting. In Russia, the richest 1% own 70% of the country’s wealth, but in New Zealand, they own only 18%. In Italy, half of young adults aged 25-34 still live with their parents, but in Norway, only 4% do. The average age in India is 27, but in Japan, it is 47. Only 10% of politicians are women in Brazil, Hungary, and Japan, but in Sweden, 44% are women.

When the real facts are so different and surprising, it is not strange that people get them wrong.

We often hear about the danger of tigers disappearing in India, orangutans struggling in Indonesia, and pandas being in trouble. These are animals that many people love and do not want to lose. However, scientists are now worried that the real problem is happening closer to us. The loss of animals like ladybirds could be the biggest threat to the variety of life on Earth.

Because of climate change, fewer animals, more people, and many species dying out quickly, more scientists now say we are living in the Anthropocene. This is a new age where humans control nature and many species are going extinct.

The WWF’s Living Planet Index (LPI) 2014 report showed that the world’s wildlife is in serious trouble. The report said that the number of vertebrates (animals with backbones) has dropped by 52% in the last 40 years. The loss of different kinds of life is now at a “critical level.” Some groups, like mammals, birds, reptiles, and amphibians, have lost even more, and freshwater species have dropped by 76% in the same time.

Scientists are especially worried about animals that give us important “ecosystem services.” For example, about 75% of the world’s food depends on bees and other pollinators like hoverflies. While pandas and tigers are beautiful, it is worms that break down waste and make soil healthy, and bats that eat mosquitoes and help control diseases like malaria. In North America, the loss of bats is expected to cost farmers over $22 billion because there will be more pests.

Dr. Nick Isaac, a scientist at the Centre for Ecology & Hydrology in Oxfordshire, says that losing common species will hurt people more than losing rare animals, because we depend on common species more. He and his team have found that insects and other small animals in Britain are disappearing as quickly as larger animals, which could have “serious consequences for humanity.” He also says it is not just about species going extinct, but also about the number of animals in each species getting smaller. This is a big change in how we understand the problem.

He also said that between 23% and 36% of all birds, mammals, and amphibians used for food or medicine are now at risk of extinction. In many places, wild animals are an important part of people’s diets, especially for poor people.

Most experts agree that the main cause is humans using too many resources, damaging nature, causing climate change, and destroying habitats much faster than before. This time, it is not just the big, well-known animals we need to worry about, but also the small, less visible creatures like insects and worms. Even if they are not going extinct right now, their numbers are going down, and this will affect everyone. Dr. Isaac says, “We are going to feel the impact of those losses. In the UK, the pattern is the same for small animals as for big ones. It’s not as simple as ‘fish die and people starve’ – it’s more complicated.”

In 2013, TV naturalist Sir David Attenborough said that humans are a “plague on earth.” But the WWF says there is still time to fix things. David Nussbaum, the head of WWF UK, said, “The amount of destruction in this report should wake us all up. We all – politicians, businesses, and people – have a responsibility to act and protect what we value: a healthy future for people and nature.”

He also said, “Humans are cutting down trees faster than they can grow back, catching more fish than the oceans can replace, taking water from rivers and underground faster than rain can refill them, and putting more carbon into the air than forests and oceans can absorb.”

Women have often been kept out of important roles in football, but this changed when France chose its first female professional team manager. It did not matter that the club was in the second division. It also did not matter if some men said it was just a trick to get attention for a small team, Clermont Foot 63, which was ranked 14th out of 20 in its league.

The important thing was that Helena Costa got the top job. She made football history by becoming the first female manager in the top two divisions of any professional European league. Véronique Soulier, president of the club’s supporters’ group, told reporters, “As a woman, I am happy. At first, I was surprised, but then we all agreed it was good news. We think a woman leading a group of men is not a bad thing.”

Clermont Foot 63, which plays in Clermont-Ferrand in south-central France, has about 3,800 fans at home games. Costa, 36, is from Alhandra, Portugal, and has a master’s degree in sports science. She is a UEFA-licensed coach. She worked as a talent scout for Celtic in Scotland, coached Benfica’s male youth teams, led the Qatar women’s team to its first international win in 2012, and recently coached the Iranian women’s national team until September 2013.

Costa was given a two-year contract by Claude Michy, the president of Clermont Foot 63, who is known for getting attention for his club. In 2013, he said the team had signed Messi. But it was not Lionel Messi from Barcelona, but Junior Messi Enguene, a 20-year-old midfielder from Cameroon.

France’s women’s minister, Najat Vallaud-Belkacem, tweeted, “Bravo to Clermont Foot for understanding that giving women a place is the future of professional football.”

Carolina Morace, an Italian who was the only other woman to coach a men’s professional team, said, “I don’t know Helena, but if she was hired, it means she knows her job. I hope one day this will be normal.” Morace was a top player in Italy, the top scorer for 12 seasons, and played 153 times for Italy. In 1999, she became coach of Viterbese, a men’s team in Serie C1, but quit after two games because of problems with the club’s owner, Luciano Gaucci, who also owned a Serie A team, Perugia.

Morace said she refused to fire her assistant and the team’s trainer, as Gaucci wanted. She said, “He told me I could work with anyone I wanted, but by then, there was no trust, and I did not want to continue in that situation.” Now, Morace works as a lawyer in Rome and as a football expert on TV and in the newspaper Gazzetta dello Sport.

She also said, “Right now, I see too many men, even in women’s football, working without the same skills as women, who are not getting jobs.” Raymond Domenech, former manager of the French national team, said, “Women know how to play and manage football. Why shouldn’t they manage men’s teams? The opposite happens and no one complains. It’s a natural choice and shows that women are equal to men. Well done to President Michy. I told myself that if I managed a club again, I would hire a woman as my assistant. He did it before me.”

Clermont Foot 63’s website said Costa’s hiring would start “a new era” for the club. On the supporters’ website, some people were surprised and some were doubtful. One fan wrote, “I think it’s just a publicity stunt and she won’t last the season. I don’t think the players will respect her, especially since she is the same age as the oldest players.” Another said, “Her CV is not bad, but now the question is: will she be good enough?” A third wrote, “I wish her success, but I think it will be hard for her as a woman in such a male world. Has our president just made a media move?”

But Soulier was hopeful: “I hope the new manager can give the club the motivation it needs. The boys in the team can be hard to manage. Maybe with a woman in charge, they will be less demanding.”

If Costa’s past is any sign, she will be the one making the demands. She did work experience at Chelsea when José Mourinho was manager between 2004 and 2007. People called her “Mourinho in a skirt,” but Costa did not like this sexist comment. She said, “Like Mourinho, I always want to win. In that way, I am happy to be compared to him.”

Loneliness is now a big topic. The Office for National Statistics says Britain is the loneliest country in Europe. People in Britain are less likely to have close friends or know their neighbours than people in other EU countries. Many British people have no one to help them in a crisis. Research by Professor John Cacioppo from the University of Chicago found that loneliness is twice as bad for older people’s health as being overweight, and it is almost as dangerous as being poor.

But these studies often forget about loneliness in young adults. In 2010, the Mental Health Foundation found that young people worry about loneliness more than older people. People aged 18 to 34 were more likely to feel lonely often, worry about being alone, and feel depressed because of loneliness than people over 55.

Sam Challis, who works for the mental health charity Mind, says, “Loneliness is a known problem for older people—there are day centres and charities to help them. But when young people turn 21, they are too old for youth services.” This is a problem because loneliness and mental health are closely linked. Loneliness can cause more stress, depression, paranoia, anxiety, addiction, and problems with thinking. It is also a known reason for suicide. Paul Farmer, the head of Mind, and Jenny Edwards, the head of the Mental Health Foundation, say loneliness can both cause and be caused by mental health problems.

So, what can young people do to fight loneliness? Dr Grant Blank from the Oxford Internet Institute says social media and the internet can help or hurt. They are good when they help us talk to loved ones far away, but not when they replace meeting people in person. Sam Challis says, “People show a perfect version of themselves online, and we expect our social lives to be like those we see in the media.” When we compare our lives to our friends’ lives online, we may feel worse and stop seeing people.

Meditation and apps like Headspace are popular for mental health, but they may not help with loneliness because they make us spend more time alone with our thoughts. Challis says, “It’s better to find out what is stopping you from going out and meeting people.”

A 2013 study at the University of Michigan found that Facebook can make people less happy, but using technology to meet new people can help. If you cannot go outside, the internet can still give comfort. For example, Maddy Matthews, a 19-year-old student with a two-month-old baby, says Mumsnet has been “an absolute godsend.” Since her baby was born, she rarely sees her university friends and her partner works most evenings. She says, “In the first few days, I was up late at night feeding her and worried I was doing something wrong. Posting on Mumsnet helped me feel less alone.”

Helplines can also help with loneliness, at least for a short time. One in four men who call the Samaritans charity talk about loneliness or feeling alone. Get Connected is a free, private helpline for young people who need help with emotional and mental health problems linked to loneliness. There are also support services on websites like Mind’s that remind you that you are not alone.

At work, it can help to tell your employer how you feel. John Binns, who advises businesses about mental health, was in hospital for stress-related depression in 2007 and took two months off work. He felt he had no one to talk to and was not close enough to his colleagues for them to notice his problems. Being more open with his employer and colleagues made it easier to return to work. He says, “Often, people find that colleagues are more supportive than they thought. My colleagues started to invite me to lunch and told me that things had not changed much since I left.”

Talking with colleagues at work may seem unimportant, but it helps protect us from the emotional and mental effects of work stress. Rick Hughes, a workplace adviser for the British Association for Counselling and Psychotherapy (BACP), says, “If you connect with your team, you might be stressed but not alone.”

Nicky Forsythe, a psychotherapist and founder of Talk for Health, says, “We think our social networks are not important, but they are key to our well-being. The most important thing is to have a regular time and place to talk about your life and have someone listen with empathy.”

Counselling can help you develop personal skills like empathy. The BACP website can help you find counsellors near you. Rick Hughes says, “A problem shared is a problem halved, and sometimes you need to talk to someone who is not a friend or family member.” Most universities offer counselling for students and many have group sessions to help with loneliness.

Research shows that loneliness is killing older people, and as the population gets older, we should try to reduce loneliness before it is too late. Ruth Sutherland, the head of the relationship counselling service Relate, says, “Getting older does not have to mean getting lonelier. But we need to build good relationships earlier in life.”

The inventor of a modern computer-assisted autopsy system, now used more and more in European hospitals, says this technique could make it impossible to commit a 'perfect murder' in the future.

The method, called 'Virtopsy', was first developed by scientists at the University of Zurich and is now used in some forensic medical centers in Europe. Instead of cutting open the body with a scalpel as in a traditional autopsy, doctors can now look at the body in 3-D on computer screens.

Michael Thali, Director of Zurich’s Institute for Forensic Medicine and one of the inventors of Virtopsy, said this method could change criminal investigations. He said, “There will be no such thing as the perfect murder anymore because a virtual autopsy lets you find every piece of evidence.”

Virtopsy uses images from strong magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), computed tomography (CT), and surface scans of dead bodies. Together, these machines are called a 'Virtobot'. This technique can find injuries like lesions and blows that are often missed in traditional autopsies, as well as air pockets, heart attacks, and even cancer.

Richard Dirndorfer, a pioneer in DNA analysis and a developer of Virtopsy, told the German science magazine PM, “Virtopsy could one day replace the traditional autopsy. I think it will happen slowly, just like DNA analysis slowly replaced blood group analysis.”

These computer imaging methods let doctors see deep inside dead bodies. The method has already helped find bleeding and broken bones that were missed in normal autopsies. At first, the goal is to use Virtopsy together with traditional autopsies.

Dominic Wichmann, a specialist at Hamburg’s University Hospital, told Spiegel, “It will help forensic scientists plan their autopsies much better.” Criminologists from around the world have visited Switzerland in recent years to see how the new method works.

The American TV show CSI has shown Virtopsies twice. In one episode, the system proved a murder victim was killed by a bullet through the cheek. In another, a Virtopsy allowed a murdered man’s wish to be cryogenically frozen because his body was not cut open.

The method has been developed over many years. At first, the scientists worked in a cold, unheated lab and were not taken seriously. Later, a donation from a wealthy eye doctor helped the project grow. Even then, some people did not like the idea because they thought it would replace the traditional skills of forensic scientists and pathologists. But now, a new generation sees Virtopsy as something that can work together with traditional methods and maybe even replace them one day, but probably not completely.

Lars Oesterhelweg, Deputy Director of the Institute of Forensic Medicine at the Charité Hospital in Berlin, which uses Virtopsy, said, “To study the color of blood, the thickness of body fluids, or smells, we still need to do the traditional cuts.”

He also said the new method is very useful for looking again at cases where the cause of death is not clear. “It means that third opinions can be given, investigations can be checked again, and cases can be reopened,” he said.

Scientists using Virtopsy said that families of the dead, who often do not want autopsies because they change the body’s appearance, prefer this non-invasive method.

You can be named Aagot, Arney, or Ásfríður; Baldey, Bebba, or Brá. Dögg, Dimmblá, Etna, and Eybjört are also allowed, as well as Frigg, Glódís, Hörn, and Ingunn. Jórlaug is fine, and so are Obba, Sigurfljóð, Úranía, and even Vagna if you want. But if you are a girl in Iceland, you cannot be called Harriet.

Tristan Cardew, who is British, said, “The whole situation is really rather silly.” He and his Icelandic wife, Kristin, are appealing a decision by the National Registry in Reykjavik. The Registry refused to renew their ten-year-old daughter Harriet’s passport because it does not accept her first name.

Harriet’s 12-year-old brother, Duncan, also has a name that the Registry does not accept. Because of this, both children have traveled with passports that call them Stúlka and Drengur Cardew, which means Girl and Boy Cardew. “But this time, the authorities have decided to follow the law exactly,” said Cardew, who moved to Iceland in 2000. “The law says that no official document will be given to people who do not have an approved Icelandic name.”

Because of this problem, the family from Kópavogur almost missed their holiday in France. They had to ask the British embassy for an emergency UK passport, which should now let them travel.

Names are very important in Iceland, a country with only about 320,000 people. The phone book lists people by their first names because most Icelandic last names just show that you are your father’s or mother’s son or daughter. For example, Jón Einarsson’s children might be called Ólafur Jónsson and Sigríður Jónsdóttir.

The law says that the names of children born in Iceland must be given to the National Registry within six months of birth, unless both parents are foreign. If the name is not on the official list of 1,853 female and 1,712 male names, the parents must ask the Icelandic Naming Committee for approval.

About 5,000 children are born in Iceland each year. The committee gets about 100 applications each year and rejects about half of them. This is because of a 1996 law that tries to protect the Icelandic language. The rules say that names must be able to have Icelandic grammar endings, must not go against the structure of the Icelandic language, and must be written using normal Icelandic spelling.

In practice, this means that names with letters not in Iceland’s 32-letter alphabet, like “c”, are not allowed. Names that cannot take the endings needed for Icelandic grammar are also usually rejected. “That was the problem with Harriet,” said Cardew.

In recent years, more people have criticized Iceland’s naming laws. In 2013, Blær (“Light Breeze”) Bjarkardóttir Rúnarsdottir won the right to use her given name instead of “Girl” after a court said denying her name broke the Icelandic constitution. The former mayor of Reykjavik, Jón Gnarr, has also called the naming law “unfair, stupid, and against creativity.”

The Cardews could solve Harriet’s problem by giving her an Icelandic middle name. “But it’s a bit late for that and way too silly,” said Cardew. “Are they saying they don’t want us here?”

Google has mapped the world’s highest mountains, the ocean floor, the Amazon rainforest, and even parts of North Korea. But until now, Google has mostly avoided the difficult Arctic region. Now, Google is starting an important project to update maps of the polar areas. The company hopes this will help millions of people understand life on the permafrost.

Google sent a small team to Iqaluit, the biggest town in Nunavut, Canada. The team brought warm clothes, laptop computers, and a special 18kg backpack camera. With help from an Inuit mapping expert and watched by curious local people, the team spent four days walking through the area. They collected images and information to give this remote community on Baffin Island the same map features that people in cities already have.

Iqaluit, with 7,000 people, will appear on Google’s Street View in July 2013. Project leader Aaron Brindle said, “I live in Toronto and I always expect everything to be on the map, but in the north, this has not been true for a long time.”

In most places, Google uses a camera on top of a car to make maps. But in Iqaluit, the team had to walk on snowy roads and little-known trails, some made of ice that melt in summer. They also walked part of a 15km road called the Road to Nowhere, even though there were warnings about polar bears and other wild animals.

Mayor John Graham said the Google team was followed by many excited and curious local people, whom he called “Google stalkers.” Graham understands why people are interested. He said the Street View project continues the work of explorers like Martin Frobisher, who sailed into the bay in 1576, and Captain Elliott Roosevelt, who flew over the area in 1941. Roosevelt’s flight led to the building of a military airbase and the founding of modern Iqaluit, which is now the government center and main transport and communication hub for Nunavut.

One of Google’s first problems was getting the data needed to update their map. Their satellite images were mostly correct, but because the town is growing quickly due to mining, they missed a new road built last year, said Arif Sayani, the town’s Director of Planning.

Another problem was that many businesses and homes get mail at the post office, not at their own address. If Google used these addresses, the map would show many places grouped around the post office in the center of town.

To fix these problems, about 30 Inuit elders, business owners, and high school students came one night to help. They used laptops and learned how to make sure their homes, shops, and meeting places would appear correctly on the map.

The project is not just for fun or charity. Sayani said the town can use the maps to attract visitors or new residents. The maps may also help with planning decisions for Iqaluit’s future growth.

Google tested this mapping project last summer in Cambridge Bay, a smaller Nunavut town with about 1,500 people, 1,700km west of Iqaluit. The online images show gravel roads and muddy puddles, but do not show what life is like in a place usually covered in snow. This is one reason Google chose to visit Iqaluit in March, a colder and more difficult month.

Brindle hopes to continue mapping other northern towns, but the high cost of travel and shipping equipment in the Arctic is a challenge for Google. The next northern town has not been chosen yet. When it is, Brindle said Google might just send a special backpack camera and ask volunteers to help map the area.

Brindle said, “I hope that in three, four, or five years, we will look back and see a very different map of Canada’s north.”

Governments in Europe hope to find an easy way to stop unemployment from rising. But in the worst areas of the EU, more and more people are losing their jobs, and talking about the problem does not help people find work.

In one poor area of Italy, a mayor thinks he has found a way to help his town, which has very high unemployment. However, some people think his idea is not a real solution, but a sign that he has given up. Valter Piscedda, the centre-left mayor of Elmas, a small town near Cagliari in Sardinia, wants to pay people to leave the town. The council will pay for ten unemployed people to take intensive English classes, buy a cheap plane ticket, and look for work in other parts of Europe.

“This idea comes from common sense and experience,” he told the Guardian. “In the last year and a half, especially in the last few months, I have met young people almost every day who are desperate to find work. Some want help to find a job here. Others have tried everything and are so discouraged that they do not want to wait anymore. They want to go abroad to get work experience and life experience too.

“So, I thought: let’s do everything the council can to help those who want to get experience abroad,” he said.

As Italy’s economy gets worse, Sardinia and much of southern and central Italy have very high unemployment. According to Italy’s National Institute of Statistics (Istat), the unemployment rate was 17.7% in the second quarter of 2014. More than 54% of people under 25 do not have jobs.

For the “Adesso Parto” (“Now I’m leaving”) program, the Elmas council has set aside €12,000. The money will go to people who apply first, and who are between 18 and 50 years old. To qualify, they must be unemployed, have lived in Elmas for at least three years, and earn no more than €15,000 a year. They do not need a university degree.

The idea of encouraging people to leave is sensitive, because many Italians—especially young, educated people—are already leaving the country every year. But Piscedda, who is in the same party as Prime Minister Matteo Renzi, says he is not causing a “brain drain.” He believes that people who leave may come back one day and give much more to the town. More importantly, he wants to help those who need it most.

“It’s a program for people who have no other options; it’s their last chance. It lets them keep their dignity, so they don’t have to ask friends for money or put pressure on families who cannot help,” he said.

Earlier in 2014, the council started another program to give money to businesses that hired young people from Elmas. “We advertised 20 jobs,” he said. “We got 120 applications.”

In Elmas, people have different opinions about the new program. “The truth is, there is little work here,” said Alessandro Macis. “Going abroad to learn about work and other cultures can be very good. The son of a friend of mine, who did not study much, went to London. He started as a waiter, now he is a cook and learning English.”

Others are confused. “I heard about it, but I thought it was strange. If you have money to pay people to leave, why not use it to help them stay?” said Consuelo Melis, who works in a local café. On Twitter, some people were shocked. “The state is admitting defeat,” wrote Marco Patavino. “Institutions are giving up,” said Carlo Mazzaggio.

Piscedda is not discouraged. He said about his critics online: “Probably, they are people who do not need help. Every day, I see people’s problems and I have to try to solve them. If these people had another choice, they would not ask for help.

“As mayor, the jobs I can create are only temporary. I can have a square cleaned, or the streets cleaned, but these jobs only last a few months and give a little money. I want to do more than that.”

Apart from big disasters like volcanoes, hurricanes, and earthquakes, there are two main natural dangers that can slowly destroy a city or even make it disappear: water and sand.

If climate change was making the Earth colder instead of hotter, ice would also be a big danger. For example, in 2013, a rare “ice tsunami” hit Ochre Beach in Canada. Strong winds pushed a wall of melting ice from Dauphin Lake onto the shore, breaking every house in its way. However, this was unusual. In most places, melting ice is making cities weaker by raising sea levels, not by dramatic events.

A hundred years ago, Venice, a beautiful city that is very close to sea level, flooded about ten times a year. Now, its lowest area, Piazza San Marco (just three feet above sea level), floods about 100 times a year.

Rising sea levels are not the only problem. In many places, the land is also sinking. In Venice, the ground dropped by 20 centimeters between 1950 and 1970 because of industrial activity. Ho Chi Minh City in Vietnam is sinking about 2 centimeters each year, but Jakarta in Indonesia is sinking much faster—10 to 20 centimeters every year. In the last 30 years, Jakarta has sunk about four meters. Its seawall, built 40 years ago, is now less useful. Jakarta has pumped out so much groundwater that the land above is drying and sinking, making a bowl shape. Rivers that used to flow through the city to the sea now have to be redirected because they cannot flow uphill.

Venice, Ho Chi Minh City, and Jakarta are trying to solve these problems, but Miami in the United States is not. Many politicians in Miami do not admit there is a serious environmental problem.

Miami has three main problems. First, it is less than ten feet above sea level. Second, more and more tropical storms are flooding the city. Third, it is built on limestone, which lets seawater come in. This water fills the city’s foundations and comes up through drains and pipes, pushing sewage up and polluting the fresh water. Miami could become impossible to live in one day.

In the Maldives, people on some islands are thinking about leaving their homes. The capital, Malé, has 153,379 people and is only four feet above sea level. With help from Japan, the city built a ten-foot sea wall for $63 million. But in the long run, only stopping sea levels from rising will save Malé and the other islands.

Rainfall is also a danger for cities. Recently, Detroit got a whole summer’s worth of rain in one morning, which was too much for its old sewer system. Because Detroit lost much of its car industry, it does not have enough money to fix the problem. The city is also at risk from diseases in the water.

In Africa, the Sahara Desert is spreading south by 30 miles each year, threatening towns in northern Mauritania. In the last 20 years, the desert has grown by more than 260 acres around Chinguetti, a trading and religious center. Its population has dropped from 20,000 in the mid-1900s to just a few thousand now. Trading has almost stopped because sand is filling the streets.

Rancho Mirage, a city near Palm Springs in California, may also have to be left in the next ten years. This is not just because of global warming, but because people have used too many resources. California’s plan to farm the desert worked when there were only about half a million people in 1870. Now, there are 38 million people, 32 million cars, and many lawns and golf courses.

People in Rancho Mirage use more than 200 gallons of water each day, causing a man-made drought. Water use has been cut by 25%, but this may not be enough to save the city, which is surrounded by sand and dust. In the future, some cities in California’s desert may have to be left, and people may have to move to other cities.

When people leave a city, nature quickly takes over. Hashima Island in Japan was turned into a concrete city in 1887 for coal mining. When the coal ran out in 1974, the city was abandoned. Now, sea spray is breaking down its concrete walls.

Fire is also a growing danger for cities in America. After big storms, forest fires cause the most damage. There have been 800 major fire disasters in the US between 1953 and 2014. A new report from the USDA Forest Service shows that more and more cities are at risk from wildfires.

In Australia, some resorts in Victoria and some suburbs of Melbourne are on a list of the 52 most at-risk places for bushfires. Long droughts make trees easy to burn. It is unlikely that a whole city will be destroyed by fire, but many fires could make a city impossible to live in, and people might leave.

Many cities are struggling against nature, but can we say which city is most at risk? Natural events are hard to predict, but Malé in the Maldives looks to be in great danger. Even if its new sea wall works, the other islands around Malé will disappear soon. If they disappear, Malé will lose its reason to exist.

Many people call living with parents as adults "the hotel of mum and dad," but few real hotels are as generous. Because of the housing crisis, one in five young adults now stays at home with their parents until at least age 26, and the same number do not pay anything for living there. A recent survey showed that the number of adults living at home is different across the country. In the East Midlands, just under 9% of young adults live at home, but in London, where houses and rent are most expensive, it is more than double that. While many young adults help with money, 20% pay nothing at all.

Young adults are struggling because wages are low and rents are higher than ever. Those who want to buy a home find it hard to save money because renting costs so much. Research from the charity Shelter found that half of renters cannot save any money for a deposit, and a quarter can only save £100 or less each month. Mortgages are cheaper now because interest rates are very low, but the best mortgage deals are only for people who have saved a lot for a deposit.

Because of these problems, more young adults are moving back in with their parents to save money. Parents who cannot give their children a large amount of money are still willing to help by letting them live at home. The survey found that 28% of adults living at home are trying to save for a deposit, but 30% are not saving any money.

A spokesman for the company that did the survey said, “The hotel of mum and dad is staying open longer than many people thought. High rent and the need to save for a deposit mean some children have to wait before they can move out. For some, moving out may never be possible.”

Michael Day, 30, lives with his parents in Bristol. He says he is stuck between paying high rent and saving for a deposit. Renting a one-bedroom home in Bristol costs between £500 and £800 a month, but buying a similar home costs about £130,000. “I don’t want to rent because it costs more than a mortgage, but you need a big deposit for a mortgage, so it’s a vicious circle,” he said.

Michael does not want to share a home with strangers, so he has few choices. At home, he pays a small amount to help with bills and keeps the rest of his money from his job at a candle shop. He plays golf at a high level and admits that instead of saving, he spends his extra money on golf and holidays. “You need so much money that I will have to save for a long time,” he said. “Because it’s so hard, I’ve been going on holiday and enjoying myself.”

Sue Green, from Saga, a company that sells insurance and products to people over 50, said most parents did not plan to have their children living with them into their 20s or 30s. “Most parents are happy to let their children live at home for free because it might help them buy a home sooner,” she said. “Children who don’t pay rent may help in other ways, like buying food, getting takeaways for the family, or doing jobs around the house.”

Angus Hanton, co-founder of the Intergenerational Foundation, said older people helped cause the housing crisis, so young people should not be blamed for living at home. “People under 30 have seen their average income fall by about 20% since 2008. Rents and car insurance are higher than ever, and it is harder for young people to get a mortgage, but not for older people who buy homes to rent out. Student debt is rising fast, and many jobs for young people are short-term or have zero hours, making life harder for them. Instead of blaming young people, we should help them so they can afford to build their own lives,” he said.

Jenna Gavin, 29, lives in Southport, Merseyside, in her childhood home. She moved out for a year to go to university but has lived with her parents since then. She works as a medical receptionist nearby and wants to stay in the area. Renting a one-bedroom flat would cost her more than £420 a month before bills, which is a lot of her pay. “I don’t want to rent because I don’t want to spend all that money and have nothing in the end,” she said. “I’ve looked at buying and talked to mortgage advisers, but I just can’t borrow enough to buy a home.”

Jenna is trying to save but finds it hard to get enough money. “You don’t see your savings grow as much as you need – even a 5% deposit is a lot of money, and I would like to save more,” she said. Her parents are happy not to charge her rent. “They want me to save, and I help in other ways – I bring food and do things around the house.”

Jenna gets along well with her parents and has her own room, which she moved into at age 14. But she always thought she would have her own place by age 30. “I don’t think that will happen, as I turn 30 next year. But hopefully, in a couple of years, I’ll have moved out.”

David Bowie, who died of cancer, continued to surprise people until the end of his life. His last album, Blackstar, was released on his 69th birthday, January 8, 2016. This album showed that he still had the talent to make dramatic and challenging music.

In the 1970s, Bowie led new musical styles and pop fashion. He started as a mime and cabaret performer in the late 1960s, then became a singer-songwriter and a leader of glam-rock. Later, he moved into “plastic soul” music and then went to Berlin to create new electronic music. Bowie was known for changing his sound and image, always driven by his curiosity and intelligence. Few people in pop music history have matched his ability to reinvent himself.

Bowie was born David Robert Jones in south London. In 1953, his family moved to Kent, where he showed talent in singing and playing the recorder. Later, he studied art, music, and design. In 1961, his mother bought him a plastic saxophone, an instrument that would often appear in his music.

At age 15, Bowie formed his first band, the Kon-rads. It was clear that he was very talented and wanted to be a solo artist. He changed his name to Bowie to avoid confusion with Davy Jones from the Monkees.

Bowie’s first album, called David Bowie, came out in June 1967. In July 1969, he released Space Oddity, the song that made him famous. The song was released at the same time as the Apollo 11 moon landing and became a top five hit in the UK.

In March 1970, Bowie married art student Angela Barnett. Artistically, he was moving forward quickly. The Man Who Sold the World was released in the US in late 1970 and in the UK in 1971. This album had bold songwriting and a dark, hard-rock sound. Its themes included immortality, insanity, murder, and mysticism, showing that Bowie was thinking beyond normal pop music.

He followed this with Hunky Dory in 1972, which had complex songwriting. The album was good but only had moderate success. Everything changed with The Rise and Fall of Ziggy Stardust and the Spiders from Mars, released later that year.

With this album, Bowie became a science-fiction character—a glam-rock star from space visiting a dying Earth. The album made him a star. The hit single Starman brought instant success, and Bowie’s colorful costumes and exciting performances made fans very enthusiastic, similar to the excitement seen with the Beatles.

Everything Bowie did was successful. His first UK number 1 album was Aladdin Sane (1973), which included the hit songs The Jean Genie and Drive-in Saturday. But Bowie was already planning new things.

He became more interested in funk and soul music, which showed in Young Americans (1975). This album gave him a number 1 hit in the US with Fame, which featured John Lennon.

Station to Station (1976) introduced a new character, the Thin White Duke, which Bowie also played in the film The Man Who Fell to Earth.

Bowie’s marriage was ending because of the pressures of fame, and he and Angela divorced in 1980. That year, he released the successful album Scary Monsters (and Super Creeps), which included the hit Ashes to Ashes. He also acted as John Merrick in The Elephant Man on Broadway. In 1981, he had a number 1 single with Queen called Under Pressure. He started working in different media, appearing in the German film Christiane F (1981) and writing its music. He had another hit with Cat People (Putting Out Fire) from the movie Cat People (1982). Bowie continued acting in films like The Hunger and Merry Christmas, Mr Lawrence, both released in 1983.

In 1983, Bowie focused on commercial success with the album Let’s Dance and a big tour. The album and its singles Let’s Dance, China Girl, and Modern Love were huge international hits. This was the time of MTV, and Bowie’s creative music videos helped his success. The Serious Moonlight tour attracted large crowds and was the most successful period of his career. His fame grew even more after performing at the 1985 Live Aid concert at Wembley Stadium. He also recorded Dancing in the Street with Mick Jagger, which became a number 1 hit. After performing at the Freddie Mercury tribute concert in April 1992, Bowie married Somali model Iman, and they bought a home in New York. This new chapter in his life matched his search for new musical ideas.

For the album Black Tie White Noise (1993), Bowie mixed soul, electronica, and hip hop. The album was number 1 in the UK and included the top 10 single Jump They Say. New technology also influenced his music. His 1999 album Hours… was based on music he wrote for a computer game called Omikron, where Bowie and Iman appeared as characters. Bowie and Iman’s daughter, Alexandria, was born in August 2000.
