Two mothers in South Africa found out they are raising each other’s daughters because the babies were accidentally switched at birth in a hospital in 2010.

One mother wants to fix the mistake and get her real daughter back, but the other mother does not want to give up the girl she has raised as her own.

Henk Strydom, a lawyer for one of the mothers, said the baby swap is a terrible mistake and a sad situation that probably will not end happily.

Both mothers gave birth on the same day in 2010 at Tambo Memorial Hospital in Boksburg, near Johannesburg. At first, nobody knew about the mistake.

In 2013, one mother, who is 33 years old and does not have a job, asked her ex-partner to pay money to help raise her daughter. The man said he was not the father. A DNA test showed that he was not the father and that the girl was not her biological daughter. The mother was very upset and did not know what to do.

Later, she met the other mother. Since December 2013, both mothers have been going to counseling sessions together, organized by the hospital. There, they have met their real daughters.

Strydom said his client noticed that her real daughter looks like her. He said it was very hard for her. She has to take care of a child who is not really hers, while her own daughter is with someone else.

The woman became unhappy with the situation and asked the children’s court to give her custody of her real daughter, but the other mother refused.

Strydom said it is a sad situation. His client wants her daughter back, but after four years, it is easy to understand why the other mother does not want to give up the child she has raised.

The High Court in Pretoria has asked the University of Pretoria’s Centre for Child Law to find out what is best for the children.

Strydom said he does not know what the court will decide, and that someone will not be happy with the result.

He also said that, for now, he and his client do not want to sue the hospital or the government health department, which is helping with the case and giving counseling.

The Centre for Child Law will talk to the mothers, fathers, and anyone else important in the girls’ lives. The children and mothers will have medical checks and may see a psychologist.

Karabo Ngidi, a lawyer at the centre, said that what happens next must be best for the children. Biology is important, but it is not the only thing to think about.

Both families are Zulu, so Zulu tradition, culture, and law will also be considered. It is also possible that the ex-partner of the mother who went to court could be the real father of the other girl.

This is not the first time babies have been switched in South Africa. In 1995, two mothers got money after their sons, born in 1989, were switched at a hospital in Johannesburg.

In 2009, in Oregon, USA, Dee Ann Angell and Kay Rene Reed found out they were switched at birth in 1953 when a nurse brought them back from a bath.

In 2013, in Japan, a 60-year-old man who was switched at birth and grew up in a poor family got money as compensation. His real brothers and sisters, and the boy who was raised in his place, went to private schools and universities, but he grew up on welfare and became a truck driver.

Bruce Laing, a psychologist in Johannesburg, said that being switched at birth can have serious, frightening, and very upsetting effects for a long time. He told The Times of South Africa that parents might always wonder, “What if?”

Two mothers in South Africa found out they are raising each other’s daughters because someone made a mistake at a hospital in 2010 and switched the babies at birth.

One mother wants her real daughter back, but the other mother does not want to give up the girl she has raised as her own.

Henk Strydom, a lawyer for one of the mothers, said this is a very sad situation and it will probably not end well.

Both mothers gave birth at Tambo Memorial Hospital in Boksburg, near Johannesburg, on the same day in 2010.

In 2013, one mother, who is 33 years old and does not have a job, wanted her ex-partner to pay money to help raise her daughter. The man said he was not the father. Strydom said, “A DNA test was done. They found out the baby was not his and not hers. She was very sad and did not know what to do.”

She met the other mother, and now both mothers go to counselling sessions together at the hospital. There, both mothers met their real daughters.

Strydom said about his client: “It is not easy for her. She has to take care of a child that is not hers, while her real child is with someone else.”

The woman became unhappy and asked the children’s court to give her custody of her real daughter, but the other mother said no.

“It is a tragedy. She wants her baby back, but it has been four years. You can understand that the other mother does not want to give up her baby,” Strydom said.

The High Court in Pretoria has asked the University of Pretoria’s Centre for Child Law to find out what is best for the children.

Strydom said, “Whatever happens, someone will not be happy.”

Karabo Ngidi, a lawyer at the centre, said, “We must do what is best for the children. Biology is important, but it is not the only important thing.”

This is not the first time babies have been switched by mistake in South Africa. In 1995, two mothers got money after their sons, born in 1989, were switched by mistake at a hospital in Johannesburg.

At the start of the final season of Downton Abbey, the mood is sad and shows that times are changing. It is the year 1925. The neighbours are selling their big house, and Lord Grantham wants to have fewer servants.

But at the real Downton Abbey, called Highclere Castle, things are better. Highclere Castle is owned by George “Geordie” Herbert, the 8th Earl of Carnarvon. Because Downton Abbey became very popular around the world, the money from the show helped pay for important repairs to the castle. Lady Fiona Carnarvon said that the show has given them free advertising and made Highclere famous. She and her husband love the castle, and now millions of people do too.

Right now, only the ground floor and first floor of Highclere Castle are used. But they have started fixing the rooms in the tower. Soon, visitors will be able to go up the tower and see an exhibition about Sir Charles Barry, the architect who rebuilt the house between 1839 and 1842. He also designed the Houses of Parliament.

When the Downton Abbey producers first came to Highclere in 2009, the family needed to do £12 million of repairs, and £1.8 million of that was urgent. By 2012, the show was helping a lot. Lord Carnarvon said that after the banking crisis, they were worried, but then Downton Abbey started and Highclere became a big tourist attraction.

The number of visitors doubled to 1,200 a day. Downton Abbey, written by Julian Fellowes, became a hit in the UK in 2010 and then in the US. Now, it is shown in 250 countries.

There is now an online booking system, which helps visitors from other countries buy tickets. Highclere’s assets have almost tripled to about £1 million since 2012. Gareth Neame, the executive producer, said that Downton Abbey helped save Highclere’s future.

Peter Fincham, ITV’s director of television, remembers when they chose Highclere for the show. He did not know about the castle and thought all big houses looked the same, but he was wrong. The castle became an important part of the show.

Tourists who visit Downton Abbey are part of a bigger trend. VisitBritain says that almost 30% of foreign visitors, or about nine million people, visit castles and historic houses. Almost half of visitors to Britain now say they want to see places from films or TV.

More than a million people tour historic buildings each year, spending over £1 billion. 51% of Brazilians, 42% of Russians and Chinese, and 35% of Indian visitors are likely to visit interesting sites during their trips.

Patricia Yates, director of VisitBritain, said that tourism, films, and TV are closely linked. She also said that period dramas have made places outside London more popular.

Downton Abbey shows a special view of Britain. It is a fantasy world set in a certain time in history. It is the first TV period drama to become a big part of popular culture.

Lady Carnarvon says that Highclere’s future is not completely safe, but the show has helped them spend more money on repairs. Highclere Castle plans to have a Tutankhamun event in 2022, 100 years after the 5th Earl of Carnarvon found Tutankhamun’s tomb with Howard Carter. Another event is the 300th birthday of Lancelot “Capability” Brown, who designed the gardens.

Lady Carnarvon says you should not take anything for granted. You have to invest in these great houses. Since the 1930s, there has been a shortage of money. In the past, the estate and house supported the family, but now it is the other way around: she and her husband must find ways to support Highclere.

She tries to show people that visiting is fun. They have special events for visitors, not just tours of an old house. They have to compete with other attractions like the London Dungeon.

Health warnings that cover almost two-thirds of cigarette packs and a ban on menthol cigarettes in the EU are closer to happening after a vote in the European Parliament.

Menthol and other flavored cigarettes will be banned from 2022. MEPs also decided that most electronic cigarettes, which are becoming more popular as alternatives to tobacco, do not need to be regulated like medicines.

Health officials and the e-cigarette industry in Britain want to know what this means. For example, they want to know if e-cigarette companies will have the same bans on sponsorship and advertising at sports events as tobacco companies.

The Department of Health did not comment on the advertising question until officials have looked at the MEPs’ decisions. But in a statement, the Department of Health said: We are happy to see stronger action on tobacco, with European rules banning flavored cigarettes and stricter rules on health warnings on the front of packs.

However, we are not happy with the decision not to regulate nicotine-containing products (NCPs), including e-cigarettes, as medicines. We think these products should be regulated as medicines and will keep saying this during more talks.

Smoking rates in England are now the lowest since records began—19.5 percent—but we want to reduce smoking even more and believe this step will help.

The UK e-cigarette industry welcomed the parliament’s vote. It said it is already talking with the Advertising Standards Authority but added that banning all advertising would not be sensible, reasonable, or useful.

MEPs decided that e-cigarettes should only be regulated as medical products if companies say they can help people stop smoking tobacco. The government’s main medicines regulator criticized this decision.

The regulator wants e-cigarettes, used by about 1.3 million people in Britain, to be treated like gums, patches, and mouth sprays that help people quit smoking. But the e-cigarette industry says that getting a license is expensive and would remove alternatives to tobacco from shops.

MEPs voted to put health warnings on 65% of each cigarette pack. Right now, warnings cover at least 30% on the front and 40% on the back. The UK government has delayed deciding whether to follow Australia by introducing plain packaging until there is proof that it reduces tobacco use.

The MEPs’ decision, which could become law in 2014, will be followed by talks with the EU Council of Ministers.

A spokesman for the Medicines and Healthcare Products Regulatory Authority said the UK still believes that regulating NCPs as medicines is the best way to improve public health.

Linda McAvan, Labour MEP for Yorkshire and the Humber and spokesperson on tobacco issues for the parliament’s Socialists & Democrats group, said: We know that children, not adults, start smoking. Even though there are fewer adult smokers in most member states, World Health Organization numbers show that young smokers are increasing in some countries.

We need to stop tobacco companies from targeting young people with special products and make sure cigarette packs have strong warnings.

Martin Callanan, the Conservative MEP for North East England, said: Forcing e-cigarettes off the shelves would have been completely wrong. These products have helped many people stop smoking more dangerous cigarettes, but some MEPs wanted to make them harder to make than normal tobacco.

British American Tobacco said the bigger health warnings demanded by MEPs were not needed and that banning menthol cigarettes would increase demand for illegal products.

The European Parliament said that health warnings must cover almost two-thirds of cigarette packs. There will also be a ban on menthol cigarettes in the EU. The EU will stop the sale of menthol and other flavored cigarettes from 2022. Members of the European Parliament (MEPs) also decided that most electronic cigarettes, which are becoming more popular instead of normal cigarettes, do not need to be regulated like medicines.

The Department of Health and e-cigarette companies in Britain want to know exactly what these new rules mean. For example, they want to know if e-cigarette companies will be banned from advertising at sports events.

The Department of Health said, “We are happy to see stronger action against smoking, with European rules banning flavored cigarettes and stricter rules for health warnings on cigarette packs. But we are not happy with the decision not to regulate nicotine products, including e-cigarettes, as medicines. We think these products should be regulated as medicines. Smoking levels in England are now the lowest ever—19.5 percent—but we want even fewer people to smoke. We believe these new rules will help.”

UK e-cigarette companies were pleased with the parliament’s vote. They said they are already talking with the Advertising Standards Authority. But they also said that banning all advertising would not be a good idea.

MEPs decided that e-cigarettes should only be regulated as medical products if the companies say their products can help people stop smoking. Some other groups want e-cigarettes, which are used by about 1.3 million people in Britain, to be regulated like gums, patches, and mouth sprays that help people quit smoking.

It is difficult to know exactly where the noise is coming from, but you can hear it everywhere in Damascus. All day and night, you hear guns, rockets, or planes attacking rebel areas. The sounds of war are getting closer to Syria’s capital. Just over two years after the Syrian crisis started, people in Damascus have learned to ignore the sounds of death and destruction only a few miles away.

“You do get used to it after some time,” said George, an IT technician. “But you never know exactly what they are hitting. Usually, you find out later from videos posted by the opposition on YouTube.”

The constant noise is more worrying because the government tries hard to make life look normal. “As you can see, everything here is fine, but we have to hit the terrorists, these extremists,” said an army officer. A government official said, “If I was afraid, I would just shut my door and stay inside. I have to work and I am not afraid. If I don’t defend my country, who will?”

In private, normal people are less confident. In the city center, a shopkeeper sadly said his baby daughter cries when she hears explosions. Zeina, a student in her twenties, is afraid she might stop feeling anything about suffering or danger. “At first, when the explosions started, I used to have nightmares,” she said. “Now I can sleep through anything.”

The risks are getting closer to home. In Sabaa Bahrat Square, which was supposed to be the safest part of Damascus, a car bomb exploded. The front of a building turned black, its windows broke, and the Syrian Central Bank next door was also damaged. The square is often used for pro-government rallies on TV, with people shouting slogans under big pictures of President Bashar al-Assad.

That bombing was not the worst Damascus has seen as things have gotten worse. In February, reports say 80 people, including schoolchildren, died near the Baath Party headquarters in Mazraa. You can still see the hole in the road, now covered with new asphalt. “I live nearby but luckily I wasn’t there,” said Munir, a university teacher.

Mortar bombs, fired from rebel areas now very close to the city, are a new and worrying problem. On March 28, these bombs killed 15 students in a university cafeteria. The real target was probably a government building.

Security has increased since the bombing of the national security crisis cell in July 2012, when four of Assad’s top aides were killed. Concrete barriers, often painted with the Syrian flag’s colors—black, red, and white—now protect official buildings, not just military ones. The Iranian Embassy in Mezze now looks like a fortress. “The regime did manage to set up a ring of steel around Damascus,” said a foreign diplomat. He added that there are now holes in that ring, which shows how real the war is.

Because of all this, moving around the city has become difficult, unpredictable, and slow. This is now a normal part of life in a city that is understandably nervous. Checkpoints on main roads stop cars to check IDs and search bags with explosive detectors. Only drivers with special security clearance can use fast lanes to avoid waiting.

However, it is hard to avoid the question everyone is thinking about: will there be a battle for Damascus—the world’s oldest city that has always been lived in, as the guidebooks say—like the one that has badly damaged Aleppo? Some parts of the city already feel like a war zone. The most expensive hotel is almost empty, although many rooms are used as offices by international agencies, with white UN vehicles parked behind barriers outside. The streets become empty soon after 9pm.

Some people think the fight for Syria’s capital is coming, but not yet—maybe in the summer, when the rebels have made more progress in the south. Others think that neither side will win completely and hope for a political solution from other countries. But few people here expect things to get better.

Passing clouds  
One nice thing about flying is seeing clouds up close. Even though clouds look light, they actually hold a lot of water—about 500 tonnes in a small cloud. Water is heavier than air. So why don’t clouds fall from the sky like rain? They do, but it happens very slowly. An average cloud would take a year to fall just one metre.

On cloud nine  
Most people call clouds “fluffy” or “black,” but weather experts, called meteorologists, have names for more than 50 types of clouds. These types are put into groups numbered one to nine. Cloud nine is a very large, tall cloud called a cumulonimbus. That’s why “on cloud nine” means feeling very happy.

Around the rainbow  
The best place to see a rainbow is from a plane. Rainbows appear when sunlight hits raindrops. On the ground, we see a bow shape because the Earth blocks the rest, but from a plane, you can see a full circle rainbow.

Mr blue sky  
Sunlight is white and has all the colours. When sunlight goes through the air, some of it is scattered by gas molecules. Blue light scatters more than other colours, so the sky looks blue.

There’s life out there  
Besides clouds and other planes, you might not expect to see much outside a plane window. But the air is full of bacteria—up to 1,800 different types have been found over cities, and they can go twice as high as planes usually fly.

Turbulence terror  
Turbulence can make even experienced flyers feel sick. It is caused by rough air and can make the plane bump or drop suddenly. The good news is that no modern passenger plane has ever crashed because of turbulence. People can get hurt if they are not wearing seatbelts or if luggage falls, but the plane itself is safe.

In-flight radiation  
When body scanners were first used at airports, people worried about radiation. But the amount of radiation from a scanner is the same as you get from one minute of flying. The Earth is always hit by cosmic rays, which are natural radiation from space, and this is stronger at high altitudes.

You can’t cure jet lag  
The world has different time zones. When you travel far, your body’s time is different from the local time, causing jet lag. You can’t cure jet lag, but you can make it better by eating plain food for 24 hours before flying, drinking lots of water, and changing to your destination’s time as soon as you get on the plane.

Supersonic 747s  
Many people have flown faster than the speed of sound. There are fast-moving air currents called jet streams high in the sky, especially between the US and Europe. Sometimes, a plane flying at 550 mph enters a jet stream moving at 250 mph, so the plane’s speed over the ground can be 800 mph—faster than sound.

Flying through time  
Time zones make it feel like you are traveling through time, but special relativity means you actually do, a little. However, it is so small that if you flew across the Atlantic every week for 40 years, you would only be 1/1,000th of a second ahead in time.

Terrible tea  
If your tea tastes bad on a plane, it’s not the flight attendant’s fault. Water should be almost 100°C to make good tea, but on a plane, water can only get to 90°C. So, it’s better to choose coffee.

I can’t hear my food  
People often say airline food tastes bland. This is not just because of the food. Planes are noisy, and loud noise can make food taste less strong.

Needle in a haystack  
With today’s technology, it seems strange that a plane like Malaysian flight MH370 could disappear. But finding a missing plane is very hard. The plane knows its location, but this information is not sent out in real time. It could be, because ships have had tracking since the 1980s. The problem is not technology, but that there is no law requiring it.

Volcanic fallout  
Volcanic eruptions can stop air travel. Ash from volcanoes melts in the hot engines and then hardens on the engine parts. Cancelling flights because of ash clouds is inconvenient, but flying through ash is very dangerous.

The wing myth  
For many years, people explained wrongly how wings keep planes in the air. Most of a plane’s lift comes from Newton’s Third Law of Motion. The wing is shaped to push air down. As the wing pushes air down, the air pushes the wing up, lifting the plane.

In October 2012, the Taliban sent a gunman to shoot Malala Yousafzai while she was riding home on a bus after school. They wanted to stop her from speaking out and fighting for girls’ education.

Nine months later, after many surgeries, Malala stood up at the United Nations on her 16th birthday to answer the Taliban. She said, “They thought the bullet would silence us. But they failed.”

Malala’s 16th birthday was very different from most. Instead of having a party, she sat in a main council room at the United Nations, in a seat usually for world leaders. She listened as Ban Ki-moon, the UN secretary-general, called her “our hero, our champion.” Gordon Brown, the former British prime minister and now a UN education envoy, wished her a happy 16th birthday and said these were words the Taliban never wanted her to hear.

The event was called Malala Day. It was the result of four amazing years for Malala, a girl from Mingora, Pakistan. She became famous after writing a blog for the BBC Urdu service about her struggle to get an education while the Taliban was gaining power.

By age 11, Malala was already very determined. She spoke directly to Richard Holbrooke, the US special representative to Pakistan, asking him to help stop the Taliban from blocking girls’ education. At 14, Archbishop Desmond Tutu noticed her and suggested her for the International Children’s Peace Prize. At 15, she became the youngest person ever nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

But this attention was dangerous. Malala received death threats. On October 9, 2012, after a meeting of Taliban leaders, a gunman was sent to silence her.

After the attack, Malala had many operations in Pakistan and the UK. Doctors put a titanium plate in her left forehead and gave her a cochlear implant to help her hear again. Now, she lives with her family in Birmingham, England, and goes to school every day, just as the Taliban tried to stop her from doing. In the UN, she said, “I am not against anyone. I am not here for personal revenge against the Taliban or any other terrorist group.”

Malala answered the Taliban’s violence with words, not hate. She said, “I do not even hate the Talib who shot me. Even if I had a gun and he stood in front of me, I would not shoot him.”

She spoke with confidence, though her left eye was injured and one side of her face drooped a little. She wore a white shawl that belonged to Benazir Bhutto, the former prime minister of Pakistan, who was also attacked by extremists but did not survive.

Malala said, “The extremists are afraid of books and pens. The power of education scares them. They are afraid of women and the power of women’s voices.”

She talked about a recent attack on a hospital in Quetta and the killing of female teachers in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. She said, “That is why they are blowing up schools every day—because they are afraid of change and afraid of equality in our society.”

Malala also explained her own view of Islam, different from the Taliban’s. She said, “They think God is small and strict and would send girls to hell just for going to school. The terrorists are using the name of Islam and Pashtun society for their own benefit. Islam is a religion of peace, humanity, and brotherhood. Islam says every child has the right and duty to get an education.”

Malala’s courage to speak out has inspired many people. The “Stand with Malala” petition, which asks for education for the 57 million children worldwide who do not go to school, has more than four million signatures. Over a million people signed after Malala’s speech.

At the start of her speech, Malala said, “I don’t know where to begin my speech. I don’t know what people expect me to say.” But she did not need to worry.

In October 2012, the Taliban sent a man with a gun to shoot Malala Yousafzai. She was going home on a bus after school. The Taliban wanted to stop Malala and her work for girls’ education.

Nine months later, after many surgeries, Malala spoke at the United Nations on her 16th birthday. She said, “They thought the bullet would silence us. But they failed.”

Malala’s 16th birthday was special. She did not have a cake or candles. She sat in the main seat at the United Nations, where world leaders usually sit. She listened as Ban Ki-moon, the UN secretary-general, called her “our hero, our champion.” Gordon Brown, the former British prime minister and now a UN education envoy, said, “the words the Taliban never wanted her to hear: happy 16th birthday, Malala.”

The event was called Malala Day. Malala is from Mingora, Pakistan. She became famous after she wrote a blog for the BBC Urdu service. In her blog, she talked about her hard life trying to go to school when the Taliban were in control.

When Malala was 11, she asked Richard Holbrooke, the US special representative to Pakistan, to help her fight the Taliban, who wanted to stop girls from going to school. When she was 14, Archbishop Desmond Tutu suggested her for the International Children’s Peace Prize. At 15, she became the youngest person ever nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize.

After this, Malala got death threats. On 9 October 2012, after a meeting of Taliban leaders, a gunman tried to kill her.

Malala had many surgeries in Pakistan and the UK after she was shot on the bus. Now, she lives with her family in Birmingham, England. She goes to school every day, which is what the Taliban tried to stop. Malala said, “I am not against anyone.”

She does not want revenge against the Taliban or any other terrorist group.

Malala answered the Taliban’s violence with words, not bullets. She said, “I do not even hate the Talib who shot me. Even if I had a gun and he stood in front of me, I would not shoot him.”

She also said, “The extremists are afraid of books and pens. The power of education scares them. They are afraid of women. The power of women’s voices scares them.”

Malala talked about an attack in June on a hospital in Quetta, the capital of Baluchistan, and about female teachers killed in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. She said, “That is why they are destroying schools every day – because they are afraid of change, afraid of the equality we will bring to our society.”

The “Stand with Malala” petition asks for education for the 57 million children in the world who do not go to school. It has more than four million signatures. More than a million people signed after Malala’s speech.

At the start of her speech, Malala said, “I don’t know where to begin my speech. I don’t know what people are expecting me to say.” But she did not need to worry.

Researchers were surprised not by how difficult people found the challenge, but by how much they wanted to avoid it. The task was simple: sit in a chair and do nothing except think.

Some people found this so uncomfortable that they chose to give themselves mild electric shocks just to stop being bored. During a 15-minute period alone, two-thirds of men pressed a button to give themselves a painful shock. In the same situation, a quarter of women did the same. Scientists think this is because men usually like new and exciting experiences more than women.

Psychologists from Virginia and Harvard Universities wrote a report to find out why most people find it so hard to do nothing. In more than 11 different studies, the researchers found that people disliked being left alone with their thoughts, no matter their age, education, income, or how much they used smartphones or social media.

Timothy Wilson, the leader of the study, said that the results were not just because of modern life or technology. Instead, he thinks that things like smartphones are popular because people always want to do something, not nothing.

In the first experiments, students were put alone in a room without phones, books, or anything to write with. They were told to sit and think for six to fifteen minutes. They had to stay seated and not fall asleep.

After the time was up, the students were asked about their experience. Most did not enjoy it. They found it hard to focus, and their minds wandered even though there was nothing to distract them.

To see if the strange setting made it harder to think, the researchers repeated the experiment at people’s homes. The results were similar. In fact, people felt even worse and often broke the rules by getting up or checking their phones.

To check if this only happened with students, the scientists tested more than 100 other people, aged 18 to 77, from a church and a farmers market. These people also did not like being left alone with their thoughts.

The most surprising result came next. The researchers wanted to see if people would rather do something unpleasant than nothing at all. So, they gave students the option to give themselves a mild electric shock.

Earlier, the students had said they would pay money to avoid the shock, which they found worse than looking at pictures of cockroaches or hearing an annoying sound.

But to the researchers’ surprise, 12 out of 18 men and 6 out of 24 women gave themselves up to four electric shocks during the test.

The scientists said the most surprising thing was that being alone with their thoughts was so difficult for many people that they chose to shock themselves, even though they had said before that they would pay to avoid it.

Jessica Andrews-Hanna from the University of Colorado said that many students might give themselves a shock to make a boring lecture more interesting. But she thinks we need to learn more about why people in Wilson’s study chose to shock themselves.

She said, imagine a person is told to sit in a chair with wires on their skin and a button that gives a harmless but uncomfortable shock. They are told to just sit and think. As they sit, their mind starts to wander, and they begin to wonder if the shock is really that bad.

The researchers were surprised by what people did to avoid the task. What was the task? People had to sit in a chair and do nothing except think.

Some people found this so boring that they gave themselves small electric shocks to stop the boredom.

Two-thirds of men pressed a button to give themselves a painful shock during 15 minutes alone. One in four women also pressed the shock button.

Psychologists from Virginia and Harvard Universities wrote a report about why most people find it hard to do nothing.

In more than 11 different studies, the researchers showed that all kinds of people did not like being alone to think. It did not matter how old they were, how much money they had, how much education they had, or how often they used smartphones or social media.

Researcher Timothy Wilson said the results were probably not because of modern life or mobile phones and social media. He said these things might be popular because people feel they need to do something and do not like doing nothing.

In the first experiments, students went into a room and were told to think. They were alone, with no phones, books, or anything to write with. The only rules were to stay sitting and not fall asleep. They had to be alone for six to 15 minutes.

After the experiment, the students answered questions. Most students did not enjoy the experience. They found it hard to concentrate and their minds wandered.

The researchers did the experiment again with people at home. The results were similar. People found it even harder and some cheated by getting up or checking their phones.

The researchers did the study again with more than 100 people, aged 18 to 77, from a church and a farmers’ market. These people also did not like just sitting and thinking.

There was an even more surprising result. To see if people would choose something bad instead of nothing, the students could give themselves a small electric shock.

Before the experiment, all the students said they would pay money to avoid an electric shock.

But 12 out of 18 men gave themselves electric shocks, and 6 out of 24 women gave themselves electric shocks.

The scientists were surprised. Being alone with their thoughts was so hard for many people that they gave themselves an electric shock, even though they said before that they would pay not to get shocked.

Jessica Andrews-Hanna at the University of Colorado said many students would probably give themselves an electric shock to make a boring lecture more interesting. But she said we need to learn more about Wilson’s study.

She said, “Imagine a person is told to sit in a chair with wires on their skin and a button that gives a safe but uncomfortable shock. They are told to just sit and think. As they sit, their mind starts to wander and they think about the shock – was it really that bad?”

Organic food has more antioxidants, which are good for health, than regular food. It also has lower levels of toxic metals and pesticides. This information comes from the biggest scientific study so far. The international team who did the study says that eating organic fruits and vegetables could give the same health benefits as eating one or two extra portions of the recommended five portions of fruits and vegetables each day.

The team, led by Professor Carlo Leifert, found that organic food has much higher levels of different antioxidants—between 19% and 69% more—than regular food. This is the first study to clearly show big differences between organic and regular fruits, vegetables, and cereals.

The researchers say that the higher antioxidants in organic food are equal to eating one or two more portions of fruits and vegetables each day. This could be important for people’s health.

These results will add to the debate about whether organic food is better for people. Tom Sanders, a nutrition professor at Kings College London, said the research does show some differences. But he asks if these differences are just normal changes, and if they really matter for health. He is not sure. He also said that Leifert has disagreed with many people before. Sanders added that organic cereals have less protein than regular cereals.

The results are based on 343 studies from around the world, more than ever before, that looked at differences between organic and regular fruits, vegetables, and cereals. Helen Browning, head of the Soil Association, which supports organic farming, said this research proves that the way we farm affects the quality of our food.

Leifert and his team say that many antioxidants are linked to a lower risk of long-term diseases, like heart disease, brain diseases, and some cancers. The researchers also found much higher levels of cadmium, a toxic metal, in regular crops. Pesticide residues were found four times more often on regular crops than on organic food.

Some people will criticize this research. Because it includes so many studies, some of them might be low quality, which could make the results less reliable. Also, the higher levels of cadmium and pesticides in regular food are still much lower than the safe limits. But the researchers say cadmium builds up in the body over time, and some people may want to avoid it. They also say that pesticide limits are set for each chemical, not for the mix of chemicals used on crops.

Another criticism is that the differences found might be because of different climates, soil, or types of crops, not because of organic farming. The biggest criticism is about the possible health benefits. The last big study in 2012, which looked at 223 studies, found little evidence that organic food is much more nutritious than regular food.

Earlier, smaller studies in 2009 and a report by the UK Food Standards Agency also said there is not strong evidence that organic food is better. The 2012 study did say that eating organic food might help people avoid pesticide residues. Sanders said he is not convinced by the new study. He said eating organic food will not make you healthier. What matters most is eating fruits and vegetables, not whether they are organic or regular.

Surveys show that most people buy organic food to eat more healthily (55%) and to avoid chemicals (53%). Many people also care about the environment (44%), animal welfare (31%), and taste (35%). Browning said this research supports what people already think about organic food. In other countries, more people support and accept the benefits of organic food and farming. She hopes these results will help the UK agree more with the rest of Europe.

Emmanuel Limal used online dating sites a lot, but he was tired of meeting women who were not ready to start a family, or who did not say they wanted children. Emmanuel is a 43-year-old actor from France. He has lived in Copenhagen for 20 years, looking for love and hoping to have children. He tried to find someone online, but he was unhappy with the results.

“I got frustrated because everyone said they were very active, always traveling, or had many hobbies, but they never talked about children,” Limal said. On some sites, you could click a button saying “I’d like kids someday,” but when you read the person’s profile, you thought, “You will never have time!” If someone goes to the gym eight times a week and travels every month, they are not putting family first.

Limal has a six-year-old daughter from a past relationship. He comes from a big family—his father has 11 brothers and sisters—so he always wanted more children. “I couldn’t find anyone who wanted to make starting a family a priority,” he said. It was hard to know when to talk about wanting kids when meeting someone new. “It’s the biggest dating taboo,” he said. One day, he read a profile from a 38-year-old woman who said she knew it was not good to admit, but she wanted children. Limal thought, “You shouldn’t be ashamed of this.”

Limal borrowed money to start Babyklar.nu, which means “baby-ready now” in English. It works like a normal dating site, but everyone must be honest about wanting to start a family soon. “We ask people if they are okay with someone who already has children and if they want another baby,” Limal said. “But we don’t ask how many children they want. That would be too much like shopping online.”

The site has had a very good response. “We had 50 people sign up every hour when we started in June, and we are already hearing from couples who met on the site and are now together. I expect the first Babyklar.nu baby by next summer.” More men have signed up than women (53% men, 47% women), with comments like, “It’s so nice to say this out loud,” and “I finally dare to be honest about what I want.”

The site has come at a good time for Denmark, a country with five million people. Danes are not having enough babies. A report from Rigshospitalet in Copenhagen says the current rate is 1.7 children per family, which is not enough to keep Denmark’s population the same. The usual reasons are that women are waiting too long to have children, and couples are living together without getting married and waiting to start families.

“Now, I hope men and women who want to start a family but haven’t met the right person will have another option,” says Limal. He says this is not just about having babies: “I want this to be about children and love. My goal is to match people who really want a family and a partner—and who will stay together. I am a romantic at heart.”

There are plans to start the site in France and the UK later in 2013, but for now, only Danes can use it. Danes do not mind having children before marriage, so things can move quickly. Also, because Denmark is small, someone from Jutland can date someone from Copenhagen without traveling too far, Limal said. And now, Limal has finally found love. “I’ve met a nice woman and she wants a baby too—so we will see.”

A subway system is home to billions of bacteria. These include bacteria from Swiss cheese and kimchi, bacteria that cause bubonic plague, drug-resistant bacteria, and bacteria from human skin. For the first time, scientists have started to list and map the bacteria in a city’s subway. They found many interesting things.

Dr. Christopher Mason, a geneticist at Weill Cornell Medical College, led a team that studied the New York City subway system for 18 months. They looked for tiny life forms on turnstiles, seats, ticket booths, and stations. The team found bacteria that cause meningitis at Times Square, a small amount of anthrax on a train handhold, and bacteria that cause bubonic plague on a trash bin and ticket machine in uptown Manhattan.

The team said people should not worry about the plague and anthrax findings. There was only a very small amount of anthrax, and rats probably carried the plague bacteria. No one has gotten sick with plague in or near New York for many years.

The study says that plague and anthrax are not common in the subway. It also says that people in New York are not at risk. Most of the bacteria found are harmless or even helpful to humans.

Some results were expected and remind people to wash their hands, Mason said. He also said they found many helpful bacteria, like the ones used to make cheese.

Bacteria in the subway showed the eating habits of different neighborhoods. Bacteria from cheeses like brie, cheddar, parmesan, and mozzarella (used on New York pizza) were found all over the subway. Swiss cheese bacteria were mostly in midtown Manhattan and the financial district. Bacteria used to ferment cabbage for kimchi and sauerkraut were found in the financial district and Bay Ridge.

Bacteria that can cause illness and infections were very common. Bacteria that cause diarrhea, nausea, E. coli, skin infections, and urinary-tract infections were found all over the city. The bacteria that cause tetanus were found in Soho, and bacteria that cause dysentery were found at stations in the Bronx and Harlem.

Mason and his team collected over 1,000 samples from all 466 open subway stations in New York. They used a DNA sequencer and a supercomputer to study the samples. They found 15,152 different species, and almost half were bacteria.

The good news is that these bacteria are not causing sickness or disease in New York. They seem to be normal parts of city life.

In short, the researchers say the subway and city are as safe as people thought. Mason said people should not worry about getting urinary-tract infections from subway seats. He advised people to wash their hands, get enough sleep, eat salads, and exercise, just as before.

He also said he feels more confident riding the subway now.

Many findings made sense. Stations like Grand Central and Times Square, which have more people, had more bacteria and more types of bacteria. The Bronx, with its many different neighborhoods and stations, had the most types of bacteria. Staten Island, with only three stops, had the least.

The researchers found sea bacteria at South Ferry, a station that flooded during Hurricane Sandy. They were surprised to find some species usually found in Antarctica and in fish.

Next, Mason said, they will study other cities, such as Paris, São Paulo, and Shanghai, and continue to study New York to see how results change with the seasons. He hopes this research will help health officials and geneticists, and help track and prevent diseases.

Nelson Mandela, a key leader in Africa’s fight for freedom and a hero to millions, has died at the age of 95. He was South Africa’s first black president. Mandela died at home in Johannesburg with his family after being sick for many years, which made him stop appearing in public.

The current president, Jacob Zuma, told the country about Mandela’s death. He said Mandela died around 8:50 pm local time and was at peace. Zuma said, “This is our deepest sorrow. Our nation has lost its greatest son. What made Nelson Mandela great was that he was human. We saw in him what we want to see in ourselves. Fellow South Africans, Nelson Mandela brought us together, and together we will say goodbye to him.” Zuma also said Mandela would have a state funeral and ordered flags to fly at half-mast.

World leaders paid tribute to Mandela. US President Barack Obama called him by his clan name, Madiba, and said, “Through his strong dignity and will to give up his own freedom for others, Madiba changed South Africa and inspired all of us.” UK Prime Minister David Cameron said, “A great light has gone out in the world,” and called Mandela a hero of our time. FW de Klerk, the South African president who freed Mandela and shared the Nobel Peace Prize with him in 1993, said the news was very sad for South Africa and the world. He said, “He lived reconciliation. He was a great unifier.”

People in South Africa gathered in the streets to celebrate Mandela’s life. In Soweto, people sang and danced near his old house. They sang songs from the fight against apartheid. Some people wore South African flags and the green, yellow, and black colors of Mandela’s party, the African National Congress (ANC).

Mandela’s death has made South Africa mourn and think deeply, almost 20 years after he led the country from racial apartheid to democracy. People around the world also feel his loss, as many saw Mandela as one of the last great leaders in history, like Gandhi and Martin Luther King.

Mandela is remembered for forgiving others after spending 27 years in prison, 18 of them on Robben Island. When South Africa was close to civil war, Mandela chose to make peace with the white minority to build a new democracy. He led the ANC to win the country’s first multiracial election in 1994. He then stepped down after one term as president.

Mandela was born Rolihlahla Dalibhunga in a small village in the Eastern Cape on July 18, 1918. A teacher gave him the English name Nelson. He joined the ANC in 1943 and helped start its youth league. In 1952, he opened South Africa’s first black law firm with his partner, Oliver Tambo.

Mandela was known for his charm, love of boxing, and interest in women. He once said, “I can’t help it if the ladies notice me. I am not going to protest.”

When the ANC was banned in 1960, Mandela went into hiding. After the Sharpeville massacre, where police killed 69 black protesters, he decided to start an armed struggle. He was arrested and charged with sabotage and trying to overthrow the government.

At his trial in 1964, Mandela defended himself and said, “I have cherished the ideal of a democratic and free society, where all people live together in harmony and with equal chances. It is an ideal I hope to live for and achieve. But, if necessary, it is an ideal for which I am prepared to die.” He was not given the death penalty but was sentenced to life in prison.

In 1990, FW de Klerk ended the ban on the ANC, and Mandela was released from prison. People around the world celebrated his release. Archbishop Desmond Tutu said, “He restored others’ faith in Africa and Africans.”

Mandela’s 91st birthday was celebrated with the first Mandela Day in his honor. He was married three times and had six children, 17 grandchildren, and 14 great-grandchildren.

Brazil had one of its biggest protests in decades when more than 100,000 people went into the streets. They were angry about aggressive police actions, bad public services, and the high costs of the World Cup.

The main protests happened in cities like Rio de Janeiro, São Paulo, Brasilia, Belem, Belo Horizonte, Salvador, and others. The protests started peacefully, but some turned violent, with fights between police and protesters, and some cars and buses were set on fire.

Earlier, during smaller protests about higher bus prices, people said the police used too much force, like rubber bullets, tear gas, and beatings.

These big protests happened at the same time as the football Confederations Cup. Many people were upset about rising prices, poor public services, a lot of money being spent on sports events, bad health care, and problems with inequality and corruption.

Most of the protests were peaceful, but some police officers were hurt, at least one car was turned over and burned, and some windows were broken.

The situation got worse at night. A large group set fires outside a government office, broke windows, and wrote graffiti on the walls saying things like "Revolution," "Down with Paes," "Down with Cabral" (the mayor and state governor), and "Hate police." Police inside used pepper spray.

People had many reasons for protesting. Oscar Jos Santos, a 19-year-old, said, "We are here because we hate the government. They do nothing for us." Nadia al Husin, an architect who had been unemployed for six months, said, "There must be something wrong with this country."

To tourists, Amsterdam still seems very open and free. Recently, the city’s Mayor told tourists that the city’s coffee shops, which sell marijuana, would stay open even though there is a new national law to stop drug tourism. However, Amsterdam’s plan to send problem neighbors to “scum villages” made from shipping containers might hurt its reputation for being tolerant.

The Mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, says his new policy, which costs 810,000 euros, is to protect people who are victims of abuse and homophobia. The camps, where antisocial families will live for three to six months, are called “scum villages” because the idea is similar to a plan from Geert Wilders, a far-right politician. Last year, Wilders said that repeat offenders should be sent to a “village for scum.”

Bartho Boer, a spokesman for the Mayor, says the plans are not against freedom. “We want to protect the liberal values of Amsterdam,” he says. “We want everyone to be themselves—whether they are gay, lesbian, or people who resist violence and then become victims of harassment. We as a society want to protect them.” According to Boer, the villages are not for neighbors who just play loud music on Saturday night, but for people who are very violent and threatening, and who keep harassing victims again and again.

People found guilty of causing serious trouble will be evicted and put in simple, temporary homes, including shipping containers in industrial areas of the city. “We call it a living container,” says Boer. Putting antisocial families in these units, which have showers and kitchens and have been used as student housing, means they are not rewarded for their bad behavior by getting better homes.

The Dutch newspaper De Parool wrote that in the 19th century, troublemakers were moved to villages in Drenthe and Overijssel, which quickly became slums. But Boer says the government has learned from past mistakes and will not put antisocial families together.

“It would be more correct to call them ‘scum houses’ instead of ‘scum villages,’” says Boer, “because we do not want to put more than one of these families in the same area.” After a maximum of six months in these houses, which are in different parts of the city, the families will be found permanent homes. The city government expects to move about ten families a year into this program, which starts in 2013.

The temporary homes will have a lot of police, but antisocial families will also get help from doctors, social workers, and parole officers. “They are taken care of so the whole situation does not happen again in their new home,” says Boer.

Tourists still think Amsterdam is a very free city. The Mayor of Amsterdam recently told tourists that coffee shops selling marijuana will stay open, even though there is a new law in the country to stop people coming just to buy drugs. But Amsterdam now has a new plan to send neighbours who behave very badly to special places called “scum villages,” which are made from shipping containers. Because of this, some people may not think Amsterdam is a free city anymore.

The Mayor, Eberhard van der Laan, says this new plan to stop bad behaviour will cost £810,000. The plan wants to protect people who are victims of abuse and homophobia. The families who behave very badly will live in these camps for three to six months. Bartho Boer, who speaks for the Mayor, says the plan is not against freedom. “We want to protect the free values of Amsterdam,” he says. “We want everyone to be themselves – if they are gay or lesbian, or if they try to stop violence and then become victims. We want to protect them.” Boer says these villages are not for people who just play loud music on Saturday night, but for people who are very violent and keep hurting others again and again.

People who are found guilty of violent harassment will have to leave their homes and live in temporary homes, including shipping containers in industrial parts of the city. “We call it a living container,” says Boer. A Dutch newspaper wrote that in the 1800s, people who behaved badly were sent to villages in Drenthe and Overijssel, but these places soon became very poor and dirty. But Boer says the government has learned from these mistakes and will not put many bad families together.

Boer says they are “scum houses,” not “scum villages,” because they do not want to put more than one bad family in the same area. After a maximum of six months in these houses, which are in different parts of the city, the families will get permanent homes. The city thinks it will move about ten families each year, starting in 2013.

Police will watch the temporary homes, but the families will also be able to see doctors and social workers. “We will help them so the same problems do not happen again in their new homes,” says Boer.

Male bosses get bonuses that are twice as big as those given to female bosses in the same jobs. This means that, over their careers, men get 141,500 more in extra pay than women.

The Chartered Management Institute (CMI) shared these numbers. In 2012, men in management jobs in the UK got average bonuses of 6,442, while women got 3,029. In the highest jobs, female directors got bonuses of 36,270 in the last year, but male directors got 63,700.

These numbers show that pay in British businesses is still not equal. Because of this, people who want equality at work are asking for changes.

Ann Francke, the head of CMI, said it is time to make this problem important for all managers. She said we need to change how we manage people. There should be more flexibility, less focus on male ways of working, more focus on results instead of time spent in the office, and more openness about how people are paid and rewarded.

She said that fixing this problem would help companies do better and make workers happier. She asked, "What are we waiting for?"

Some of the pay difference may be because women often work in jobs where bonuses are not common. But the big difference in bonus size makes the pay gap in Britain worse. The government says the pay gap is getting smaller, but full-time male workers still earn 10% more than women.

Maria Miller, the Minister for Women and Equalities, said the CMI numbers show again that women still get less than men at work. She said things are changing and the pay gap is closing, but there is still more to do before men and women are equal at work.

The government is helping. It has 120 companies in its Think, Act, Report scheme, which asks companies to improve how they hire, promote, and pay women. The government is also looking at other reasons for the pay gap, like women having to balance work and family. They have started shared parental leave and the right for all workers to ask for flexible working hours.

Big companies like Tesco, BT, Unilever, and the law firm Eversheds have joined Think, Act, Report. But only 120 companies have joined in almost two years.

The CMI's data also shows that the pay gap is getting smaller: the difference between what male and female bosses earn has become less since 2012.

A group of 17,000 managers, whose pay has been tracked for years, showed that men's earnings are now rising faster than women's for the first time in five years. Men's pay went up by 3.2%, while women's pay went up by 2.8%, including both salary and bonuses.

At the highest level, male directors' pay went up by 5.3% in the last year, but female directors' pay only went up by 1.1%.

Male bosses get bonuses that are twice as big as the bonuses given to female bosses in the same jobs. This means that, over their working lives, men get £141,500 more in bonuses than women.

The Chartered Management Institute (CMI) gave these numbers. In 2012, men in management jobs in the UK got an average bonus of £6,442, but women got only £3,029. Female directors got bonuses of £36,270 in the last 12 months, but male directors got £63,700.

These numbers show that pay in British businesses is still not equal. People who want more equality at work say we need to make changes. Ann Francke, the boss of CMI, said there should be more flexible working and less focus on a “masculine” work culture. She said that good work should be more important than how long people stay in the office. She also said there should be more openness about how bonuses are given.

Ann Francke said, “If we fix this problem, companies will do better and people will be happier at work. What are we waiting for?”

Maria is sitting on a black plastic chair in a community centre on a cold Tuesday afternoon. She is waiting for someone to call her number. Her number is 34.

When it is her turn, Maria goes to get a brown paper bag filled with important food like pasta, eggs, and cornflakes. She can choose butternut squash or carrots for this week’s vegetables.

Maria is the 34th person today at the East Hampton Food Pantry. This food pantry is close to some of the most expensive houses in the world.

Every day at this time of year, more than 400 families come to the food pantry to get their weekly food bag. This food helps them live through the cold, dark winter in Long Island.

The Hamptons are old towns and villages by the ocean, 100 miles from Manhattan. In the summer, rich people come here to have fun. But in early September, the rich people leave and go back to Manhattan or Beverly Hills. Then, life becomes hard for the mostly immigrant people who live here all year.

Maria says, “The people who come here are rich and famous, but we who live here are not.” Maria works 14 hours a day in the summer cleaning big houses, but in the winter, she often has no work.

Maria laughs when someone asks if she has enough money. “There is no work in the winter, only in the summertime,” says Maria, who is from Latin America, like many workers in the Hamptons. Many people live in one room because they cannot pay the rent.

She says some families with up to five children have to live in basements and still pay more than $1,000 a month for rent. People come here looking for work, but in the winter, there is no work.

Many of Maria’s friends cannot pay for heating or medicine. Many would not have enough food if the East Hampton Food Pantry did not exist. This is just one of several food pantries in the town.

Vicki Littman is the chairperson of the East Hampton Food Pantry. In 2015, the pantry gave out more than 31,000 food bags. She says more and more people are coming to the food pantry.

Littman says that when she talks to people who visit in the summer about the food pantries, they are always surprised. They only know the glamorous side of the Hamptons, with big parties, beaches, and mansions.

But people do not realize that there are many workers here. Landscapers, nannies, and waitresses all need the money they earn in the summer to live through the winter.

Littman says the town has lost many important workers, like teachers, police officers, doctors, and dentists, because they cannot afford to live here.

Housing is the biggest cost in the Hamptons. Larry Cantwell, who has lived in East Hampton all his life, says houses often sell for more than $25 million. “Finding your first home is very hard in a place like this,” Cantwell says. “If you can find a home to buy in East Hampton for $500,000, you are very lucky.”

Cantwell says more than half the homes in the town are empty for most of the year. The population goes from 80,000 in August to 10,000 in the winter.

“There is a lot of wealth here, but almost all of it is in second homes only used in the summer,” says Cantwell, whose father was a fisherman and mother was a house cleaner. “But the rest of us live here all year.”

There are famous and very rich people, but also hard-working and poor people who have a difficult life. This community used to be a farming and fishing community, with people who lived off the land and water—a real working-class community.

Eddie Vallone, 22, says, “People see the Hamptons as a rich town, but there are a lot of problems here, especially drugs. It’s hard to understand—OK, the summer is ending. What am I going to do for the winter?” Vallone says. “I want to work, but there is no work.”

Vallone cleans pools and does small jobs on luxury estates. If he saves his money well, his summer earnings can last until November. But work does not start again until May or the beginning of June.

Robert Myslajek stops. On a muddy mountain path, the scientist finds what he is looking for between two wolf paw prints. Droppings! he says happily. Seeing a wolf is very rare, so finding its faeces makes it a good day.

But now it is getting easier to find signs of wolves. There are about 1,500 wolves in Poland, and their number has doubled in 15 years. Wolves, along with brown bears, lynxes, and wolverines, are Europe’s last big meat-eating predators. Conservationists from Britain, Germany, and the Netherlands come to Poland to learn how the country has protected wolves, which are often seen as bad animals, even in fairy tales.

Bits of bone and hair stick out from the black faeces. It ate a red deer, says Myslajek, a biologist from the University of Warsaw. In my lab, I can tell you a lot about this wolf—not only what it eats, but also its gender, sexual habits, age, health, and family.

DNA tests show that Polish wolves travel far. One wolf reached the Netherlands, but sadly, it was hit by a car. Wolves need a lot of space. The average area needed by a Polish wolf pack is 250 square kilometres, says Myslajek.

Can we ever bring wolves back to Scotland? asks Alex Entwisle, a 23-year-old student from the UK, who is on a study trip to southern Poland. He and other animal science students have spent the day looking for droppings and paw prints in the Beskidy mountains of the Polish Carpathians.

They are discussing if wolves should return to the British Isles for the first time since the 18th century.

Myslajek visited the Scottish Highlands in 2015 for the Wolves and Humans Foundation and answered questions from villagers about the Polish experience. The big difference between Scotland and Poland is that we eat pork. We do not have many sheep here.

But we have many wild animals—300,000 red deer and more than 800,000 roe deer. In Poland, we also have too many wild boar—about 200,000—and these animals eat and destroy farmers’ cereal crops. Here, wolves help solve this problem, he says.

The scientist says wolves can travel up to 30 kilometres in one hunt. The Beskidy pack is strong, with eight or nine animals. This year, we have recorded five cubs, two young wolves, and two adults.

We track them using cameras in the forest and by following their prints in the mud and snow. In each family group, only one pair of adults has cubs each year. All pack members help care for the young.

Myslajek, the son of a shepherd, does not understand why wolves have a bad reputation. Why did we need the fairy tale Little Red Riding Hood, with its big bad wolf?

He is fascinated by these shy animals, who stayed wild 33,000 years ago when other wolves became domestic dogs.

Myslajek says only scientific reasons—like the need to help forests grow and control wild animal numbers—can save Europe’s wild meat-eaters, especially the unpopular wolf. Natural predators keep the ecosystem balanced. They reduce the number of plant-eating animals, which helps trees grow tall for birds to nest in.

The ban on wolf hunting in the western Carpathians became law in 1995, and in all of Poland in 1998. Now, there are wolf packs in almost all of the country’s big forests, where wolves live together with humans.

The Polish government pays money to farmers whose animals are killed by wolves. Myslajek tells farmers to use electric fences. He has also helped bring back two things that, for unknown reasons, scare wolves: strings of small red flags (hung around sheep pens) and the Tatra Mountain Sheepdog.

Poland’s wolves have also been helped because the country developed its roads and buildings later than other countries. In 1989, when the communists left power, Poland had only one motorway. Big road projects started after Poland joined the European Union in 2004, and these projects must consider wild animals.

People’s attitudes have also changed. For many years, hunting was part of the culture. In 1975, there were fewer than 100 wolves in Poland. From the 1950s, the government encouraged hunting wolves and paid a reward for killing one, equal to a month’s salary. It was a massacre.

Myslajek says that Polish wolves are much safer now, but not completely safe. Wolf packs cross country borders, and hunting still happens in Russia, Lithuania, Belarus, Ukraine, and Slovakia.

He says Poland’s new government, elected in October 2015, does not like wolves. The Environment Minister, Jan Szyszko, is a hunter. There are 120,000 licensed hunters in Poland, and they have a lot of influence.

Being a wolf supporter is not easy. You cannot tell politicians that wolves are a big tourist attraction. Most tourists want to see the animals, but wolves stay away from humans. They have a very good sense of smell.

The 12 British animal science students leave the Polish Carpathians without seeing a wolf. Entwisle does not believe that Scotland will ever be as successful as Poland.

It would be great for the environment to have wolves back in Scotland because there are too many deer. But it would not be possible because of the roads and sheep.

There would also be problems with farmers. In Britain, we like predators to be far away and to watch them on television, said Entwisle.

There are worse things to do in life than walk along Rio’s Copacabana beach in the sun on your way to watch a World Cup match. So it was not surprising that England fan Anthony McDowell from Liverpool was happy. “The place is lovely. The people are great. There’s a party feeling,” said McDowell. “The only thing that could be better is the England team.”

He and about six friends are among thousands of fans from around the world who have turned the beach into a party with national colors and songs. Some people danced, some took photos, some drank, but most just walked and talked about football, waiting for the next game to start on the big screen nearby. The last time so many people were here during the day was when the pope visited.

The happy and mostly peaceful mood was very different from the protests, transport problems, and stadium issues before the World Cup. But now that the football has started, visiting fans want to enjoy the experience. “If I had known, when I started planning, how complicated and expensive it would be, I wouldn’t have come. But now that we’re here, it’s great,” said Brian Hill, an England fan from Sunderland.

The trip has not been perfect. Hill traveled for more than 20 hours to get to Rio. His son, Andrew, had his sunglasses stolen almost as soon as he sat on the beach. They were also surprised that many bars do not have big screens for the games. But like many fans, they said they love the atmosphere of this tournament, which has started very well on the field.

Everyone must have enjoyed Robin van Persie’s amazing diving header for the Netherlands against Spain. There have also been many goals: 28 in the first eight games—almost three times as many as at the same stage in South Africa in 2010. Adding to the party feeling in the streets, where most fans are from nearby countries, Latin American teams have done very well so far.

So far, the tournament has avoided the worst problems, though it is not completely trouble-free. The stadiums were finished late and some were not fully ready, but there have been no reports of big problems or trouble getting into the stadiums since the games started.

As in past World Cups, tickets have been a problem, with many empty seats at some games. FIFA spokesman Saint-Clair Milesi said that only 48,000 of the 51,900 seats at the Netherlands versus Spain game were filled.

The Globo newspaper listed several problems in the 12 host cities. Almost all had worse traffic than usual. The worst transport problems were in Natal, where bus drivers were on strike. In Salvador, some trips took five times longer than normal. “Traffic was already bad but this week it is chaotic,” said Jecilda Mello, a local resident.

But protests have become smaller since the opening day, when small demonstrations happened in several cities and police used tear gas and pepper spray. Since then, the only security problems have been small thefts and fans who are too excited. A sudden street party of Argentinian fans was stopped with pepper spray after they blocked roads.

The long distances between cities have led to very different World Cup experiences. The tournament has not changed much in São Paulo, South America’s biggest city, but far away in Manaus—the remote Amazon city where England played Italy—visitors said there was World Cup excitement, with decorated streets and flags on many cars.

The FA chairman, Greg Dyke, said there was a big difference in atmosphere. “We’ve had a really warm welcome in Manaus. It’s a big thing for them, even if it is a bit strange to spend so much on a stadium with no one to play in it. But we were in São Paulo for four or five days before the opening match and you wouldn’t have known until the last day that there was even a World Cup on. It was strange.”

Walking along Rio’s Copacabana beach in the sun before a World Cup match is a very nice thing to do. So, it was not a surprise that Anthony McDowell, a football fan from Liverpool, England, was happy. “This place is beautiful. The people are friendly. There is a party feeling,” said McDowell. “The only thing that could be better is the England team.”

He and six friends were part of the thousands of fans from many countries who turned the beach into a party place. Some people danced, some took photos, some drank, but most just walked and talked about football, waiting for the next match to start on the big screen nearby.

The friendly and mostly calm mood was very different from the protests, transport problems, and stadium issues before the World Cup started. Now that the football games have begun, visitors want to enjoy themselves. “If I knew before how difficult and expensive it would be, I would not have come. But now that we are here, it is great,” said Brian Hill, another England fan.

The trip was not perfect. Hill traveled for more than 20 hours to get to Rio. His son’s sunglasses were stolen almost as soon as they sat on the beach. They were also surprised that many bars did not have big screens for the games. But, like many fans, they said they loved the feeling of this tournament, which started very well.

Everyone enjoyed Robin van Persie’s amazing diving header for the Netherlands against Spain. There have also been many goals: 28 in the first eight games—almost three times more than at the same time in South Africa in 2010. Latin American teams have done very well so far, and because most fans are from nearby countries, this has made the party feeling even stronger.

So far, the tournament has not had the big problems that many people thought would happen, but there are still some issues. The stadiums were finished late and some were not completely ready, but there have been no big problems with the buildings or getting inside.

Like other World Cups, tickets have been a problem, with many empty seats at some games. FIFA spokesman Saint-Clair Milesi said that only 48,000 of the 51,900 seats were filled at the Netherlands vs. Spain game.

The Globo newspaper listed some problems in the 12 cities hosting games. Almost all had worse traffic jams than usual. The worst transport problems were in Natal, where bus drivers were on strike. In Salvador, some trips took five times longer than normal. “Traffic was already bad, but this week it is very bad,” said Jecilda Mello, a local person.

There have been fewer protests since the first day, when small protests happened in some cities and police used pepper spray. Since then, the only security problems have been small thefts and fans who are too excited. Police used pepper spray on Argentinian fans when they started a street party and blocked roads.

But far away in Manaus, the Amazon city where England played Italy, visitors said there was a strong World Cup feeling, with colorful streets and flags on many cars.

Greg Dyke, the chairman of the English Football Association, said the atmosphere was very different in each city. “We had a very warm welcome in Manaus. It is a big event for them. But we were in São Paulo for four or five days before the first match, and it was hard to see that the World Cup was happening until the last day. It was strange.”

A girl born today in the UK can expect to live almost 82 years, and her brother can expect to live 78 years. In Andorra, they would live even longer (85 years for girls and 79 for boys). In the US, they would live a little less (81 for girls and 76 for boys). But if they lived in the Central African Republic, they would die much younger, at 49 for girls and 44 for boys. Almost everywhere in the world, except in countries like Lesotho that have problems with HIV and violence, people are living longer lives. The best news is that young children are much less likely to die than forty years ago. The number of children under five who die has dropped by almost 60%, from 16.4 million in 1970 to 6.8 million in 2010.

This last number shows why the big project by the Institute of Health Metrics and Evaluation (IHME) in Seattle is important. Over the past five years, almost 500 researchers have worked to study the effects of diseases around the world. Knowing how many children die and why helps the world focus on saving their lives. There are many things to learn from the huge database they have made, which will help world organizations and governments take better care of people.

The project was very large and not everyone agrees with it. IHME used some new methods. For example, when there were no official death records, they used "verbal autopsies," which means they asked families about how someone died. The most surprising result was about malaria. IHME said 1.2 million people die from malaria every year, which is twice as many as people thought before. Most of the increase is in adult deaths. Many people believe malaria mostly kills children under five.

Dr. Christopher Murray, the IHME Director, said that doctors are taught that adults in areas with malaria become partly immune. At first, IHME believed this too, but then they started to follow the data. African doctors often write that adults are dying from malaria, but sometimes their fever could be from another cause. These findings have led to more studies.

Margaret Chan, the Director General of the World Health Organization (WHO), officially welcomed the IHME study, but some WHO staff are careful. Colin Mathers, a senior scientist, said they need to check if the numbers are correct and wait for more proof. Dr. Tiers Boerma, another WHO director, said people should know that some of the numbers are very different, and the WHO cannot accept every new number from academic studies. However, Mathers said IHME has tried new things, which is exciting. Murray said one main finding is that the main causes of death are changing much faster than expected.

Because people are having fewer children and living longer, the average age of people in the world has gone up from 26 to almost 30 in just ten years. In Latin America, for example, countries like Brazil and Paraguay had an average life expectancy below 30 in 1970, but almost 64 in 2010. That is a 35-year increase in average age of death in forty years. In Brazil, the change is so fast that most organizations cannot keep up, Murray said.

Another important change is that, outside Africa, people are dying less from infectious diseases and problems with mothers and babies, and more from "lifestyle diseases" like heart disease, stroke, diabetes, and cancer. Some of these diseases are also caused by genes. This change is especially strong in Latin America, the Middle East, and south and southeast Asia.

The third big finding, Murray said, was a surprise. There is a lot of disability, and it affects people who are living longer but not healthier lives. The main causes of disability are not the same as the causes of death. The main problems are mental health issues like anxiety and depression, and conditions like arthritis, lower back pain, anemia, loss of sight and hearing, and skin diseases. There is also substance abuse. The numbers for these problems are not going down. We are not making progress in reducing these conditions.
